[S1] Comment by Ismael Juma (2025-02-26)
Thanks for the report. Can you specify the version you tested?
[S2] Comment by Colin McCabe (2025-02-26)
Controller registration doesn’t have anything to do with the quorum. It can only be successfully done once the quorum is already established and there is a leader. If you are not able to form a quorum you should check the raft logs to see why that is.

You can also turn up logging for kafka.server.ControllerRegistrationManager to TRACE to see more logs about what is happening.
[S3] Comment by Daniel Fonai (2025-03-31)
[~ijuma] the version is 3.9.0, I updated the Affects Version field.

[~cmccabe] I might have described it incorrectly. What we see is that the controller registration times out (due to transient network/DNS issues) then the controller does not retry the registration and the KRaft migration could not be finished successfully. I uploaded the controller logs, there are a lot of 
UnknownHostExceptions but those are intermittent and related to the network/DNS issues (the cluster is in Kubernetes and sometimes DNS is slow). Maybe that has nothing to do with the quorum.
[S4] Comment by Daniel Fonai (2025-03-31)
I think we might have found the root cause. There is a flag in ControllerRegistrationManager (pendingRpc) which is set when the controller registration request is queued. In case the request is not sent but timeout occurs, the flag is not reset and and request is not rescheduled: [https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/c095faa5783b3b2f37f0be590eca7a3ab9aabc99/core/src/main/scala/kafka/server/ControllerRegistrationManager.scala#L211-L214]

I created a PR to reset the flag on timeout: [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/19321].

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-770: Replace "buffered.records.per.partition" & "cache.max.bytes.buffering" with "{statestore.cache}/{input.buffer}.max.bytes"
Status
Current state: Partially Done in 3.4: new cache size config and metrics
Discussion Thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-13152
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The current config "buffered.records.per.partition" controls how many records in maximum to bookkeep per partition, and hence when this value is exceeded for any subscribed partition, the consumer pauses this partition However this config has two issues:
It's a per-partition config, so the total memory consumed is dependent on the dynamic number of partitions assigned.
Record size could vary from case to case.
The above 2 reasons makes it hard to bound the memory usage for this buffering.
Proposed Changes
This KIP proposes to deprecate the per partition (buffered.records.per.partition) and introduce a new one called input.buffer.max.bytes. This would be a global config applicable per Kafka Streams instance. This parameter controls the number of bytes allocated for buffering. Specifically, for a processor topology instance with T threads and C bytes allocated for buffering, each thread will have an even C/T bytes to construct its own buffer. Following points describes some of the characteristics of the new config:
Whenever all the tasks belonging to a particular Stream Thread have amassed bytes more than what has been allocated to it, the underneath consumer would pause consuming from all partitions that have some data already. What this also means, is that partitions with empty buffers wouldn't be paused.

Default local endpoints are useful for command-line clients:

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-795: Add public APIs for AbstractCoordinator
Status
Current state: Discarded
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
After Kafka moved the rebalancing responsibilities from brokers to clients, many other applications (Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, Confluent Schema Registry) have relied on the Group Membership Protocol to implement resource allocation amongst distributed processes.
Kafka Connect's WorkerCoordinator class extends AbstractCoordinator, and uses the rebalance mechanism to distribute tasks to its workers. In the same spirit, Confluent Kafka Registry - and its SchemaRegistryCoordinator - relies in the AbstractCoordinator class for leadership election (which instance of a Schema Registry cluster can accept writes). These two are in addition to the ConsumerCoordinator that the Kafka Consumer uses internally, and indirectly Kafka Streams.
We've adopted this generic, extensible protocol to implement a framework that solves both the distributed resource management and leader election use cases our engineering teams face when building their systems. The powerful primitives exposed by the AbstractCoordinator class have made it relatively easy to build distributed resource management systems on top of Apache Kafka.
A good example of how other projects can leverage AbstractCoordinator APIs to implement resource management is this PR to add HA capabilities to Kafka Monitor. We're looking into adding these capabilities to other systems in our Kafka Infrastructure (Kafka Cruise Control being the next one).
We think it's time for the AbstractCoordinator to become part of Kafka's public API, so we can ensure backwards compatibility in future versions of the client libraries. In fact, we were inspired by Gwen Shapira's talk at the strangeloop conference in '18 [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MmLezWRI3Ys] which gave us a new perspective when redesigning our existing distributed leader election system. 
Finally, we feel that the protocol is well designed and extensible, so advertising Kafka's Coordinator capabilities might be a good idea, as it's applicable to many use cases.
Public Interfaces
This KIP introduces a new Coordinator interface in the org.apache.kafka.consumer.clients.consumer package.javaCoordinator.java
It also moves several classes from the org.apache.kafka.consumer.clients.consumer.internals package to the org.apache.kafka.consumer.clients.consumer package, as …

Motivation
Tools kafka-console-producer.sh and kafka-console-consumer.sh have the multiple option --property to setup the MessageReader for Producer (defined by --line-reader) or the MessageFormatter for Consumer (defined by --formatter).
To setup the KafkaProducer/KafkaConsumer they have the multiple option --producer-property/--consumer-property and the config file option --consumer.config/--producer.config.
The idea is to offer the same possibility to use a config file option to setup the MessageReader/MessageFormatter in addition to the existing option --property.
It will be useful in different use cases:
when having multiple --property (the default reader can have up to 11 properties)
when passing properties with sensitive data (like schema.registry.ssl.truststrore.password for kafka-avro-console-producer) (could also be mitigated by using env vars)

--formatter-config to tool kafka-console-consumer.sh

bash

[S1] Comment by Shantanu (2026-08-26)
I looked at current trunk (ConfigurationControlManager) and confirmed the policy map with unit tests that capture AlterConfigPolicy.RequestMetadata.configs() on incremental DELETE/SUBTRACT.

AlterConfigPolicy runs on the controller. The map passed to the policy is built from the ConfigRecords generated for the request, not from the Admin ops directly. DELETE sets newValue = null. A record is generated when currentValue differs from newValue, or when the resource type is BROKER (brokers reload dynamic config).

Unit tests on trunk:

|| Scenario || ConfigRecord generated? || Policy map ||
| TOPIC DELETE of a key that is currently stored | yes | key present, value null |
| TOPIC DELETE of a key that is not stored | no | empty map (key absent) |
| BROKER DELETE of a key that is currently stored | yes | key present, value null |
| BROKER DELETE of a key that is not stored | yes | key present, value null |
| BROKER SUBTRACT on an unset LIST key whose schema default is "1", subtracting "1" | yes | key present, value empty string (computed result, not the default) |
| TOPIC DELETE of a stored BOOLEAN whose schema default is "true" | yes | key present, value null (not "true") |

Example: DELETE retention.ms on a topic that already has a topic-level override → policy sees retention.ms=null. The same DELETE on a topic with no override → policy sees an empty map. The same DELETE on a broker resource always sees retention.ms=null.

A. Document current behavior, no code …

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-844: Transactional State Stores
Status
Current state: Discarded (in favor of )
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Right now, a stream processor with EOS has to delete all data from the local state stores after crash failure because the state stores might be in a partially updated state. The partial update of a state store can happen during a crash failure because the changes to the local state are not atomic with respect to Kafka Streams commit. If an application with EOS crashes between commits, it cannot reset the state to the previously committed, so it wipes the state stores and replays the changelog from scratch.
This KIP proposes making writes to the state stores transactional so that they atomically commit only after the corresponding changes are committed to the changelog topic. As a result, Streams applications configured with EOS will no longer need to wipe the state stores on crash failure.
Public Interfaces
Changed:
org.apache.kafka.streams.processor.StateStore
org.apache.kafka.streams.state.Stores
org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.Materialized.StoreType
Proposed Changes

Background
This section briefly describes relevant parts of a stateful task's write lifecycle with EOS.
The task (StreamTask, StandbyTask) registers its state stores. State stores load offset metadata from the checkpoint file (link). That step aims to establish a mapping between data in the state store and the offset of the changelog topic.
In case of crash failure, if the state store has data, but the checkpoint file does not exist, ProcessorStateManager throws an exception for EOS tasks. This is an indicator to throw away local data and replay the changelog topic (link).
The task processes data and writes its state locally.
The task commits EOS transaction. TaskExecutor#commitOffsetsOrTransaction calls StreamsProducer#commitTransaction  that sends new offsets and commits the transaction.
The task runs a postCommit method (StreamTask, StandbyTask) that:
flushes the state stores and
updates the checkpoint file (link) for non-EOS tasks (link).
Go to step 2 until task shuts down. During shutdown, the task stops processing data, then writes its current offset to the checkpoint file and halts.
If the failure happens at steps 2 or 3, the state store might contain records that have not yet been committed by EOS transaction. These uncommitted records violate the EOS guarantees and are …

AlterConfigPolicy runs on the controller. The map passed to the policy is built from the ConfigRecords generated for the request, not from the Admin ops directly. DELETE sets newValue = null. | BROKER DELETE of a key that is not stored | yes | key present, value null |
| BROKER SUBTRACT on an unset LIST key whose schema default is "1", subtracting "1" | yes | key present, value empty string (computed result, not the default) |
| TOPIC DELETE of a stored BOOLEAN whose schema default is "true" | yes | key present, value null (not "true") |

Example: DELETE retention.ms on a topic that already has a topic-level override → policy sees retention.ms=null. The same DELETE on a topic with no override → policy sees an empty map. The same DELETE on a broker resource always sees retention.ms=null.

ACCEPT ONLY IF: the page states the status (a 'Current state' line, a vote result, 'accepted', 'adopted', 'under discussion', 'superseded by' ...). If the page says rejected, discarded, withdrawn or dormant, or says nothing, reject: the schema has no value for those.

<<<TEXT
SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-845: 'HasField' predicate for kafka connect
Status
Current state: Discarded
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Today's connect predicates enables checks on the record metadata. However, this can be limiting considering many inbuilt and custom transformations that we have are more key/value-centric.
Some use-cases this can solve:
Data type conversions of certain pre-identified fields for records coming across datasets only if those fields exist. [Ex: TimestampConverter can be run only if the specified date field exists irrespective of the record metadata]
Skip running certain transform if a given field does/does not exist. A lot of inbuilt transforms raise exceptions (Ex: InsertField transform if the field already exists) thereby breaking the task. Giving this control enable users to consciously configure for such cases.
Even though some inbuilt transforms explicitly handle these cases, it would still be an unnecessary pass-through iteration.
Considering each connector usually deals with multiple datasets (Even 100s for a database CDC connector), metadata-centric predicate checking will be somewhat limiting when we talk about such pre-identified common fields in the records from across the datasets.
Public Interfaces
New:
org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.predicates.HasField$Key
org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.predicates.HasField$Value
Proposed Changes

Overview
This KIP proposes to have a new HasField predicate class that works for records with or without schema.
The predicate takes a field path configuration option string (Ex: abc.xyz). Hence supports nested field checks.
Return true/false based on whether the path exists in the record.
Configuration changes

Predicate Settings in Kafka Connect Config:
predicates.<predicateName>.field.path
Examples
Converting a timestamp only if created_at  field exists
Inserting only if the field testField doesn't exist
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Fully respects the current predicate interfaces and there is no need for deprecation/migration.
Test Plan / Cases
field.path setting is mandatory when the predicate is enabled
The predicate will return false for records with null keys/values.
The predicate returns true if the field exists in the record, even if the field is set to null.
Rejected Alternatives
Creating multiple custom transforms to handle the field checks.

Severity: moderate

Affected versions:

- Apache Kafka 3.7.0 through 4.1.2
- Apache Kafka 4.2.0 through 4.2.1
- Apache Kafka 4.3.0

Description:

The broker-side PushTelemetry API (KIP-714) validates only the
compressed size of a client's metrics payload against
telemetry.max.bytes (default 1 MB) before decompressing it.
ClientTelemetryUtils.decompress() then decompresses the payload with
no limit on the decompressed output size, growing a heap buffer until
the compressed input is exhausted. A small, highly compressible
payload (for example gzip-compressed zeros) can therefore expand to
hundreds of megabytes of broker heap.

Impact:

An authenticated client can send a PushTelemetry request with a small
compressed payload that decompresses to a very large size, consuming
broker heap out of proportion to the request size. Repeated or
concurrent requests can exhaust the broker heap and cause an
OutOfMemoryError, degrading or crashing the broker; a client that
targets multiple brokers can affect cluster availability.
PushTelemetry is available to any authenticated client and is not
gated by an ACL.

Mitigation:

Upgrade to Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.1, or 4.4.0. On affected versions
there is no configuration that fully prevents the amplification,
because telemetry.max.bytes bounds only the compressed size; lowering
telemetry.max.bytes reduces the worst-case decompressed size
proportionally and is a partial mitigation.

[S1] Review by showuon (2026-10-19)
Thanks for adding the tests. LGTM, Only one minor comment.
[S2] Comment by OmniaGM (2026-10-20)
Thanks @fvaleri for the pr, quick comment the pattern and ACL configs (`topics.include/exclude`, `groups.include/exclude`, `topic.properties.exclude`, `acls.include/exclude`) are defined without a validator, so `AbstractConfig` would accept any string for them. They're only checked later, in the constructor, when compilePatternList and parseAclRules run.

I believe here when a value is invalid, the exception thrown at that point is not a `ConfigException`:
- `topics.include=foo[` throws `PatternSyntaxException`, which is a plain `RuntimeException`.
- `acls.include=TOPIC;.*;REED` throws `IllegalArgumentException` from `AclOperation.valueOf`.

So once the create-mirror path uses this config, a typo wouldn't come back `INVALID_CONFIG`, or the mirror would be accepted and only break later, once the link starts on the brokers.

Could we add validators to these `define(...)`? the same way as `TopicCreationConfig::REGEX_VALIDATOR` in Connect (catching `PatternSyntaxException`)? Each entry would then be checked whenever the config is parsed, and a bad one would fail with `ConfigException(name, value, reason)`, which maps to `INVALID_CONFIG`. It would also name the entry that's wrong. same with rest of regex configs,  and the ACL ones could have a similar validator that calls `MirrorAclRule.parse`. 

WDYT?

 - validation for the regex/ACL configs (so invalid values fail with ConfigException)

 - splitting the broker-level and mirror-level configs into separate classes

[S1] Page: KIP-856: KRaft Disk Failure Recovery
Status

Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/ytv0t18cplwwwqcp77h6vry7on378jzj
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-14113
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
KIP-595 introduced KRaft topic partitions. These are partitions with replicas that can achieve consensus on the Kafka log without relying on the Controller or ZK. The KRaft Controllers in KIP-631 use one of these topic partitions (called cluster metadata topic partition) to order operations on the cluster, commit them to disk and replicate them to other controllers and brokers.
The cluster metadata partition is stored in the metadata.log.dir. If this directory doesn't contain a valid meta.properties file the Kafka node fails to start. The user can create a valid meta.properties file by executing the format command of the kafka-storage tool. The format only creates a meta.properties if it doesn't exists.
If the metadata.log.dir was prevously formatted, it was lost because of a disk failure and the user runs the format commmand of the kafka-storage tool then it is possible for the cluster metadata partition to establish a leader with inconsistency or data loss. To safely reformat a metadata.log.dir the user needs to make sure that the new voter node has a superset of the previous voter's on-disk state. This solution to disk failure is manual and error prone.
This KIP describes a protocol for extending KIP-595 and KIP-630 so that the Kafka cluster can detect disk failures on the minority of the nodes in the cluster metadata topic partition. This KIP also describe the mechanism for the user to programmatically replace the failed voters in a way that is safe and available.
Key Terms
These are the definition of some important terms that are used through the document.
Voters: A voter is any replica that can transition to the candidate state and to the leader state. Voters are required to have an ID and UUID. Each replica keeps their own set of voters that are part of the topic partition. For a replica, the voters are the replica ID and UUID is in its own voter set. A candidate needs to get votes from the majority of its own voter set before is can become the leader of an epoch. When a voter becomes a leader it will use its voter set to determine when an offset has been committed.
Observers: An observer is any replica that is not in the voter set. …

<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Nicholas Telford (2026-10-06)
A simple solution would be to change the way our internal transaction buffers work.

Currently, our RocksDBTransactionBuffer works by maintaining two structures:
1. a WriteBatch of pending writes to apply to RocksDB; this is the native memory and is the primary reason statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes was introduced, because this memory is not counted against the block cache or write buffers.
2. a Java TreeMap that is used to serve reads of buffered writes. This essentially mirrors the contents of the WriteBatch, but in the JVM, and indexed.

The main reason the WriteBatch exists is to pay for the cost of writes during the put/delete operation; but this cost is very small (WriteBatch is very cheap).

Instead of holding this WriteBatch in-memory for the lifetime of the transaction, we can simply construct it during commit, by iterating the TreeMap and adding its contents to the WriteBatch.

This shifts more of the cost of writes from put/delete to commit; although I expect the total throughput to be similar.

Actually, there's one scenario where throughput might be improved: a low cardinality of keys with a high replacement/deletion rate. Since we would only replace them in the TreeMap, and then write only the most recent values in the WriteBatch, instead of replacing them in both.

Edit: actually, this would not really resolve the core problem, although it might help when there are many updates of the same key. Memory usage of the on-heap transaction buffer …
[S2] Comment by Nicholas Telford (2026-10-06)
A more brute-force, but much simpler, approach would be for the StreamThread to halt processing once the statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes limit has been reached and not continue until the next commit succeeds.
[S3] Comment by Nicholas Telford (2026-10-06)
As an aside: pausing processing under this circumstance could also be extended to a TimeoutException during commit: we would then wait for a successful commit before continuing processing, to prevent OOM issues.

I'm starting to lean towards both fixes: pausing processing until the next successful commit and deferring the WriteBatch to commit-time.

CONVERSATION: Ticket KAFKA-21230: Long rebalances can cause OOM errors with transactional state stores enabled
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Nicholas Telford (2026-10-06)
A simple solution would be to change the way our internal transaction buffers work.

Currently, our RocksDBTransactionBuffer works by maintaining two structures:
1. a WriteBatch of pending writes to apply to RocksDB; this is the native memory and is the primary reason statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes was introduced, because this memory is not counted against the block cache or write buffers.
2. a Java TreeMap that is used to serve reads of buffered writes. This essentially mirrors the contents of the WriteBatch, but in the JVM, and indexed.

The main reason the WriteBatch exists is to pay for the cost of writes during the put/delete operation; but this cost is very small (WriteBatch is very cheap).

Instead of holding this WriteBatch in-memory for the lifetime of the transaction, we can simply construct it during commit, by iterating the TreeMap and adding its contents to the WriteBatch.

This shifts more of the cost of writes from put/delete to commit; although I expect the total throughput to be similar.

Actually, there's one scenario where throughput might be improved: a low cardinality of keys with a high replacement/deletion rate. Since we would only replace them in the TreeMap, and then write only the most recent values in the WriteBatch, instead of replacing them in both.

Edit: actually, this would not really resolve the core problem, although it might help when there are many updates of the same key. Memory usage of the on-heap transaction buffer …
[S2] Comment by Nicholas Telford (2026-10-06)
A more brute-force, but much simpler, approach would be for the StreamThread to halt processing once the statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes limit has been reached and not continue until the next commit succeeds.
[S3] Comment by Nicholas Telford (2026-10-06)
As an aside: pausing processing under this circumstance could also be extended to a TimeoutException during commit: we would then wait for a successful commit before continuing processing, to prevent OOM issues.

I'm starting to lean towards both fixes: pausing processing until the next successful commit and deferring the WriteBatch to commit-time.
TEXT>>>

CONVERSATION: Pull request #23855: KAFKA-21302:  Sort copartition groups and indexes for consistent Streams topology comparison
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by lucasbru (2026-10-20)
Thanks for the fix! I think we should also fix this on the client. `StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestManager#getCopartitionGroupsFromStreams` builds the index lists and the list of groups by iterating a `Set`, which is where the nondeterministic order comes from. Could you sort the indexes within each group and then the groups there too, the same way we already sort source/sink/repartition topics in `fromStreamsToHeartbeatRequest`? Clients would then always send a canonical topology. We'd still keep the broker-side normalization permanently, both on join and on replay, because of older clients and already-persisted unsorted records. A test in `StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestManagerTest` that checks the sorted output would be good too.

It might also be worth sorting in `convertToStreamsGroupTopologyRecord`, so that newly written topology records are canonical too. The record format doesn't change, and it means a broker downgrade won't reject newer, sorted clients against a stored record. `fromRecord` would still normalize for groups created before this change.
[S2] Comment by chickenchickenlove (2026-10-20)
@lucasbru 
Thanks for taking the time to review! 

I agree that we should fix the client side as well. Given the backport implications, would it make sense to track that change in a separate ticket and PR?

AFAIK, Copartition groups are persisted, including their ordering. If an existing client is upgraded to send sorted groups while the broker remains unpatched, the broker could reject the topology because its ordering differs from the persisted record, even though the topology is semantically unchanged.

Separating the client-side change would let us backport the broker normalization independently and evaluate the client-side backport with this compatibility concern in mind.

What do you think?
[S3] Comment by lucasbru (2026-10-20)
Good point, I hadn't thought about the unpatched-broker case. Agreed, let's keep this PR broker-only so it can be backported on its own, and handle the client side in a separate ticket.

The same argument applies to my suggestion of writing sorted records: if a patched broker writes sorted records and is later downgraded, existing clients sending the old order would be rejected. So let's drop that and keep persisting what the client sent.
[S4] Comment by chickenchickenlove (2026-10-20)
Thanks for the clarification! 
First of all, I've created new ticket for client side. (https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21320)

Currently, I'm working on addressing your comments in this PR.
I'll be back ASAP with new commit!
[S5] Comment by lucasbru (2026-10-20)
Small addition after looking at how the client builds the groups: the order comes from `HashSet` iteration in `InternalTopologyBuilder#copartitionGroups`, which is deterministic for the same topology code. So instances running the same code always send the same order, and the mismatch only happens when equivalent topologies are written differently (e.g. join order swapped) and the topic names collide in the same hash bucket.

That also means existing records generally match what current clients send, which makes your point about sorting on the client even stronger. A sorting client would usually differ from the persisted order on an unpatched broker.
[S6] Comment by chickenchickenlove (2026-10-20)
@lucasbru 

I've pushed a new commit that incorporates most of your suggestions!

I left out the `matches()` optimization for now, as I think it would be better to address it in a separate issue. However, if you consider it a minor change, I'm also happy to include it in this PR. Just let me know what you think!

I also added a comment at the end of KAFKA-21302. Even when running the exact same code, the ordering of copartition groups can vary across JVM runs if the source nodes are defined using `Set.of(...)`.

I wanted to highlight this again, as I thought it might be helpful when determining the priority of this issue.

When you get a chance, please take another look! 🙇‍♂️
[S7] Comment by lucasbru (2026-10-21)
Thanks for the update and for checking the `Set.of` case, you are right. This can happen without code changes, in some cases (more detail in the ticket).
[S8] Comment by chickenchickenlove (2026-10-21)
@lucasbru 
Thanks for taking the time to review this carefully! 
I reverted change for the normalization and implemented matches method and some test cases.
When you get a chance, please take another look. 🙇‍♂️
TEXT>>>

[S1] Comment by Muralidhar Basani (2026-10-07)
[~prakhar1801] thanks for the report.

Could you sort the indexes within each group and then the groups there too, the same way we already sort source/sink/repartition topics in `fromStreamsToHeartbeatRequest`? SUBJECT
[S1] Email from Manikumar Reddy: CVE-2026-111496: Apache Kafka: Kafka Streams StreamThread hang from  integer overflow in stream-time punctuation
Severity: low

Affected versions:

- Apache Kafka 1.1.0 through 4.1.2
- Apache Kafka 4.2.0 through 4.2.1
- Apache Kafka 4.3.0 through 4.3.1

Description:

Kafka Streams derives its stream-time clock from record timestamps.
PunctuationSchedule.next() computed the next punctuation time as
timestamp + (intervalsMissed + 1) * interval with no overflow check. A
record with a timestamp at or near Long.MAX_VALUE advances stream time
to that value, so the next stream-time punctuation overflows to a
negative time. PunctuationQueue then re-queues that time and loops on
it indefinitely while holding a lock, stalling the StreamThread.

Impact:

A single record is enough. The affected StreamThread stops processing,
and because the record stays in the topic the hang returns on restart;
an application whose partitions are all affected becomes unresponsive.
Only the Streams application is affected, not the brokers or the
cluster. Triggering it needs write access to a source topic whose
topology uses stream-time punctuation, and a broker that stores the
record: brokers from Apache Kafka 4.0.0 reject such a timestamp by
default (log.message.timestamp.after.max.ms, one hour), so it is
reachable only on older brokers or where that bound has been relaxed.

Mitigation:

Upgrade Kafka Streams to 4.2.2, 4.3.2, or 4.4.0. As defense in depth,
keep log.message.timestamp.after.max.ms bounded on source topics and
restrict write access to them.

Resolution:

>From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, and 4.4.0: …

CANDIDATES
[C1] Proposal: KIP-1334 : Introduce max.future.record.timestamp.difference.ms to Protect Stream-Time from Future Record Poisoning
[C2] Proposal: KIP-1385: Measure local.retention.ms from remote upload time instead of record timestamps
[C3] Proposal: KIP-1293: Add Time-Shift Parameter to Kafka Streams Punctuation Scheduling
[C4] Proposal: KIP-424: Allow suppression of intermediate events based on wall clock time

My understanding is, that we currently present stale group metadata to the assignor, and thus, the assignor might incorrectly assign a standby to a member in the group, even if a "sibling member" (ie, member of a different thread within the same Kafka Streams clients) hold a corresponding active task. This triggers an assignor run, and we pass in M1 with the old member m1-old and old processId p-old, while we did re-map M2 onto an new memberId m2-new and use the new processId p-new. The assignor now incorrectly thinks there is two clients, and incorrectly assigns t-standby to M2. Later, when M1 re-joins, before this fix we incorrectly give t-active to M1, and with this fix, we hold off to give t-active to M1. When M1 re-joins, it also triggers a rebalance (which might be delayed base on assignment-interval config), and when the second rebalance runs, it now correctly sees both member using processId p-new, and would only assign t-active and omit t-standby again. [S2] Review by lucasbru (2026-10-27)
Agree with the analysis. It’s a corner case and it heals itself, but we should still fix it since one process briefly gets told to run the same task twice. One small correction from trying it out: once the second rebalance runs, the sticky assignor promotes M2’s standby to active, and M1 ends up empty. So it recovers, but not by M1 getting the active task back.

I’m not keen on remapping all members of p-old to p-new. Besides the case where a client comes back with more members, we’d be guessing about members that aren’t heartbeating. Nothing guarantees the instance IDs from p-old all come back on the same new process.

I’d go for something simpler than the current fix. When a static member rejoins from a different process, don’t copy its current assignment at all, and only keep the relabeled target assignment. The reconciler then grants the tasks with its usual checks, so we don’t need a second copy of the one-process check in the static join path. We also don’t lose anything, because the new process has no local state for those tasks anyway. Conflicting tasks wait for the next rebalance exactly as they do with the current PR.

I agree the root cause is the new process ID. That only happens for apps without persistent stores, because with persistent stores the process ID is kept in the state directory. Fixing it would mean the client keeps its process ID across restarts, which I’d treat as a separate change.

[S1] EmailMessage by Junaid (2026-08-24)
Hi all,

TL;DR: Apache Beam has merged a Kafka Streams runner, which turns a Beam
pipeline into a Kafka Streams topology. Because Beam is portable, this
means a Kafka Streams application no longer has to be written in Java: the
runner is Java, but your code can be Python, Go or YAML. It is an
experimental skeleton, opt-in at build time and in no Beam release. I also
have a question at the end about forwarding records from a punctuator under
EOS, which is the one thing currently blocking us.

I wrote this over the summer as a Google Summer of Code project.

The portability is the part worth explaining. Beam runs user code in a
separate process over gRPC, whichever SDK it was written in, so the runner
never executes your code itself. A pipeline written in Python runs on a
runner written entirely in Java. So you can write what is really a Kafka
Streams application in Python and deploy it like any other Kafka Streams
application: no job manager, no second cluster, scale by starting more
copies of the process. Java and Python are covered by tests; the other SDKs
should work by construction, but I have not run them.

Stateless ParDo, GroupByKey, Combine, fixed and sliding windows, Flatten
and metrics work. Side inputs, stateful ParDo with user timers, merging
windows and splittable DoFn do not yet.

Now the question. Beam executes user code in bundles, and a bundle must be

Thanks for reaching out:

> is forwarding records from a wall-clock punctuator under EOS expected to be safe

I don't know anything about Beam, or "bundles", but in general 
punctuation in combination with EOS are tricky. EOS guarantees that you 
read some messaged, producer the corresponding output, and atomically 
commit the result records plus the advanced input topic offsets.

Punctuations, wall-clock and event-time, don't really fit into this 
pattern. It might still be ok to use them, but w/o more details it's 
very hard to say if this could work or not. -- EOS in general does not 
cover side-effects, and punctuation (depending on their implementation) 
are most likely a side-effect.

> and is there a supported way to run work just before a commit

No, that's not supported.

> We want to flush buffered output exactly at the commit boundary, so the
> records produced and the offsets consumed commit together. If there is an
> idiom for that, I would rather use it than work around it.

to do this. A transaction gets committed by the runtime in the 
background, and this process is totally agnostic to punctuations. I 
cannot say why you would see duplicates though (assuming your buffer is 
persistent storage), but there is no guarantee when a punctuation runs 
exactly, and if you take input records and buffer them, if the TX 
commits the offset will get advanced, so the buffer must ensure it does

separate process over gRPC, whichever SDK it was written in, so the runner
never executes your code itself. A pipeline written in Python runs on a
runner written entirely in Java. So you can write what is really a Kafka
Streams application in Python and deploy it like any other Kafka Streams

copies of the process. Java and Python are covered by tests; the other SDKs
should work by construction, but I have not run them.

> is forwarding records from a wall-clock punctuator under EOS expected to be safe

I don't know anything about Beam, or "bundles", but in general 
punctuation in combination with EOS are tricky. EOS guarantees that you 
read some messaged, producer the corresponding output, and atomically 
commit the result records plus the advanced input topic offsets.

Punctuations, wall-clock and event-time, don't really fit into this

Update: This KIP was discarded in favor of moving the code from the kafka  (aka core) module to other modules. Once that effort is completed, kafka  (aka core) will be empty and a separate KIP will propose its removal (along with proposed alternatives).
Since Scala 2 is not binary compatible across minor versions, a separate kafka  (aka core ) artifact is published for each supported Scala version (as is typical for Scala projects). More concretely, we currently publish kafka_2.12 and kafka_2.13 for Scala 2.12 and 2.13 respectively. This requires building the project and running all the tests once for each supported Scala version. In addition, it's not uncommon for contributors to have to fix pull requests so that they work on both Scala versions.
Projects written in Java can use any of the two jars (i.e. there is no benefit in having both artifacts), but projects written in Scala should use the jar with the matching Scala version. It is worth noting that the kafka  jar does not expose any public API, so we are doing extra work to support Scala users who access internal APIs. That said, it's not uncommon for users and other projects to depend on internal broker classes to start an embedded kafka cluster for testing purposes (we should have a public API for testing, but that's a subject for another KIP).
As part of KIP-751, we deprecated support for Scala 2.12 with the goal to remove it in Apache 4.0 – that is, a single Scala version would be supported at that point. I propose we take the chance to formalize that only a single Scala version will be supported by the kafka  (aka core ) module from Apache Kafka 4.0 and the artifact name should be changed to be simply kafka  (i.e. the Scala version suffix will be removed).

[S2] Comment by Avishek Das (2026-10-09)
[~showuon] I have a few questions:
 * What is the actual goal? Is it latency (keep the leader in a particular DC), durability (every commit must reach C), or a C-as-witness setup? Notethat with 2-2-1, losing any single DC already leaves at least 3 voters, so the current design already survives one DC outage. Why AB is a problem needs to be stated.
 * Is leader preference enough? If so, it's a small, low-risk change built on the existing PreferredCandidates and backoff mechanism.
  {}If quorum rules really have to change{*}, how should it interact with KIP-853 voter add and remove? Should groups and weights be stored in the voter set inside the log?

It's reliability I would say. In our example, the DC c is a resource constraint node, which we don't want it to be elected as the leader. I've updated the expected behavior in the description above.

 

> Is leader preference enough? If so, it's a small, low-risk change built on the existing PreferredCandidates and backoff mechanism.

> {}If quorum rules really have to change{}, how should it interact with KIP-853 voter add and remove? Should groups and weights be stored in the voter set inside the log?

 

Yes, in KIP-853, the source of truth for the voter info is the metadata log, not the kafka proerties file anymore. So I'd also expect the weight store in the metadata log. Of course, it needs more discussion in the community.

 

Thank you for picking it up.

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-906: Tools migration guidelines
Status
Current state: Accepted
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The tools migration effort is ongoing and being tracked in KAFKA-14525. This is part of a bigger initiative to split the core module into multiple modules (e.g. storage, network, security, tools), which is being tracked in KAFKA-14524. 
The plan is to migrate tools and related classes in a fully compatible way from kafka.tools and kafka.admin packages (core module) to org.apache.kafka.tools package (tools module).
While kicking off this activity, we identified a number of potential compatibility issues:
Missing wrapper: some tools do not have a wrapper script.

[S2] Review by AndrewJSchofield (2026-10-21)
Thanks for the PR. An AI-assisted review suggests this PR is a regression in behaviour.

The skip drops the partitions that currently have first claim on the budget (DelayedShareFetch.java:849). The new comment says "the already fetched records are handed out first". They are not. The merge at the end of `combineLogReadResponse` does `missingTopicPartitionsLogReadResponse.putAll(existingFetchedData)`, so the missing partitions sit first in the combined map, and processFetchResponse acquires in map order with `maxFetchRecords - acquiredRecordsCount`. So before this change the missing partitions were acquired first and the already-fetched ones got the remainder. After it, the already-fetched span is used to decide the missing ones get nothing. Concrete scenario, one consumer, tp0 and tp1 both with deep backlogs:
- tp0 is served, so its next fetch offset moves and its cached fetch-offset metadata goes stale. It is read in tryComplete and lands in the already-fetched set every time.
- tp1 is not served, so its offset and cached metadata stay valid. It is never read in tryComplete and is always a "missing" partition.
- Before the change, tp1 was acquired first on each fetch and the two alternated naturally. After it, tp0's span is at least maxFetchRecords, so tp1 is skipped on every fetch for as long as tp0 has a backlog. That is indefinite starvation of tp1.

CONVERSATION: Ticket KAFKA-21283: Fix StreamThreadTest teardown race causing thread leaks and cascading test failures
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Kuan Po Tseng (2026-10-15)
Happy to work on this issue, thanks!
[S2] Comment by Lucas Brutschy (2026-10-20)
Can this only happen in the test or in prodcution as well? If the latter, this should probably be a bug ticket not a test ticket
[S3] Comment by Ken Huang (2026-10-20)
In production, TaskManager.shutdown() is only called from {{{}StreamThread#completeShutdown(){}}}. This happens either on the stream thread itself after its run loop exits, or from StreamThread#shutdown() when the thread is still in the CREATED state and was never started. In either case, no other thread is accessing the TaskManager concurrently.

The race comes from the test teardown, which calls thread.taskManager().shutdown(false) from the test thread while the StreamThread may still be running and picking up restored tasks from the StateUpdater. Production code never shuts down the TaskManager from another thread like this, so I think fixing the test is right.
[S4] Comment by Lucas Brutschy (2026-10-20)
thanks!

Motivation
Note: This KIP required leader election change, which will be proposed in another KIP.
In Kafka, Producers have the option of either waiting for the message to be committed or not, depending on their preference for tradeoff between latency and durability. This preference is controlled by the acks setting that the producer uses.
Currently, the acks config accepts these values:
acks=0
If set to zero then the producer will not wait for any acknowledgment from the server at all.
acks=1
This will mean the leader will write the record to its local log but will respond without awaiting full acknowledgement from all followers.
acks=all
This means the leader will wait for the full set of in-sync replicas to acknowledge the record.
For acks=all case, the simple flow is like this:
It looks perfect. But there's a caveat here. Like the doc said, acks=all will "wait for the full set of in-sync replicas to acknowledge the record", so if there's only 1 replica in in-sync replicas, it will have the same effect as acks=1 (even though we have replication-factor set to 3).
To get the expected durability, users also need to set min.insync.replicas  (default is 1) config correctly. In the doc of min.insync.replicas config:
When min.insync.replicas  and acks  used together, it allows you to enforce greater durability guarantees. A typical scenario would be to create a topic with a replication factor of 3, set min.insync.replicas to 2, and produce with acks of "all". This will ensure that the producer raises an exception if a majority of replicas do not receive a write. 
In the typical scenario: replication factor = 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, we ensure at least 2 replicas acks, which means, we can tolerate 1 replica out-of-sync or down (ex: rolling update) and still make the write process successfully. This keeps high availability and durability in Kafka.
Let's step back and think again. In the case of replication factor = 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, we can allow 1 replica doesn't ack, and still have durability guarantee

[S2] Comment by Gergely Harmadás (2026-10-15)
This seems like a genuine bug. As mentioned in the description Kafka has some restrictions on certain config value changes. While the broker is running, going from num.io.threads 16->8->6 pass the validation check "{}value should be at least half the current value{}". However after the restart the situation changes:
 # After startup the broker first operates with the static config from server.properties (16)

Thanks for the changes. 
However, I think this behaviour is introducing another case of starvation. The case isn't a very regular way of share fetch but it can occur and trunk was protected earlier, so seems like a regression. The case is when a share fetch hands its record budget to partitions in response order, so the first partition with enough data takes all of it. That order comes from two stacked mechanisms:

1. LRU order: the share session moves the partition it just served to the end of its list.
2. Epoch rotation: the broker then rotates the list by `sessionEpoch % numPartitions`.

The client advances the session epoch on every ShareFetch and every ShareAcknowledge. In a `poll(); commitSync();` loop the epoch therefore moves by 2 per fetch, so the rotation never changes. If the epoch is odd, rotation 1 puts the just-served partition first on every fetch with 2 partitions. That partition takes the whole budget each time, and the other starves for as long as the first has at least one fetch’s worth of records. With 4 partitions and odd parity, one partition is never served at all.

A single unpaired request is enough to make the epoch odd:

an empty fetch (for example, before the share partitions finish initializing, or during lock contention with another member),
or an extra acknowledge, which is how the test triggers it.

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-941: Range queries to accept null lower and upper bounds
Status
Current state: ["Adopted"]
Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/wnn2qrb7vglw11bdm2cdlkm1430b75zc
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-15126
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Within the RangeQuery class in the Interactive Query API (which allows you to leverage the state of your application from outside your application), there are methods for getting the upper and lower bounds. When web client requests come in with query params (which become those bounds), it's common for those params to be null. We want developers to just be able to pass in the upper/lower bounds if they want instead of implementing their own logic to avoid getting the whole range. 
An example of the logic they can avoid after this KIP is implemented is below:
`
Public Interfaces
We are not explicitly changing the public interface, but a KIP is appropriate because there's a behavior change. As it stands on 6/26/23, if you pass in a null value to the RangeQuery without a specified upper and lower bound, it will perform a full range scan. After this proposed change, you will need to specify an upper and lower bound of null in order to perform a full range scan. This change in behavior will need to be documented.
Proposed Changes
The proposed change takes line 57 of the RangeQuery java class from: 
to:
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
This will not affect users who are implementing a check of their nulls in their own code. 
Users who send a web request with no parameters will still receive a full scan. This is mostly an improvement for new adopters of range queries. 
New users will have the convenience of using the upper and lower bounds, and the docs will need to be updated to let users know they get the benefit of a full range scan when they insert null values.
Test Plan
Relevant unit tests will be added to demonstrate the functionality.
Rejected Alternatives
N/A.

We have a job that checks the offset and fetches latest records if there are any, latest record fetched had offset 69530. So that indicates that no records had actually been added to the partition.

Hi all,

I have a Jira account request waiting for review in the self-serve queue and
was hoping a PMC member could take a look when there is a moment.

  Requested username: kevinyoo
  Real name:          Seokmo Yoo
  Submitted:          September 1, 2026

I am asking here because the self-serve queue is the only route since public
signup was disabled, and I do not want the request to sit unnoticed.

The account is for two SASL/OAUTHBEARER issues I ran into while running Kafka
clients inside a container that gives each deployment its own class loader.
Both have a fix and tests ready, rebased on current trunk.

1. LoginManager is shared across class loaders

   LoginManager is cached by JAAS configuration, login class, login callback
   class and the sasl.* configs, but not by the class loader of the caller.
   When two deployments in one JVM use the same JAAS configuration they share
   a LoginManager, so its reference count never reaches zero and the
   OAUTHBEARER refresh thread outlives the deployment that created it. That
   thread keeps the discarded class loader as its context class loader, and
   because LoginContext resolves login modules through ServiceLoader, every
   later re-login fails the same way:

<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Sharad Garg (2025-08-26)
Hello, could someone please check this?
[S2] Comment by David Arthur (2026-07-16)
[~gargsha] we will look into adding some docs around this. 

In general, I would not recommend running in dual-write mode for too long. The mode with the most risk is hybrid mode when you have ZK brokers but a KRaft controller. Once the brokers have come up as KRaft (dual write mode), things are pretty much the same as they would be in a pure-KRaft system.

I would suggest only being in hybrid mode as long as it takes to restart the brokers as KRaft. In other words, the least amount of time as necessary. You can stay in dual write mode for a few hours, days, or weeks. It's really up to you. Just note that once you finalize the migration, there is no going back.

The validations that you perform are up to you. Generally, we like to see that client traffic is unaffected and broker health is stable. 

I can share an anecdote from when I was migrating a lot of clusters back in 2024. We rolled through hybrid mode as quickly as possible. After triggering the migration, we would immediately start restarting brokers as KRaft. Once in dual write mode, we would leave clusters there for at least one week before doing the next restart to finalize the migration. While in dual write mode, we would check that client throughput was normal and that we didn't have things like sustained URPs or under min ISR partitions.

[S2] Comment by David Arthur (2026-07-16)
[~gargsha] we will look into adding some docs around this. 

In general, I would not recommend running in dual-write mode for too long. The mode with the most risk is hybrid mode when you have ZK brokers but a KRaft controller. Once the brokers have come up as KRaft (dual write mode), things are pretty much the same as they would be in a pure-KRaft system.

I would suggest only being in hybrid mode as long as it takes to restart the brokers as KRaft. In other words, the least amount of time as necessary. You can stay in dual write mode for a few hours, days, or weeks. It's really up to you. Just note that once you finalize the migration, there is no going back.

The validations that you perform are up to you. Generally, we like to see that client traffic is unaffected and broker health is stable. 

I can share an anecdote from when I was migrating a lot of clusters back in 2024. We rolled through hybrid mode as quickly as possible. After triggering the migration, we would immediately start restarting brokers as KRaft. Once in dual write mode, we would leave clusters there for at least one week before doing the next restart to finalize the migration. While in dual write mode, we would check that client throughput was normal and that we didn't have things like sustained URPs or under min ISR partitions.

[C1] Ticket KAFKA-21363: Streams EOS: member cut off from the group coordinator keeps committing punctuator writes unfenced, and its store diverges from the changelog after a clean restart
With exactly_once_v2 and the classic group protocol, a Streams instance that cannot reach the group coordinator keeps its active task and keeps committing what its wall clock punctuator writes, while the group has already given the same task to another instance. [S2] Comment by Pankraz76 (2026-10-24)
More detail on the retry loop mentioned above, in case it helps the review:

While a marker waits in the unknown-broker queue (leader endpoint is `Node.noNode()`), the `TxnMarkerSenderThread` re-checks it in a tight loop until the partition has a leader again:
- `generateRequests()` drains the unknown-broker queue and calls `addTxnMarkersToBrokerQueue()` for each parked marker.
- The leader is still unavailable, so the marker is parked again.
- `addTxnMarkersToBrokerQueue()` always ends with `wakeup()`, so the next `pollOnce(Long.MAX_VALUE)` returns immediately and the thread loops straight back.

With one parked marker I measured about 30,000 `getPartitionLeaderEndpoint` calls per second (0 when nothing is parked). It does not affect correctness: the marker is sent as soon as the partition has a leader, which the integration test in this PR verifies.

This already happens on trunk when a leader has no endpoint for the inter-broker listener, and it was the behavior for offline partitions before KAFKA-17573. So I kept it out of this fix. A possible follow-up would be to call `wakeup()` only when markers reach a real broker queue, and retry parked markers after a backoff (e.g. `retry.backoff.ms`) or on a metadata update. Happy to file a JIRA for that if reviewers agree.

Status
Current state: Withdrawn, this should have been included in KIP-944.

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Design goal
The goal of this KIP is to allow consumer callbacks to call the consumer again from another thread.
Motivation
Rebalances cause a lot of message duplication. This can be prevented by doing commits in the partition-revoked callback. This KIP will make it much easier to do work in that callback when an async runtime is used.
The JVM based KafkaConsumer contains a check that rejects nested invocations from different threads (in method acquire). For programs that use an async runtime, this is an almost impossible requirement. Also, the check is more strict than is required; we only need to validate that there is no concurrent access to the consumer.
Examples of affected async runtimes are Kotlin co-routines (see KAFKA-7143) and Zio.
Here follows a condensed example of how we'd like to use ZIO in the rebalance listener callback from the zio-kafka library.scala1onRevoked callbacktrue

Look at line 6 of the first code block. In method end the stream will try to call consumer::commitAsync(offsets, callback). In awaitCommitsCompleted() (line 7) we call consumer::commitSync(Collections.emptyMap) to wait untill all callbacks are invoked.
Since this code is running in the rebalance listener callback, KafkaConsumer enforces that the commit methods must be invoked from the same thread as the thread that invoked onPartitionsRevoked. Unfortunately, the ZIO runtime is inherently multi-threaded; tasks can be executed from any thread. There is no way Zio could support this limitation without a major rewrite.

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-962: Relax non-null key requirement in Kafka Streams
Current state: Merged
Voting thread: here
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-12317ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-14748
Motivation
Kafka Streams enforces a strict non-null-key policy in the DSL across all key-dependent operations (like aggregations and joins).
 For left-joins, it makes sense to still accept a `null`, and add the left-hand record with an empty right-hand-side to the result.
Similarly, for outer-joins it makes sense to keep the record.
The defined semantics for left/outer join are: keep the stream record if no matching join record was found.
Thus, Kafka Streams today's behavior is inconsistent with the defined semantics.
Public Interfaces / Proposed Changes
This KIP won't change any public interfaces. However, it will change the behavior of the following:
Operators
left join Kstream-Kstream: no longer drop left records with null-key and call ValueJoiner with 'null' for right value.
outer join Kstream-Kstream: no longer drop left/right records with null-key and call ValueJoiner with 'null' for right/left value.
left-foreign-key join Ktable-Ktable: no longer drop left records with null-foreign-key returned by the ForeignKeyExtractor and call ValueJoiner with 'null' for right value.
left join KStream-Ktable: no longer drop left records with null-key and call ValueJoiner with 'null' for right value.
left join KStream-GlobalTable: no longer drop records when KeyValueMapper returns 'null' and call ValueJoiner with 'null' for right value.
Repartition of null-key records
Currently, repartitioning causes records with 'null'-keys to be dropped.
This behavior needs to be changed. 
The above described change in behavior would otherwise not work for topologies with repartitioning.
Going forward, they will be sent to an arbitrary partition.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

Keeping the old behavior
Users who want to keep the current behavior can prepend a .filter() operator to the aforementioned operators and filter accordingly.
Examples
//left join Kstream-Kstream
leftStream

//outer join Kstream-Kstream
rightStream
    .filter((key, value) -> key != null);
leftStream
    .filter((key, value) -> key != null)
    .outerJoin(rightStream, (lv, rv) -> join(lv, rv), windows);
//left-foreign-key join Ktable-Ktable

check group membership on the transactional commit even when there are no offsets to send

There is no explicit "check group membership"; but we could add offsets to the TX to enforce such a check. It's the only fix I can think off.
or treat a coordinator that stays unknown past the session timeout as losing the assignment, or let the poll timeout leave run outside the coordinatorUnknown() branch

Don't think these would be bullet proof, but both would be subject to race conditions, and thus they would only reduce the time window this issue can happen, but not fully close it.

[~mjsax] Thanks , makes sense. I also checked whether an empty TxnOffsetCommit could do the job, but the broker answers it straight away without going to the group coordinator (same on 3.0 and 4.4), so we do need real offsets in there.

One thing to be careful about is which offset gets sent. If it's the consumer position, records that were fetched but not processed yet would be skipped after a failover. StreamTask.findOffsetAndMetadata already gives the head of the task's queue and committableOffsetsAndMetadata already commits all input partitions when processor metadata needs a commit. Maybe the same path can be reused when a task has writes under eos v2 but consumed nothing? Then the extra AddOffsetsToTxn/TxnOffsetCommit only happens in that case.
[S3] Comment by Matthias J. Sax (2026-10-27)

On the broker side, KafkaApis.handleTxnOffsetCommitRequest looks like it answers a TxnOffsetCommit without topics by itself, without going to the group coordinator (I saw the same on 3.0 and trunk). So my understanding is that allowing an empty map would need a broker change too, and older brokers would still skip the check. Please correct me if I missed something there.

That makes me think one real offset might be the simpler route. From what I see the group coordinator validates member id and generation once per request (OffsetMetadataManager.commitTransactionalOffset), so one offset could already be enough for the check.

It takes the head of the task's queue, or the next offset from the last fetch when the queue is empty, not the consumer position. If nothing was processed since the last commit, I think that comes out as the offset committed last time (maybe moved past control records), so the commit would be idempotent. It returns empty for a partition where nothing was fetched yet since the assignment, which might need some thought.

Just an …
[S5] Comment by Matthias J. Sax (2026-10-28)
On the producer side, if I read it right, sendOffsetsToTransaction returns straight away when the map is empty, so neither AddOffsetsToTxn nor TxnOffsetCommit goes out. That seems to have come in with KAFKA-13319 (3.1.0), to avoid markers piling up in __consumer_offsets.

That's what I expected...
On the broker side, KafkaApis.handleTxnOffsetCommitRequest looks like it answers a TxnOffsetCommit without topics by itself, without going to the group coordinator (I saw the same on 3.0 and trunk). So my understanding is that allowing an empty map would need a broker change too, and older brokers would still skip the check.

That would be a pickle... Maybe [~jolshan] can chime in? (Given that punctuations and EOS are in general kind of an anti-pattern, I would personally be ok to only fix for newer version is we need a broker change).
[S6] Comment by Eswarar Siva (2026-10-28)
??That would be a pickle... Maybe Justine Olshan can chime in? (Given that punctuations and EOS are in general kind of an anti-pattern, I would personally be ok to only fix for newer version is we need a broker change).??

Could I ask for your view on the anti-pattern point, since it's how we run expiry today? Two of our EOS v2 services keep a large key-value store (over 200 million keys in our load tests) whose entries have to go after a fixed retention say for ex 100 days ... A persistent key-value store has no TTL, and expiring at the RocksDB level would bypass the changelog, so the entries would come back after a restore. So we keep a second store as an expiry index (expiry bucket plus key) and a wall-clock punctuator every few minutes that range-scans it up to now and deletes from both stores through the store API, so both changelogs get the tombstones.

We already learned one lesson there: a cleanup run of 14 to 18 seconds held the transaction open past the 10 second transaction timeout, the producer got fenced and the task restored from scratch, again and again. Each run now has a time budget and keeps a watermark, so the next run picks up where the last one stopped.

Status

Motivation
During the discussion for KIP-980, which proposed the creation of connectors in STOPPED state, there was a suggestion to also allow setting the initial offset for a connector in the connector creation API. The proposal was deemed valid (point no.4) but was deferred to a future KIP. This KIP proposes to implement that change.
This feature will be helpful to users who want to create a connector and start from a specific offset.
To do this today, user will have to
first create a connector in STOPPED state and check the response for errors
alter the offsets for said connector and check the response for errors
finally set the connector state to RUNNING.

A new optional field "initial_offsets"  will be added to the request body format for the POST /connectors endpoint. The value for this field has to adhere to format specified in KIP-875 else a 400 Bad Request response will be returned.

CreateConnectorRequest
{
    "name": "file-src-1",

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-996: Pre-Vote
Status
Current state: Implementing
Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/pqj9f1r3rk83oqtxxtg6y5h7m7cf56r2
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-16164
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
This KIP will go over scenarios where we might expect disruptive servers and discuss how Pre-Vote (as originally detailed in the extended Raft paper and in KIP-650) can ensure correctness when it comes to network partitions.  
Pre-Vote is the idea of “canvassing” the cluster to check if it would receive a majority of votes - if yes it increases its epoch and sends a disruptive vote request. If not, it does not increase its epoch and does not send a vote request. 
Throughout this KIP, we will differentiate between Pre-Vote and the original Vote request behavior with "Pre-Vote" and "standard Vote".
Disruptive server scenarios
When a follower becomes partitioned from the rest of the quorum, it will continuously increase its epoch to start elections until it is able to regain connection to the leader/rest of the quorum. When the server regains connectivity, it will disturb the rest of the quorum as they will be forced to participate in an unnecessary election. While this situation only results in one leader stepping down, as we start supporting larger quorums these events may occur more frequently per quorum.
For instance, here's a great example from https://decentralizedthoughts.github.io/2020-12-12-raft-liveness-full-omission/ which demonstrates a scenario where we could have flip-flopping leadership changes.
Let's say server 3 is the current leader. Server 4 will eventually start an election because it is unable to find the leader, causing Server 2 to transition to Unattached. Server 4 will not be able to receive enough votes to become leader, but Server 2 will be able to once its election timer expires. As Server 5 is also unable to communicate to Server 2, this kicks off a back and forth of leadership transition between Servers 2 and 3.
While network partitions may be the main issue we expect to encounter/mitigate impact for, it’s possible that bugs and user error create similar effects to network partitions that we need to guard against. For instance, a bug which causes fetch requests to periodically timeout or setting controller.quorum.fetch.timeout.ms and other related configs too low.

Here is a list of tools we have been told about that integrate with Kafka outside the main distribution. We haven't tried them all, so they may not work!

Distributions & Packaging
Confluent: Confluent Cloud (SaaS, fully managed) and Confluent Platform (software download for self-managed/on-premise)

EmblocSoft distribution and CPFA training - https://www.emblocsoft.com/pages/en/solutions/kafka/support/
IBM Event Streams - https://www.ibm.com/cloud/event-streams - Apache Kafka on premise and the public cloud
Strimzi - http://strimzi.io/ - Apache Kafka Operator for Kubernetes and Openshift. Downloads and Helm Chart - https://github.com/strimzi/strimzi-kafka-operator/releases/latest 
TIBCO Messaging - Apache Kafka Distribution - https://www.tibco.com/products/apache-kafka Downloads - https://www.tibco.com/products/tibco-messaging/downloads
Stream Processing
- the built-in stream processing library of the Apache Kafka project
Documentation in Apache Kafka
Documentation in Confluent Platform
Kafka Streams code examples in Apache Kafka
Kafka Streams code examples provided by Confluent

Azkarra Streams - A lightweight java framework to make it easy to build and manage streaming microservices based on Kafka Streams.
Storm - A stream-processing framework.
Samza - A YARN-based stream processing framework.

Flink - Apache Flink has an integration with Kafka
IBM Streams - A stream processing framework with Kafka source and sink to consume and produce Kafka messages 
Spring Cloud Stream - a framework for building event-driven microservices, Spring Cloud Data Flow - a cloud-native orchestration service for Spring Cloud Stream applications
Apache Apex - Stream processing framework with connectors for Kafka as source and sink.
Logstash - Input and Output plugins to enrich events and optionally store in Elasticsearch
Logagent - Kafka Input and Kafka Output plugins

Flume - Contains Kafka source (consumer) and sink (producer)
KaBoom - A high-performance HDFS data loader
Database Integration
Confluent JDBC Connector - A source connector for the Kafka Connect framework for writing data from RDBMS (e.g. MySQL) to Kafka
Oracle Golden Gate Connector - Source connector that collects CDC operations via Golden Gate and writes them to Kafka
Search and Query
Elasticsearch - This project, Kafka Standalone Consumer will read the messages from Kafka, processes and index them in Elasticsearch. There are also several Kafka Connect connectors for Elasticsearch.
Presto - The Presto Kafka connector allows you to query Kafka in SQL using Presto.
Hive - Hive SerDe that allows querying Kafka (Avro only for now) using Hive SQL
OpenMLDB Kafka Connector - This project allows you to define and extract features from data streams using SQL for ML applications.

CMAK - A tool for managing Apache Kafka clusters (previously known as Kafka Manager).
kafkat - Simplified command-line administration for Kafka brokers.

Doctor Kafka - Service for cluster auto healing and workload balancing.
Cruise Control - Fully automate the dynamic workload rebalance and self-healing of a Kafka cluster.
Burrow - Monitoring companion that provides consumer lag checking as a service without the need for specifying thresholds.
Chaperone - An audit system that monitors the completeness and latency of data stream.
Sematext integration for Kafka monitoring that collects and charts 200+ Kafka metrics
Xinfra Monitor - A framework that monitors and exposes metrics showing availability and performance of Kafka clusters and mirrored pipelines.
Kafdrop - A web UI for viewing Kafka topics and browsing consumer groups. It displays brokers, topics, partitions and consumers, and lets you view messages.
AKHQ - A Kafka GUI to manage topics, topic data, consumer groups, Schema Registry, Kafka Connect and more.
Kafbat UI - A free, open-source web UI to monitor and manage Apache Kafka clusters.
LibreDB Studio - An open-source web-based multi-database IDE with a read-only Kafka provider for browsing topics, consumer group lag and messages.
AWS Integration
Automated AWS deployment
Kafka -> S3 Mirroring tool from Pinterest.
Alternative Kafka->S3 Mirroring tool

Metrics

Ganglia Integration

Dropwizard packaging
Kafka Camel Integration

Misc.
Kafka Websocket - A proxy that interoperates with websockets for delivering Kafka data to browsers.
KafkaCat - A native, command line producer and consumer.
Kafka Mirror - An alternative to the built-in mirroring tool
Ruby Demo App 
Apache Camel Integration
Infobright integration
Riemann Consumer of Metrics
stormkafkamom – curses-based tool which displays state of Apache Storm based Kafka consumers (Kafka 0.7 only).
uReplicator - Provides the ability to replicate across Kafka clusters in other data centers
Mirus - A tool for distributed, high-volume replication between Apache Kafka clusters based on Kafka Connect
libbeat - All Elastic Beats (Metricbeat, Filebeat, etc) have Kafka outputs

[S1] EmailMessage by Chia-Ping Tsai (2026-09-14)
Hi all,

I'd like to raise a discussion about our system test dependencies. I'm not
sure this needs a KIP, happy to write one if people think so. We keep
hitting the same issues in each release:

   1. We forgot to upload files to the S3 mirror, and not every RM has
   access to it.
   2. We forgot to update both the Dockerfile and vagrant file.
   3. The Dockerfile has 44 curl lines for the same thing, so each release
   adds two more.

Therefore, I'd like to propose a base image on GitHub Container Registry
that contains only the released Kafka binaries. The benefits are:

   1. It is built and pushed by a GitHub workflow that can be triggered
   after each release, so no manual upload is needed.
   2. Only one file needs to be updated for each release.
   3. Both the Dockerfile and vagrant can pull everything from the base
   image.

Since the image is built once per release, we can fetch from ASF download
links directly and drop the S3 mirror.

Also, is anyone still using vagrant? If not, we could drop it.

Any thoughts?

Chia-Ping :)

[S1] EmailMessage by Chia-Ping Tsai (2026-09-14)
Hi all,

I'd like to raise a discussion about our system test dependencies. I'm not
sure this needs a KIP, happy to write one if people think so. We keep
hitting the same issues in each release:

   1. We forgot to upload files to the S3 mirror, and not every RM has
   access to it.
   2. We forgot to update both the Dockerfile and vagrant file.
   3. The Dockerfile has 44 curl lines for the same thing, so each release
   adds two more.

Therefore, I'd like to propose a base image on GitHub Container Registry
that contains only the released Kafka binaries. The benefits are:

   1. It is built and pushed by a GitHub workflow that can be triggered
   after each release, so no manual upload is needed.
   2. Only one file needs to be updated for each release.
   3. Both the Dockerfile and vagrant can pull everything from the base
   image.

Since the image is built once per release, we can fetch from ASF download
links directly and drop the S3 mirror.

Also, is anyone still using vagrant? If not, we could drop it.

Any thoughts?

Chia-Ping :)
