<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1365: Transform Observability and Skipped Record Handling for Kafka Connect
Status
Current state: "Under Discussion"
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka Connect's Single Message Transform (SMT) framework allows users to build chains of transformations that process records between the connector and Kafka. Transforms can modify records, route them to different topics, or drop them entirely by returning null (a filter operation). When combined with the error tolerance framework (errors.tolerance=all), records can also be diverted to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) before reaching the connector.
Today, the transform layer has two significant gaps: no operational observability and no mechanism for sink connectors to learn about records they never received. This KIP addresses both with two complementary enhancements.
Problem 1: No Per-Transform Operational Metrics
Kafka Connect provides no operational metrics at the transform layer. The existing connector-transform-metrics group only exposes static metadata:
Existing MetricTypeDescription
transform-classGauge (string)The class name of the transformation
transform-versionGauge (string)The version of the transformation
This creates several operational pain points:
No visibility into filtering — When using the Filter transform (or any transform that drops records by returning null), operators have no way to know how many records are being filtered. The only workaround is subtracting task-level source-record-poll-total from source-record-write-total (or sink-record-read-total from sink-record-send-total), which provides only an aggregate across the entire transform chain.
No per-transform throughput — In a chain of 3-5 transforms, operators cannot determine the throughput contribution or bottleneck of each individual transform. If a transform has a bug that silently drops records, it goes undetected.
No error attribution — While task-error-metrics tracks aggregate errors, operators cannot determine which transform in a chain is causing failures without correlating with debug-level logs.
Capacity planning gap — Without per-transform record counts, operators cannot make informed decisions about whether a transform is cost-effective (e.g., "is this filter dropping 90% of records, or 1%?").
The consumer group protocol and other Kafka subsystems have rich per-component metrics. The transform layer is a notable gap.
Problem 2: Offset Gap for Sink Connectors When Records Are Skipped
The SinkTask.preCommit() API allows sink connectors to control which offsets are committed to Kafka. Many production connectors override this method to implement exactly-once or at-least-once delivery guarantees with external systems. These connectors track offsets based on records they receive in put() and only return offsets from preCommit() after durably writing to the external system.
When transforms or error tolerance drop records before put(), these connectors have no visibility into the dropped records. The result:
Offset gap — The consumer position advances past the dropped records, but the sink's committed offset does not include them.
Reprocessing after rebalance — On rebalance, the consumer seeks to the last committed offset and re-fetches the dropped records. The transforms drop them again, and the cycle repeats.
Infinite reprocessing loop — If all records for a partition are dropped, the sink returns an empty map from preCommit(), the framework skips commit entirely, and no progress is ever made for that partition.
This problem affects widely-used connectors in production:
ConnectorOffset StrategyImpact
S3 SinkReturns offsets only after flushing to S3 (rotation interval / record count)Filtered records create offset gaps. Rebalance reprocesses all records since last S3 flush
IcebergSinkConnectorWorkers commit offset only after coordinator signalTrailing filtered records never committed. Gap grows with each poll cycle
Any connector using preCommit() returning {}Full offset opt-outIf all records filtered, partition offset permanently frozen
How the Two Problems Relate
The two problems form a diagnose → fix pair:
Without Part A, operators cannot diagnose where records are being dropped. Without Part B, connectors cannot act on records they never received. Together, they provide complete observability and correctness for the transform pipeline.
The use of SMTs and Predicates in production has grown significantly since their introduction. Common patterns that trigger these problems:
Filter SMT — Drop records not matching criteria (e.g., filter by record type, tenant, region)
RegexRouter + Predicate — Route and filter based on content
errors.tolerance=all — Tolerate conversion errors, send to DLQ
HeaderFilter + Predicate — Drop records missing required headers
Multi-tenant pipelines — Filter per-tenant records across shared topics
Success Criteria
AreaCriterion
ObservabilityOperators can query per-transform record-in, record-out, and record-filtered counts via JMX
ObservabilityOperators can compute per-transform filter rates for alerting and dashboards
CorrectnessSink connectors that override preCommit() can track offsets for all consumed records, including those dropped before put()
SafetyZero risk of data loss — the framework never overrides the sink's offset decisions
CompatibilityFull backward compatibility — existing connectors work identically without code changes
PerformanceZero performance regression for connectors with no transforms configured
UniversalityMetrics are available for all transforms (built-in and custom) without any transform code changes
SimplicityConnectors need minimal code changes to incorporate skipped record awareness
New or Changed Public Interfaces

New SkipReason Enum Types
Module: connect/api
TypePackageDescription
SkipReasonorg.apache.kafka.connect.sinkEnum: FILTERED, ERROR_TOLERATED
Full definition:
New Public API: SinkTask.onRecordSkipped():
Module: connect/api
File: org.apache.kafka.connect.sink.SinkTask
Full signature and Javadoc:
onRecordSkipped Method
The onRecordSkipped(TopicPartition, long, SkipReason) method is declared as a default no-op on SinkTask in New or Changed Public Interfaces → SinkTask API Changes. Sink tasks that override preCommit() and track offsets internally should override it to fold skipped-record offsets into their tracking. See that section for the full signature and Javadoc.
API Design Rationale
DecisionRationale
Default method (no-op)Backward compatible — existing connectors compile and work without changes
TopicPartition+ long offsetparametersMatches the granularity of preCommit(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata>). The sink needs partition and offset to update its tracking
SkipReasonenumSinks may want to log, metric, or handle filter vs DLQ differently. Extensible for future skip reasons
No SinkRecordparameterThe record may have failed conversion — a valid SinkRecord may not exist. Partition + offset is the minimum viable information
Called per-record, not batchedSimpler contract. Sinks that want batching can accumulate internally
Called before put()Sink can merge skipped offsets with delivered offsets in a single pass
Exceptions caught by frameworkNotification is advisory — a bug in onRecordSkipped()must not break the pipeline
Framework Integration: WorkerSinkTask Changes
The change to WorkerSinkTask is minimal — a single notification call in the existing else branch of convertMessages():
Changes Summary
LocationChange
convertMessages()else branchAdd onRecordSkipped()call with try/catch
SinkTaskMetricsGroupAdd skip counters by reason
No changes to commitOffsets()Framework offset logic unchanged
No changes to deliverMessages()Delivery logic unchanged
No changes to preCommit() callSink retains full control
New JMX Metrics: Per-Transform
Six new attributes added to the existing connector-transform-metrics MBean:
MBean: kafka.connect:type=connector-transform-metrics,connector={name},task={id},transform={alias}
Metric NameTypeDescription
transform-record-in-ratedoubleRecords/second entering this transform
transform-record-in-totaldoubleTotal records entering this transform
transform-record-out-ratedoubleRecords/second produced by this transform
transform-record-out-totaldoubleTotal records produced by this transform
transform-record-filtered-ratedoubleRecords/second filtered (dropped) by this transform
transform-record-filtered-totaldoubleTotal records filtered (dropped) by this transform
New JMX Metrics: Task-Level Skipped Records
Eight new attributes added to the existing sink-task-metrics MBean:
MBean: kafka.connect:type=sink-task-metrics,connector={name},task={id}
Metric NameTypeDescription
sink-record-skipped-totaldoubleTotal records skipped (all reasons)
sink-record-skipped-ratedoubleRecords skipped per second
sink-record-filtered-totaldoubleRecords dropped by transforms/predicates
sink-record-filtered-ratedoubleFiltered records per second
sink-record-error-tolerated-totaldoubleRecords …

[S1] EmailMessage by Aditya Kousik (2026-07-08)
Hi all,

I’d like to start a discussion on KIP-1364 as a follow-up to KIP-1306.

KIP link: https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/x/jYE_Gg

A Kafka consumer client today cannot tell why a rebalance happened without grepping logs. The rebalance trigger can help with triaging:

* max.poll.interval.ms exceeded implies misconfig or delayed poll loop;

[S1] Page: KIP-1365: Transform Observability and Skipped Record Handling for Kafka Connect
Status
Current state: "Under Discussion"
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka Connect's Single Message Transform (SMT) framework allows users to build chains of transformations that process records between the connector and Kafka. Transforms can modify records, route them to different topics, or drop them entirely by returning null (a filter operation). When combined with the error tolerance framework (errors.tolerance=all), records can also be diverted to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) before reaching the connector.
Today, the transform layer has two significant gaps: no operational observability and no mechanism for sink connectors to learn about records they never received. This KIP addresses both with two complementary enhancements.
Problem 1: No Per-Transform Operational Metrics
Kafka Connect provides no operational metrics at the transform layer. The existing connector-transform-metrics group only exposes static metadata:
Existing MetricTypeDescription
transform-classGauge (string)The class name of the transformation
transform-versionGauge (string)The version of the transformation
This creates several operational pain points:
No visibility into filtering — When using the Filter transform (or any transform that drops records by returning null), operators have no way to know how many records are being filtered. The only workaround is subtracting task-level source-record-poll-total from source-record-write-total (or sink-record-read-total from sink-record-send-total), which provides only an aggregate across the entire transform chain.
No per-transform throughput — In a chain of 3-5 transforms, operators cannot determine the throughput contribution or bottleneck of each individual transform. If a transform has a bug that silently drops records, it goes undetected.
No error attribution — While task-error-metrics tracks aggregate errors, operators cannot determine which transform in a chain is causing failures without correlating with debug-level logs.
Capacity planning gap — Without per-transform record counts, operators cannot make informed decisions about whether a transform is cost-effective (e.g., "is this filter dropping 90% of records, or 1%?").
The consumer group protocol and other Kafka subsystems have rich per-component metrics. The transform layer is a notable gap.
Problem 2: Offset Gap for Sink Connectors When Records Are Skipped
The SinkTask.preCommit() API allows sink connectors to control which offsets are committed to Kafka. Many production connectors override this method to implement exactly-once or at-least-once delivery guarantees with external systems. These connectors track offsets based on records they receive in put() and only return offsets from preCommit() after durably writing to the external system.
When transforms or error tolerance drop records before put(), these connectors have no visibility into the dropped records. The result:
Offset gap — The consumer position advances past the dropped records, but the sink's committed offset does not include them.
Reprocessing after rebalance — On rebalance, the consumer seeks to the last committed offset and re-fetches the dropped records. The transforms drop them again, and the cycle repeats.
Infinite reprocessing loop — If all records for a partition are dropped, the sink returns an empty map from preCommit(), the framework skips commit entirely, and no progress is ever made for that partition.
This problem affects widely-used connectors in production:
ConnectorOffset StrategyImpact
S3 SinkReturns offsets only after flushing to S3 (rotation interval / record count)Filtered records create offset gaps. Rebalance reprocesses all records since last S3 flush
IcebergSinkConnectorWorkers commit offset only after coordinator signalTrailing filtered records never committed. Gap grows with each poll cycle
Any connector using preCommit() returning {}Full offset opt-outIf all records filtered, partition offset permanently frozen
How the Two Problems Relate
The two problems form a diagnose → fix pair:
Without Part A, operators cannot diagnose where records are being dropped. Without Part B, connectors cannot act on records they never received. Together, they provide complete observability and correctness for the transform pipeline.
The use of SMTs and Predicates in production has grown significantly since their introduction. Common patterns that trigger these problems:
Filter SMT — Drop records not matching criteria (e.g., filter by record type, tenant, region)
RegexRouter + Predicate — Route and filter based on content
errors.tolerance=all — Tolerate conversion errors, send to DLQ
HeaderFilter + Predicate — Drop records missing required headers
Multi-tenant pipelines — Filter per-tenant records across shared topics

[S1] EmailMessage by Aditya Kousik (2026-07-08)
Hi all,

I’d like to start a discussion on KIP-1364 as a follow-up to KIP-1306.

KIP link: https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/x/jYE_Gg

A Kafka consumer client today cannot tell why a rebalance happened without grepping logs. The rebalance trigger can help with triaging:

* max.poll.interval.ms exceeded implies misconfig or delayed poll loop;
* Member fencing points at session timeout
* Coordinator-initiated rebalances are regular occurrences due to join and leave requests.
* Application calls to Consumer.enforceRebalance()are expected and the application owns the context.

Existing rebalance metrics describe frequency and latency but carry no cause dimension:

rebalance-rate-per-hour, rebalance-latency-{avg,max}, rebalance-total
last-rebalance-seconds-ago, last-poll-seconds-ago

So, the cause would be useful in diagnosing issues by surfacing the event to the user.

Looking forward to hearing your thoughts on this.

Best,
Aditya Kousik
[S2] EmailMessage by Andrew Schofield (2026-07-16)
Hi Aditya,
Thanks for the KIP.

I can see the idea behind the KIP but I'm not convinced that it's possible to work out a coherent set of RebalanceCause cases, in particular for the consumer group protocol. In this protocol, rebalances are always "coordinator-initiated". Just because the application calls Consumer.subscribe() resulting in a ConsumerGroupHeartbeat request being sent to the GC, it's not certain that the next ConsumerGroupHeartbeat response will contain the newly assigned partitions. Assignment is asynchronous and the GC makes various optimisations to avoid excessive rebalances for groups with a lot of churn. I'm not sure I could tell the difference between "coordinator-initiated" and "subscription-changed". If you can explain in more detail how each of the cases corresponds to ConsumerGroupHeartbeat response, it would help.

We do need to put more work into the broker-side metrics for rebalance for the consumer group protocol. We'd like more visibility than we have today for sure.

Thanks,
Andrew

Status
Current state: Rejected
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: KAFKA-6583 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Currently, in StreamPartitionAssignor, assignment takes place without regards to which tasks are stateful and which are not. Thus potentially creating a situation where we have an unbalanced assignment of tasks. For StreamPartitionAssignor to factor in stateful tasks, the current rebalance protocol's metadata should be upgraded so that it contains the number of state stores that exists for a certain task. In this manner, when metadata is decoded in StreamPartitionAssignor#assign(Cluster metadata, Map<String, Subscription> subscription), the data for stateful tasks are now available for more even distibution to clients.
Public Interfaces
The class in which the rebalance protocol's metadata is contained is SubscriptionInfo which encodes information into a ByteBuffer. What this upgrade would require is to change the format of the encoding and decoding to the ByteBuffer in SubscriptionInfo, which would require us to give an upgrade strategy for older Kafka versions. A new encoding and decoding format will be introduced: mainly the addition of an extra integer for each TaskId in SubscriptionInfo.
Proposed Changes
The following changes will be made to TaskId to facilitate the recording of the number of state stores for a specific task:javaFadeToGrey29TaskId.javatruetrue
In this manner, when TaskId#encode() and TaskId#decode() is called in SubscriptionInfo, the number of state stores will also be processed.  Note that setNumberOfStateStores(...) will also be called during StreamTask instantion to set the number of state stores to the given ProcessorTopology's state store list size.
It would also be helpful to know that in the older version of encoding TaskId, only the topic group id and partition number was included. In this newer version, the number of state stores is also made available.

Since we are updating metadata, this will undoubtedly necessitate an upgrade path which has been provided in KIP-268.

<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1366: Configurable Segment Interval for Window and Session Stores
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka Streams window and session state stores are internally divided into time-based segments, each backed by a separate RocksDB instance. The segment interval controls how wide each segment is in time. Currently, the segment interval for window and session stores is computed automatically as max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms) and is not configurable through the public API.
This creates two problems:
Changing retention requires a full state store restore.
Because the segment interval is derived from the retention period, any change to retention also changes the segment boundaries. Since segment boundaries determine the on-disk directory structure and key layout, a retention change invalidates the existing state store data and requires restoring from the changelog topic. This is unnecessarily disruptive — a user who simply wants to keep data longer or shorter should not have to pay the cost of a full restore.
The default segment size is suboptimal for common access patterns.
Many streaming applications need a long retention or grace period (e.g., 7 days) but access recent data the vast majority of the time. With the current formula, a 7-day retention produces segments of ~3.5 days. This means the active segment — the one receiving all writes and most reads — is very large, leading to heavier RocksDB compaction and lower cache-hit ratios. A user who knows their access pattern could benefit from smaller segments (e.g., 1 hour), keeping the active segment compact while still retaining historical data across many smaller segments.
Notably, Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore already accepts an optional segmentInterval parameter, introduced in KIP-889: Versioned State Stores. KIP-889 established both the API pattern and the rationale for user-configurable segments. This KIP extends the same capability to window and session stores, where the internal plumbing already supports a configurable segment interval — it is simply not exposed in the public API.
Public Interfaces

New method overloads in `org.apache.kafka.streams.state.Stores`

Window stores
java
Session stores
java
Validation
The following constraints are enforced on segmentInterval:
Must be at least 60,000 milliseconds (1 minute). This matches the minimum already used by the default formula (max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms)). Segments smaller than 1 minute would create an excessive number of RocksDB instances for any practical retention period.
For window stores: must be greater than or equal to windowSize. A segment smaller than the window size would cause a single window's data to span multiple RocksDB segments, degrading read performance.
An IllegalArgumentException is thrown if these constraints are violated.
Javadoc for `segmentInterval`
The only added parameter is segmentInterval. The Javadoc is adapted from the existing Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore parameterjava
For the new overloads, the existing note about retentionPeriod is replaced by a note about segmentInterval, since changing retentionPeriod alone no longer impacts the underlying storage format when segmentInterval is set explicitly:java
Proposed Changes
The changes are minimal because the internal plumbing already supports a configurable segment interval.
Stores.java : Add the new overloads listed above. Each delegates to the existing private persistentWindowStore(...) method (or equivalent), passing the user-provided segmentInterval instead of the computed default. Add validation as specified.
RocksDbSessionBytesStoreSupplier.java: add a constructor overload that accepts an explicit segmentInterval and adapt segmentIntervalMs() to return the segmentInterval set
No changes needed to:
WindowBytesStoreSupplier interface — already defines segmentIntervalMs()

[S1] Page: KIP-1366: Configurable Segment Interval for Window and Session Stores
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka Streams window and session state stores are internally divided into time-based segments, each backed by a separate RocksDB instance. The segment interval controls how wide each segment is in time. Currently, the segment interval for window and session stores is computed automatically as max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms) and is not configurable through the public API.
This creates two problems:
Changing retention requires a full state store restore.
Because the segment interval is derived from the retention period, any change to retention also changes the segment boundaries. Since segment boundaries determine the on-disk directory structure and key layout, a retention change invalidates the existing state store data and requires restoring from the changelog topic. This is unnecessarily disruptive — a user who simply wants to keep data longer or shorter should not have to pay the cost of a full restore.
The default segment size is suboptimal for common access patterns.
Many streaming applications need a long retention or grace period (e.g., 7 days) but access recent data the vast majority of the time. With the current formula, a 7-day retention produces segments of ~3.5 days. This means the active segment — the one receiving all writes and most reads — is very large, leading to heavier RocksDB compaction and lower cache-hit ratios. A user who knows their access pattern could benefit from smaller segments (e.g., 1 hour), keeping the active segment compact while still retaining historical data across many smaller segments.
Notably, Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore already accepts an optional segmentInterval parameter, introduced in KIP-889: Versioned State Stores. KIP-889 established both the API pattern and the rationale for user-configurable segments. This KIP extends the same capability to window and session stores, where the internal plumbing already supports a configurable segment interval — it is simply not exposed in the public API.
Public Interfaces

New method overloads in `org.apache.kafka.streams.state.Stores`

Window stores
java
Session stores
java
Validation
The following constraints are enforced on segmentInterval:
Must be at least 60,000 milliseconds (1 minute). This matches the minimum already used by the default formula (max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms)). Segments smaller than 1 minute would create an excessive number of RocksDB instances for any practical retention period.
For window stores: must be greater than or equal to windowSize. A segment smaller than the window size would cause a single window's data to span multiple RocksDB segments, degrading read performance.
An IllegalArgumentException is thrown if these constraints are violated.
Javadoc for `segmentInterval`
The only added parameter is segmentInterval. The Javadoc is adapted from the existing Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore parameterjava
For the new overloads, the existing note about retentionPeriod is replaced by a note about segmentInterval, since changing retentionPeriod alone no longer impacts the underlying storage format when segmentInterval is set explicitly:java
Proposed Changes
The changes are minimal because the internal plumbing already supports a configurable segment interval.
Stores.java : Add the new overloads listed above. Each delegates to the existing private persistentWindowStore(...) method (or equivalent), passing the user-provided segmentInterval instead of the computed default. Add validation as specified.
RocksDbSessionBytesStoreSupplier.java: add a constructor overload that accepts an explicit segmentInterval and adapt segmentIntervalMs() to return the segmentInterval set
No changes needed to:
WindowBytesStoreSupplier interface — already defines segmentIntervalMs()

RocksDbWindowBytesStoreSupplier — already accepts segmentInterval in its constructor

Users who want to set it use Materialized.as(WindowBytesStoreSupplier) with a custom supplier.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Backward compatible All existing methods retain their current signatures and behavior. The new overloads are purely additive.
No deprecations
Migration. Users who currently instantiate internal suppliers directly (e.g., new RocksDbWindowBytesStoreSupplier(...)) to control segment interval can migrate to the new public API overloads.
State store compatibility. As noted in the Javadoc, changing the segment interval for an existing store requires clearing local state, since it changes the on-disk segment layout. This is the same constraint that already applies when retention changes today — the difference is that with this KIP, users can change retention without triggering a segment layout change.
Test Plan

Correct segment interval is passed through to the underlying supplier.
Validation rejects invalid values (below 60 seconds, smaller than window size for window stores).
Default behavior is preserved when using the existing overloads without segmentInterval.

Apache Kafka is a distributed streaming platform with four core APIs:

** The Producer API allows an application to publish a stream of records to
one or more Kafka topics.

** The Consumer API allows an application to subscribe to one or more
topics and process the stream of records produced to them.

consuming an input stream from one or more topics and producing an
output stream to one or more output topics, effectively transforming the
input streams to output streams.

consumers that connect Kafka topics to existing applications or data
systems. For example, a connector to a relational database might
capture every change to a table.

The role of "{{{}kafka-storage --add-scram{}}}" is to allow brokers to use SCRAM to talk with each other without having to use another authentication scheme to bootstrap.

<<<TEXT
SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-263: Allow broker to skip sanity check of inactive segments on broker startup
Status
Current state: Discarded. Withdrawn because the solution we agreed on does not require interface change.
Discussion thread: 
JIRA:
Motivation
Currently broker will sanity check index files of all log segments in the log directory after the broker is started and before it becomes leader or follower for any partition. Sanity check a index file can be slow because broker needs to open index file and read data into page cache. Even if we apply time-based retention policy, the number of inactive log segments will still increase as the usage (e.g. number of partition and total-bytes-in-rate) of the Kafka cluster increases. As a result, the time to restart a broker will increase proportional to the number of segments in the log directory.
The problem with prolonged broker start time is that it will take a long time to rolling bounce a large cluster in order to deploy a new config or hotfix a config or bug. In one of our cluster, we observed that each broker spends around 8 minutes on LogManger.loadLogs(). And then the next broker needs to wait more than 8 minutes for URP to drop to 0 before it can shutdown itself. For a large cluster with 30 brokers, the total time to rolling bounce the cluster will be (8+8)*30 = 360 minutes, or 8 hours.
Ideally we would like broker startup time not to be proportional to the number of inactive segments. Most inactive segments will not be consumed, and even if it is consumed, its index files most likely will not require recovery after clean broker shutdown. This KIP proposes a way to lazy load log segments in order to reduce the cluster rolling bounce time.
Public Interfaces
Add broker config sanity.check.all.logs.enabled. This config value will be true by default.
If it is set to true, sanity check all log segments on broker startup. Otherwise, sanity check only the active log segments on broker startup. Inactive segments will be sanity checked  after broker becomes leader for those partitions, either by the background threads, or by the request handler thread if the log segment has not been sanity checked when the request handler thread tries to access the log segment.
Proposed Change
This KIP proposes the following changes:
1) When we instantiate LogSegments and AbstractIndex instances, we skip the instantiation of variables that require disk access, such as MappedByteBuffer, length etc. We will instantiate these variables when we actually need their values. Thus the instantiation of these objects will be much faster. …

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1367: Reserve apiKey values for private use
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1367: Reserve apiKey values for private use
Status
Current state: Under discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Released: <Kafka Version>
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Message types in Kafka are keyed by a unique apiKey to uniquely identify them. These include all RPC types used by the brokers and controllers, metadata records stored in the KRaft metadata log and the data stored by coordinators.
Kafka contributors regularly introduce new message types in order to evolve the Kafka protocol. However, contributors run the risk of adopting an apiKey that is subsequently claimed by another proposal while they prototype their work. This is a problem shared by other Apache projects as well [0]
A workaround for this is for contributors to use a large value for apiKey which is currently unused and is unlikely to be used in the near future. apiKey is represented as a short with non-negative range from [0, 32767]. This KIP proposes formalising the reservation of the last 1024 values, i.e. [31744, 32767] for private use, ensuring future protocol changes would take the reserved values into account.
Public Interfaces
javaMessageGenerator
javaMessageSpec
groovybuild.gradle
Proposed Changes
The change involves modifying MessageGenerator to accept a boolean flag --allow-custom which defaults to false. In addition, we add a new method, MessageSpec#isCustom which returns true if the apiKey is in the private reserved range.
MessageGenerator would only generate Java types for MessageSpecs with apiKey >= CUSTOM_MIN_API_KEY if --allow-custom is set to true and fail with a runtime exception otherwise.
The Gradle task processMessages is also modified to read a property allowCustomSpecs and pass --allow-custom flag appropriately.
Having this opt-in ensures that upstream PRs with a private spec inadvertently will result in the Gradle task failing.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The change is completely backwards compatible and incurs no cost to existing users. The range for apiKeys is quite large with about ~100 values being currently used. Reserving the last 1024 entries for private use should not cause any issues to existing users.
Test Plan
MessageGeneratorTest will be updated to ensure the correctness of --allow-custom
Documentation Plan
The documentation in Kafka Protocol section will be updated to note that the last 1024 values for apiKeys are reserved.
The change will also be mentioned in the release notes.
Rejected Alternatives
Using negative values
While this will work, it will make any future work that tries to transform the value into the negative space more involved.

[S1] EmailMessage by Nicole Du (2026-10-26)
Hi all,

I'd like to start a discussion on KIP-1388, which proposes adding a
request-side filter to the ListGroups API to allow Admin.listGroups to
return only groups with at least one committed offset.

Tools that replicate consumer group offsets across clusters, such as
MirrorMaker 2 and the group offset sync in KIP-1279, typically list all
groups before fetching their offsets. In large deployments, many groups may
have active members but no committed offsets, resulting in unnecessary
OffsetFetch requests and additional load on group coordinators.

This KIP proposes filtering these groups on the server side by introducing
a new request field in ListGroups v6 and exposing it through
ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(boolean).

KIP:
https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-1388%3A+Add+a+committed-offsets+filter+to+ListGroups

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21366

I'd appreciate any feedback or suggestions.

Thanks,
Nicole

Thanks for the KIP! I have only two comments:

DJ01: What's the reasoning for not including groups with only pending offsets?
DJ02: I wonder if we should simplify the "State of the group at the
read snapshot" table. For instance, "is visible in the snapshot" is an
implementation detail. We should rather say that the condition is
applied to the committed state and simplify the table.

[S3] EmailMessage by Nicole Du (2026-10-28)
Hi David,

Thanks for taking a look and for the suggestions!

For DJ01: My reasoning was to keep the predicate focused on offsets that
have already been committed. Pending transactional offsets may still be
aborted, so they do not count on their own. A group with an existing
committed offset still matches even if it also has pending offsets.

I’ve clarified this in the KIP. One trade-off is that a pending-only group
that commits after the listing is evaluated needs a subsequent listing to
be discovered. I’d appreciate your thoughts on whether including
pending-only groups would be more useful for callers.

For DJ02: That makes sense. I’ve replaced the snapshot-specific wording
with a definition based on the coordinator’s committed state and simplified
the table to three cases: at least one committed offset, pending offsets
only, and neither. A separate sentence clarifies that offsets eligible for
expiration continue to count until their deletion takes effect.

I’ve also made two small updates to the existing test plan: explicitly
covering pending offsets through transaction commit and abort, and
describing the visibility test in terms of committed state.

Best,
Nicole

<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1367: Reserve apiKey values for private use
Status
Current state: Under discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Released: <Kafka Version>
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Message types in Kafka are keyed by a unique apiKey to uniquely identify them. These include all RPC types used by the brokers and controllers, metadata records stored in the KRaft metadata log and the data stored by coordinators.
Kafka contributors regularly introduce new message types in order to evolve the Kafka protocol. However, contributors run the risk of adopting an apiKey that is subsequently claimed by another proposal while they prototype their work. This is a problem shared by other Apache projects as well [0]
A workaround for this is for contributors to use a large value for apiKey which is currently unused and is unlikely to be used in the near future. apiKey is represented as a short with non-negative range from [0, 32767]. This KIP proposes formalising the reservation of the last 1024 values, i.e. [31744, 32767] for private use, ensuring future protocol changes would take the reserved values into account.
Public Interfaces
javaMessageGenerator
javaMessageSpec
groovybuild.gradle
Proposed Changes
The change involves modifying MessageGenerator to accept a boolean flag --allow-custom which defaults to false. In addition, we add a new method, MessageSpec#isCustom which returns true if the apiKey is in the private reserved range.
MessageGenerator would only generate Java types for MessageSpecs with apiKey >= CUSTOM_MIN_API_KEY if --allow-custom is set to true and fail with a runtime exception otherwise.
The Gradle task processMessages is also modified to read a property allowCustomSpecs and pass --allow-custom flag appropriately.
Having this opt-in ensures that upstream PRs with a private spec inadvertently will result in the Gradle task failing.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The change is completely backwards compatible and incurs no cost to existing users. The range for apiKeys is quite large with about ~100 values being currently used. Reserving the last 1024 entries for private use should not cause any issues to existing users.
Test Plan
MessageGeneratorTest will be updated to ensure the correctness of --allow-custom
Documentation Plan
The documentation in Kafka Protocol section will be updated to note that the last 1024 values for apiKeys are reserved.
The change will also be mentioned in the release notes.
Rejected Alternatives
Using negative values
While this will work, it will make any future work that tries to transform the value into the negative space more involved.

[S1] EmailMessage by Nicole Du (2026-10-26)
Hi all,

I'd like to start a discussion on KIP-1388, which proposes adding a
request-side filter to the ListGroups API to allow Admin.listGroups to
return only groups with at least one committed offset.

Tools that replicate consumer group offsets across clusters, such as
MirrorMaker 2 and the group offset sync in KIP-1279, typically list all
groups before fetching their offsets. In large deployments, many groups may
have active members but no committed offsets, resulting in unnecessary
OffsetFetch requests and additional load on group coordinators.

This KIP proposes filtering these groups on the server side by introducing
a new request field in ListGroups v6 and exposing it through
ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(boolean).

KIP:
https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-1388%3A+Add+a+committed-offsets+filter+to+ListGroups

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21366

I'd appreciate any feedback or suggestions.

Thanks,
Nicole

read snapshot" table. For instance, "is visible in the snapshot" is an
implementation detail. We should rather say that the condition is

David

[S3] EmailMessage by Nicole Du (2026-10-28)
Hi David,

Thanks for taking a look and for the suggestions!

For DJ01: My reasoning was to keep the predicate focused on offsets that
have already been committed. Pending transactional offsets may still be
aborted, so they do not count on their own. A group with an existing
committed offset still matches even if it also has pending offsets.

I’ve clarified this in the KIP. One trade-off is that a pending-only group
that commits after the listing is evaluated needs a subsequent listing to
be discovered. I’d appreciate your thoughts on whether including
pending-only groups would be more useful for callers.

For DJ02: That makes sense. I’ve replaced the snapshot-specific wording
with a definition based on the coordinator’s committed state and simplified
the table to three cases: at least one committed offset, pending offsets
only, and neither. A separate sentence clarifies that offsets eligible for
expiration continue to count until their deletion takes effect.

I’ve also made two small updates to the existing test plan: explicitly
covering pending offsets through transaction commit and abort, and
describing the visibility test in terms of committed state.

Best,
Nicole

[S1] Page: KIP-1368: Client framework name and version
Status
Current state: Under discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The Apache Kafka clients are often wrapped by frameworks such as Spring. Kafka does this itself in Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect. There is no architected way of identifying clients running within such frameworks which can hinder problem determination.
When diagnosing an issue from the client logs, the application code is not directly calling the Kafka client. This means there's a mismatch between what the application developer wrote and how the Kafka client is being used. Behaviors such as retries or transactions can be implemented in the framework rather than the application. Having the information about whether a framework is being used can illuminate why the application is appearing to behave in a particular way.
Proposed Changes
Three client configurations are added which can be set by frameworks embedding Kafka clients (producer, consumer and admin). The configurations are client framework name (the name of the framework), client framework version (the version of the framework) and client framework ID (additional framework-specific context which may not be relevant to all frameworks). These are flowed to the broker in the ApiVersions request alongside the client software name and version providing more comprehensive context information about clients wrapped by frameworks.
The values are set using the CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_NAME_CONFIG , CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_CONFIG  and CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_ID_CONFIG  keys in the usual way. These configs are not intended to be set by regular applications. Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams both disallow setting these configuration properties and treat them as invalid configurations if set. If other frameworks provides a way for the application to set its own Kafka configs, they should also prevent the application from setting values for the client framework name, version and ID. 
The framework name should begin with the reversed Internet domain name for the framework owner, followed by the framework's name. For a framework such as Spring, the framework name would be chosen by Spring and the framework version would reflect the version of Spring.
For Kafka's own frameworks, Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect, Apache Kafka automatically sets the configs as follows:
Kafka StreamsKafka Connect
client.framework.name org.apache.kafka.streams org.apache.kafka.connect 
client.framework.version Kafka client version, such as 4.5.0 Kafka client version, such as 4.5.0 
client.framework.id Logical identifier used to group connections for the same Kafka Streams instance (process id)Connect worker ID
For example, let’s say that Kafka Streams is using the producer in Apache Kafka 4.5.0. It would set the following configurations:
"client.framework.name" = "org.apache.kafka.streams"
"client.framework.version" = "4.5.0"
"client.framework.id" = "F0DDEDA5-C8C6-493A-B026-F38A13C4E4D8"  (the Kafka Streams process id)
Then, in ApiVersions request, the following fields would be set:
ClientSoftwareName: "apache-kafka-java"
ClientSoftwareVersion: "4.5.0"
ClientFrameworkName: "org.apache.kafka.streams"
ClientFrameworkVersion: "4.5.0"
ClientFrameworkId: "F0DDEDA5-C8C6-493A-B026-F38A13C4E4D8" 
Here's an example of Kafka Connect configurations:
"client.framework.name" = "org.apache.kafka.connect"
"client.framework.version" = "4.5.0"
"client.framework.id" = "192.168.86.66:8083"
The framework ID in this case is the Connect worker ID.
Metrics
Kafka brokers today do collect metrics for client connections (see o.a.k.common.network.Selector ) and connections are counted by each <clientSoftwareName, clientSoftwareVersion>  pair, with a limit of 100 keys. The potential cardinality increase if we also key by client framework name and version could be significant, so these metrics are not augmented with client framework information.
KIP-714 introduced client metrics observability in the brokers. The client matching selectors are augmented by the addition of three new selectors:
client_framework_name  - client framework name.
client_framework_version  - client framework version.
client_framework_id  - client framework ID.
These new selectors can be included in the match  configuration property of client-metrics resources, and can also be specified on the kafka-client-metrics.sh  tool in the --match  option, such as the following which registers a client-metrics resource to collect consumer metrics for all Kafka Streams clients:shell
The broker metrics plugin will also add client_framework_name , client_framework_version  and client_framework_id  labels for clients which provide this information in their ApiVersions request. This is the natural extension of KIP-714 with this new client information.
Public Interfaces

Kafka protocol

ApiVersions RPC
Tagged fields are added to the most recent version of the ApiVersions RPC request, which is v6 (introduced in Apache Kafka 4.5 as part of KIP-1313).
Request schema
The KIP adds three tagged fields to v6. The maximum length of each of the new fields is 249 characters (see KIP-1233), and the request will fail with INVALID_REQUEST  if the length is exceeded.
Starting with Apache Kafka 5.0, the broker will also enforce the maximum length of 249 characters to both the client software name and client software version.
Response schema
The v6 response schema is unchanged.
Client API changes

ClientTelemetryContext
The org.apache.kafka.server.telemetry.ClientTelemetryContext  interface is augmented with methods to provide the client telemetry exporter a proper way of obtaining the information it needs to add resource labels to the metrics pushed by the clients. Only the new methods are shown below. Note that the principal is mentioned in KIP-714 as one of the broker-added resource labels, but that is already available to the exporter via the AuthorizableRequestContext  and it is not replicated here.java
Configuration

Client configuration
The configuration keys are defined in org.apache.kafka.clients.CommonClientConfigs  as CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_NAME_CONFIG , CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_CONFIG  and CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_ID_CONFIG . The maximum length of these configs is 249 characters.

client.framework.version For a client embedded in a framework, the version of the framework. User applications should not set this configuration directly. Importance: LOW
Type: STRING, default: null. If specified, must match the regular expression ”[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\\-.]*[a-zA-Z0-9])?"
client.framework.id For a client embedded in a framework, an optional framework-specific ID. User applications should not set this configuration directly. Importance: LOW
Type: STRING, default: null. If specified, must match the regular expression ”(?:[A-Za-z0-9\\-._~+]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})+"
Client metrics configuration
The valid values for the match configuration property of client metrics resources are augmented by this KIP.
ConfigurationDescriptionValue
match The match criteria for selecting which clients the subscription matches. If a client matches all of these criteria, the client matches the subscription.
A list of key-value pairs.
The valid keys are:
client_instance_id - client instance ID.
client_id  - client ID.
client_framework_id  - client framework ID.
client_framework_name  - client framework name.
client_framework_version  - client framework version.
client_software_name  - client software implementation name.
client_software_version  - client software implementation version.
client_source_address  - client connection's source address from the broker's point of view.
client_source_port  - client connection's source port from the broker's point of view.
The values are anchored regular expressions.
Metrics

Broker-added resources labels for client metrics

Label nameDescription
client_framework_idThe client's framework ID as reported in ApiVersionsRequest.
client_framework_nameThe client's framework name as reported in ApiVersionsRequest.
client_framework_versionThe client's framework version as reported in ApiVersionsRequest.
Tools

kafka-client-metrics.sh
The set of valid keys in the --match option is augmented by the addition of client_framework_id , client_framework_name  and client_framework_version .
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
No impact on existing users.

Motivation
KIP-247 adds support for testing a complete topology, but authors of Processor, Transformer, and ValueTransformer implementations can benefit from writing lighter and faster unit tests.
This isn't impossible today, but it requires writing some fairly complicated mock code for the ProcessorContext. We want to simplify this task by providing a general purpose ProcessorContext for unit testing.
Public Interface
java
Proposed Changes
We add the above new class to the kafka-streams-test-utils artifact (introduced in 1.1.0).
In the initial release, we mark our new class with annotation @Evolving.
All the methods annotated with @Override are implementing the ProcessorContext interface. 
We add new methods for the purposes of setting some properties (like topic, partition, etc.) that the processor may want to access.
We also capture data that the processor may put into the context, like k/v pairs in calls to forward(), but also state stores that get registered, punctuators that get scheduled, and whether commit() gets called.
We provide a mechanism to reset the commit and forwarded data captures to make it easy to make assertions about the behavior of the processor after various calls to Processor#process().
There is one method we plan not to implement:
void schedule(long interval): it's not possible to implement it without providing a handle on the processor to the context. This is a little tricky, since the mocked ProcessorContext may be used to test not just a Processor, but also a Transformer or a ValueTransformer. Since this method is deprecated in the interface, we feel it's reasonable to update client code to use Punctuators instead. This method will throw an UnsupportedOperationException.
Also note that we won't automatically trigger sheduled punctuators. Instead, we'll just capture them so test code can retrieve and trigger them if desired. This keeps the mock truly a "mock" and not a "driver", which maintains the simplicity of the code and enables users to write linear and sensible tests. …

[S1] EmailMessage by ? (2026-07-09)
Hi everyone,

I would like to start the discussion for KIP-1362: Add a
rollback-compatible storage format option for KRaft migration.

KIP:
https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/440303727/KIP-1362+Add+a+rollback-compatible+storage+format+option+for+KRaft+migration
Jira: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20762
PR/reference implementation: https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22751

In summary: this KIP proposes closing a current gap, where the ability to
do rollback of an ongoing KRaft migration breaks when cluster member nodes
are replaced. The proposed solution is to add a CLI flag to the storage
formatting tool that causes the resulting storage to not break when rolled
back.

I'm looking forward to feedback on this proposal.

Thanks,
Anton

Because of the way we want to use the archives later, we've configured our tooling to put up to 100,000 records in a single Avro file in the S3 bucket. While we were working on this, we experienced some connectivity issues to S3. Every time one of these connectivity failures occurred, the S3 client library would eventually throw a TimeoutException, the Connector task would die, and a rebalance would be triggered.
That rebalance would cause all other tasks to lose any forward progress they had made since their last commit and rewind. Because of the nature of our intermittent connection issues we would actually see this happen frequently enough to end up lagged by hundreds of millions of records.
To put it another way what we were seeing was something like:
Connect spins up with Tasks 1 thru 4
Task 1, 2, 3 each consume about 50,000 records. Task 4 consumes 100,000.
Task 4 decides to try and commit to S3, but starts timing out.
In the interim Task 1, 2, 3 each consume 10,000 more records.
Task 4 finally throws a TimeoutException from the S3 client and crashes
A rebalance triggers. Task 1, 2, and 3 are told to close and get no signal that they should attempt to commit what they have. They drop the records they have consumed.
The rebalance finishes and Task 1, 2, and 3 come back up in the same state they were in when the connector first spun up. At this point, they have to re-consume the records they already tried to consume.
Due to the connectivity issues this process repeated many, many times. Commits from some nodes would work fine, others wouldn't. But the nodes that were not having connectivity issues would still lose forward progress when the rebalance was triggered.
After some code analysis, we determined that there wasn't an existing API that a Connector could use to determine that the task was about to be shut down for a rebalance. <<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1369: API-Contract Annotations for Nullity/Thread Safety
Status
Current state: Draft
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20833
Motivation
Kafka's null-safety and thread-safety contracts live only in Javadoc, so nothing enforces them. A method that starts returning null, or a field read without its lock, compiles clean and breaks at runtime. Concurrency is also affected: Kafka is heavily threaded, and the lock-ownership reasoning behind many classes lives only in javadoc.
This proposal annotates Kafka's public API with existing contract annotations. A typed @Nullable or @GuardedBy("lock") beats a Javadoc sentence: it is uniform, greppable, shows in the IDE and generated docs, and tools read it without parsing prose. These concepts are already duplicated across the ecosystem, so rather than issue Kafka's own we can reuse the CLASS-retained SpotBugs and JSR-305 annotations, which the build's existing tools already recognise.
Public Interfaces
Kafka annotates its public API with existing annotations, added compileOnly via spotbugs-annotations (which also brings jsr305). All are @Retention(CLASS): read by build tooling and dropped by the JVM, so there is no runtime footprint. compileOnly keeps the jars out of the shadow jar and the published runtime dependencies.
Null-safety
edu.umd.cs.findbugs.annotations.@Nullable and @NonNull, applied where a value can be null:
java
These are SpotBugs' own annotations, so SpotBugs recognizes them directly, and IntelliJ, Kotlin, and NullAway recognize them too. They are CLASS-retained, so unlike javax.annotation.@Nullable (RUNTIME) they leave no dangling reference in shipped bytecode (JSpecify has this known limitation). For non-null-by-default a package may add @ReturnValuesAreNonnullByDefault or @DefaultAnnotation(NonNull.class) from the same jar.
Thread-safety
javax.annotation.concurrent.@GuardedBy, @Immutable, @ThreadSafe, @NotThreadSafe
java
@GuardedBy is in Error Prone's recognized set, so if Kafka ever adds Error Prone its GuardedBy checker verifies lock discipline with no upstream change.
Proposed Changes

Enforcement
SpotBugs (already in the check phase) recognizes the nullness annotations, so they are checked with no new setup. Flow-sensitive checks (a @Nullable dereferenced unchecked, or a @GuardedBy lock actually held) need Error Prone or the Checker Framework and are out of scope; both already recognize these annotations, so adopting them later needs no upstream change. -Werror is unaffected: the annotations add no javac warnings.
Checkstyle keeps the vocabulary consistent, with no new tooling. Each module's import-control.xml allows edu.umd.cs.findbugs.annotations and javax.annotation.concurrent, and disallows the rest of javax.annotation; most-specific-match means the concurrency package stays allowed while the RUNTIME-retained javax.annotation.@Nullable/@Nonnull are banned, so nullness always uses the CLASS-retained findbugs types.
Rollout
Pilot clients, package by package, starting with the consumer and producer public API. spotbugs-annotations is added compileOnly to clients (it is already compileOnly in several server-side modules). Generated generator classes wait until the generator emits annotations.
Set the non-null default per package with @DefaultAnnotation(NonNull.class) in package-info.java, rather than on individual classes, so a package opts in as a unit. Expect a cleanup pass: the default surfaces every field, return, and parameter that is actually nullable, each of which then gets an explicit @Nullable.
Compatibility
Additive and compile-time only: no runtime behavior, wire format, or signature changes. The annotations are CLASS-retained and their jars are compileOnly, so nothing reaches a consumer's runtime classpath or the shadow jar. jsr305 (pulled compileOnly via spotbugs-annotations) is Apache-2.0 and already resolves transitively in the build.
ScenarioBehavior
Existing Java consumerNo change; annotations are invisible at runtime.
Contributor in IntelliJNullness inspections fire; IntelliJ recognizes these annotations by default.
Kotlin consumerKotlin reads the CLASS-retained findbugs nullness annotations from the compiled bytecode and infers nullability
Scala consumerScala 2.13 does not read nullability annotations; no change.
Test Plan
SpotBugs flags a dereferenced @Nullable and a violated @NonNull
Checkstyle rejects an import of javax.annotation.Nullable and allows javax.annotation.concurrent
the annotations render in generated Javadoc
no spotbugs-annotations/jsr305 classes appear in the clients shadow jar or runtime classpath
clients consumer/producer public API compiles clean under -Werror once annotated
existing build and tests pass
Rejected Alternatives
Define Kafka-owned annotations. Custom @Nullable/@GuardedBy/etc. under org.apache.kafka.common.annotation (the KIP-1265 pattern) was considered. Rejected because these concepts are already duplicated across JSR-305, SpotBugs, the Checker Framework, and Error Prone; a Kafka set is one more duplicate that tools would not recognize without extra work (SpotBugs by name, Error Prone only via an upstream PR). Reusing the existing CLASS-retained annotations is less code and immediately recognized.
JSpecify. The modern nullness standard, but @Retention(RUNTIME): as compileOnly it leaves a dangling reference in shipped bytecode, and it covers nullness only, not thread-safety. The CLASS-retained findbugs annotations avoid the residue and pair with the javax.annotation.concurrent set.
javax.annotation.@Nullable for nullness. It matches the thread-safety package, but is @Retention(RUNTIME), so it leaves the dangling reference the CLASS-retained findbugs @Nullable avoids.
Do nothing. The status quo that left KAFKA-9234 open since 2019.
Relationship to Other KIPs
KIPRelationship
Created Kafka-owned annotations for API audience; this reuses existing annotations for API contracts, since nullness and concurrency are already standardized.

<<<TEXT
[S1] EmailMessage by SunMin Lee (2026-10-28)
Hi all,

I would like to start a discussion on KIP-1389:
https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/462815689/KIP-1389+Surface+effective+group+configurations+to+clients

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20848

With the consumer group protocol (KIP-848), share groups (KIP-932) and the
Streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071), settings such as the session timeout
are group configurations owned by the broker, and a stored group override can
be clamped to the broker's bounds (KIP-1240). Today the client cannot see the
values in effect, nor that an override was not applied.

This KIP adds an optional list of effective group configurations to the
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat, ShareGroupHeartbeat, StreamsGroupHeartbeat, ShareFetch
and ShareAcknowledge responses, each reported by the broker that applies the
configuration. The list is sent as tagged fields and only when its content
changes, using a content token echoed by the client. Clients log the values on
first receipt and on change, and warn when a stored override differs from the
value in effect. Client behavior does not change.

On the release: KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in 4.5. If this
KIP lands in the same release, I would like to add the fields to those
versions in coordination with KAFKA-20925. Andrew, I would appreciate your view
on whether that works.

Feedback is welcome.

Thanks,
Sunmin Lee
[S2] EmailMessage by David Jacot (2026-10-28)
Hi Sunmin,

Thanks for the KIP!

I agree with the fundamental issue that you describe in the KIP --
there is no way to see the effective value today because the
DescribeConfigs API returns the stored value -- but I disagree with
the proposed approach. Passing the configs to the clients via all
those APIs does not seem right to me. Each API should stay focused on
its main responsibility, and distributing configs is not the job of
the heartbeat or the share fetch APIs. The configs that they return
today, like the heartbeat interval, are there because the client uses
them. This approach also adds a lot of complexity, and I don't think
it is worth it just to log the values. Finally, it lets any member
read the group configs without the DESCRIBE_CONFIGS permission, which
is the one that controls this.

We should definitely look into whether we could improve the
DescribeConfigs API to return the effective values though. I am happy
to help on that front. If we really want to log them on the client, we
should just use the DescribeConfigs API to get them.

Another question is whether we really need to log all those configs on
the client side. I am not sure that I fully understand the benefit of
it. The group configs do not change that often and they are easily
accessible via the command line tool and the admin client. The
effective value also only differs from the stored one when an
administrator changes the broker bounds so that they exclude an
existing override, which is uncommon …

Hi David,

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

I agree with your points. Most of the list in this KIP is configuration

Hi Chia,
Thanks for taking another look. From what I understand, pruning has to wait
for the slowest group on the state partition to snapshot before it can
delete old records.

For ex: if groups A and B share a state partition:
- A snapshots frequently .. its latest snapshot is at offset 900.
- B has low traffic ... its latest snapshot is still at offset 100.

So the prune point is min(900, 100) which is 100, so only offsets 0–99 can
be deleted. Everything A writes after that stays on disk until B snapshots
again. So B's threshold is controlling the size than A's snapshots, whether
it's in bytes or a count.

I had moved the KIP to bytes after your earlier suggestion (chia_01), but I
agree the pruning behaviour makes bytes much less useful here than in a
buffering case like KIP-1325, where a byte limit directly bounds memory.

I think we had earlier calculations showed update records are a fairly
constant size, so a count gives nearly the same result.

I shall revise the KIP back to a count based approach and follow up here.

Thanks,
Murali

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1369: API-Contract Annotations for Nullity/Thread Safety
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1369: API-Contract Annotations for Nullity/Thread Safety
Status
Current state: Draft
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20833
Motivation
Kafka's null-safety and thread-safety contracts live only in Javadoc, so nothing enforces them. A method that starts returning null, or a field read without its lock, compiles clean and breaks at runtime. Concurrency is also affected: Kafka is heavily threaded, and the lock-ownership reasoning behind many classes lives only in javadoc.
This proposal annotates Kafka's public API with existing contract annotations. A typed @Nullable or @GuardedBy("lock") beats a Javadoc sentence: it is uniform, greppable, shows in the IDE and generated docs, and tools read it without parsing prose. These concepts are already duplicated across the ecosystem, so rather than issue Kafka's own we can reuse the CLASS-retained SpotBugs and JSR-305 annotations, which the build's existing tools already recognise.
Public Interfaces
Kafka annotates its public API with existing annotations, added compileOnly via spotbugs-annotations (which also brings jsr305). All are @Retention(CLASS): read by build tooling and dropped by the JVM, so there is no runtime footprint. compileOnly keeps the jars out of the shadow jar and the published runtime dependencies.
Null-safety
edu.umd.cs.findbugs.annotations.@Nullable and @NonNull, applied where a value can be null:
java
These are SpotBugs' own annotations, so SpotBugs recognizes them directly, and IntelliJ, Kotlin, and NullAway recognize them too. They are CLASS-retained, so unlike javax.annotation.@Nullable (RUNTIME) they leave no dangling reference in shipped bytecode (JSpecify has this known limitation). For non-null-by-default a package may add @ReturnValuesAreNonnullByDefault or @DefaultAnnotation(NonNull.class) from the same jar.
Thread-safety
javax.annotation.concurrent.@GuardedBy, @Immutable, @ThreadSafe, @NotThreadSafe
java
@GuardedBy is in Error Prone's recognized set, so if Kafka ever adds Error Prone its GuardedBy checker verifies lock discipline with no upstream change.
Proposed Changes

Enforcement
SpotBugs (already in the check phase) recognizes the nullness annotations, so they are checked with no new setup. Flow-sensitive checks (a @Nullable dereferenced unchecked, or a @GuardedBy lock actually held) need Error Prone or the Checker Framework and are out of scope; both already recognize these annotations, so adopting them later needs no upstream change. -Werror is unaffected: the annotations add no javac warnings.
Checkstyle keeps the vocabulary consistent, with no new tooling. Each module's import-control.xml allows edu.umd.cs.findbugs.annotations and javax.annotation.concurrent, and disallows the rest of javax.annotation; most-specific-match means the concurrency package stays allowed while the RUNTIME-retained javax.annotation.@Nullable/@Nonnull are banned, so nullness always uses the CLASS-retained findbugs types.
Rollout
Pilot clients, package by package, starting with the consumer and producer public API. spotbugs-annotations is added compileOnly to clients (it is already compileOnly in several server-side modules). Generated generator classes wait until the generator emits annotations.
Set the non-null default per package with @DefaultAnnotation(NonNull.class) in package-info.java, rather than on individual classes, so a package opts in as a unit. Expect a cleanup pass: the default surfaces every field, return, and parameter that is actually nullable, each of which then gets an explicit @Nullable.
Compatibility
Additive and compile-time only: no runtime behavior, wire format, or signature changes. The annotations are CLASS-retained and their jars are compileOnly, so nothing reaches a consumer's runtime classpath or the shadow jar. jsr305 (pulled compileOnly via spotbugs-annotations) is Apache-2.0 and already resolves transitively in the build.

Existing Java consumerNo change; annotations are invisible at runtime.

Scala consumerScala 2.13 does not read nullability annotations; no change.
Test Plan
SpotBugs flags a dereferenced @Nullable and a violated @NonNull
Checkstyle rejects an import of javax.annotation.Nullable and allows javax.annotation.concurrent
the annotations render in generated Javadoc
no spotbugs-annotations/jsr305 classes appear in the clients shadow jar or runtime classpath
clients consumer/producer public API compiles clean under -Werror once annotated
existing build and tests pass
Rejected Alternatives
Define Kafka-owned annotations. Custom @Nullable/@GuardedBy/etc. under org.apache.kafka.common.annotation (the KIP-1265 pattern) was considered. Rejected because these concepts are already duplicated across JSR-305, SpotBugs, the Checker Framework, and Error Prone; a Kafka set is one more duplicate that tools would not recognize without extra work (SpotBugs by name, Error Prone only via an upstream PR). Reusing the existing CLASS-retained annotations is less code and immediately recognized.
JSpecify. The modern nullness standard, but @Retention(RUNTIME): as compileOnly it leaves a dangling reference in shipped bytecode, and it covers nullness only, not thread-safety. The CLASS-retained findbugs annotations avoid the residue and pair with the javax.annotation.concurrent set.
javax.annotation.@Nullable for nullness. It matches the thread-safety package, but is @Retention(RUNTIME), so it leaves the dangling reference the CLASS-retained findbugs @Nullable avoids.
Do nothing. The status quo that left KAFKA-9234 open since 2019.
Relationship to Other KIPs

[S1] EmailMessage by SunMin Lee (2026-10-28)
Hi all,

I would like to start a discussion on KIP-1389:
https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/462815689/KIP-1389+Surface+effective+group+configurations+to+clients

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20848

With the consumer group protocol (KIP-848), share groups (KIP-932) and the
Streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071), settings such as the session timeout
are group configurations owned by the broker, and a stored group override can
be clamped to the broker's bounds (KIP-1240). Today the client cannot see the
values in effect, nor that an override was not applied.

This KIP adds an optional list of effective group configurations to the
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat, ShareGroupHeartbeat, StreamsGroupHeartbeat, ShareFetch
and ShareAcknowledge responses, each reported by the broker that applies the
configuration. The list is sent as tagged fields and only when its content
changes, using a content token echoed by the client. Clients log the values on
first receipt and on change, and warn when a stored override differs from the
value in effect. Client behavior does not change.

On the release: KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in 4.5. If this
KIP lands in the same release, I would like to add the fields to those
versions in coordination with KAFKA-20925. Andrew, I would appreciate your view
on whether that works.

Feedback is welcome.

Thanks,
Sunmin Lee
[S2] EmailMessage by David Jacot (2026-10-28)
Hi Sunmin,

Thanks for the KIP!

I agree with the fundamental issue that you describe in the KIP --
there is no way to see the effective value today because the
DescribeConfigs API returns the stored value -- but I disagree with
the proposed approach. Passing the configs to the clients via all
those APIs does not seem right to me. Each API should stay focused on
its main responsibility, and distributing configs is not the job of
the heartbeat or the share fetch APIs. The configs that they return
today, like the heartbeat interval, are there because the client uses
them. This approach also adds a lot of complexity, and I don't think
it is worth it just to log the values. Finally, it lets any member
read the group configs without the DESCRIBE_CONFIGS permission, which
is the one that controls this.

We should definitely look into whether we could improve the
DescribeConfigs API to return the effective values though. I am happy
to help on that front. If we really want to log them on the client, we
should just use the DescribeConfigs API to get them.

Another question is whether we really need to log all those configs on
the client side. I am not sure that I fully understand the benefit of
it. The group configs do not change that often and they are easily
accessible via the command line tool and the admin client. The
effective value also only differs from the stored one when an
administrator changes the broker bounds so that they exclude an
existing override, which is uncommon …

[S7] EmailMessage by ? (2026-10-08)
Hi Chia,
Thanks for taking another look. From what I understand, pruning has to wait
for the slowest group on the state partition to snapshot before it can
delete old records.

For ex: if groups A and B share a state partition:
- A snapshots frequently .. its latest snapshot is at offset 900.
- B has low traffic ... its latest snapshot is still at offset 100.

So the prune point is min(900, 100) which is 100, so only offsets 0–99 can
be deleted. Everything A writes after that stays on disk until B snapshots
again. So B's threshold is controlling the size than A's snapshots, whether
it's in bytes or a count.

I had moved the KIP to bytes after your earlier suggestion (chia_01), but I
agree the pruning behaviour makes bytes much less useful here than in a
buffering case like KIP-1325, where a byte limit directly bounds memory.

I think we had earlier calculations showed update records are a fairly
constant size, so a count gives nearly the same result.

I shall revise the KIP back to a count based approach and follow up here.

Thanks,
Murali
