[S1] Page: KIP-1370: Include Instance and Rack IDs in kafka-streams-groups.sh Member Output
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20888, ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20883
Motivation
KIP-1071 (https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=393677857) introduced Streams groups, the StreamsGroupDescribe API, and the  kafka-streams-groups.sh command-line tool.
The StreamsGroupDescribe response and the corresponding Admin API representation already expose the optional instance ID and rack ID of each Streams group member. However, kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --members does not currently display either field.
The instance ID identifies a static group member and remains stable when the member restarts. Displaying it is useful for mapping dynamically generated member IDs to application instances and for diagnosing static membership issues. The rack ID is primarily useful when investigating rack-aware task placement. Since it is optional and is generally needed only for detailed diagnostics, it should be included only in verbose member output.
This KIP proposes the following behavior:
The GROUP-INSTANCE-ID column will be displayed when --members is specified only if at least one group member has instance ID.
The rack ID is displayed only when --members and --verbose are specified together.
  This also makes verbose member output an additive extension of the regular member output: information available in the regular output, including the instance ID, is not omitted when verbose output is requested.
Public Interfaces
This KIP introduces no new command-line options and does not change any public Java API, network protocol, configuration, metric,  or persisted data format.
It changes the human-readable output of the existing kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --members command by adding member instance and rack information. Although console tool output is not considered a formal public interface under the Kafka KIP process, the output changes are documented in this KIP because they are user-visible and may affect scripts that parse the command output.
Proposed Changes
The member output of kafka-streams-groups.sh will expose the instance ID and rack ID already available in StreamsGroupMemberDescription.
CommandGROUP-INSTANCE-IDRACK-ID
--describe --membersIncludedNot included
--describe --members --verboseIncludedIncluded
The column order will change as follows:
CommandFromTo
--describe --members
(at least one group member has instance Id. non-empty string)
GROUP → MEMBER → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
GROUP → MEMBER → GROUP-INSTANCE-ID → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
--describe --members
GROUP → MEMBER → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
--describe --members --verbose
(at least one group member has instance Id. non-empty string)
GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 
MEMBER → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH → PROCESS →
CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 
MEMBER → GROUP-INSTANCE-ID → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH 
→ PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → RACK-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
--describe --members --verbose
GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 
MEMBER → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH → PROCESS 
→ CLIENT-ID → RACK-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
The instance ID will be displayed whenever --members is specified. The rack ID will only be displayed when --members and --verbose are specified together.
Instance IDs and rack IDs will be rendered as follows:
Source ValueConsole output
null or Optional.empty()-
Empty String ("")-
Non-empty stringThe value as reported
Although a null protocol value is converted to Optional.empty() by the Admin client, an empty string may be represented as a present optional value. The command will treat both cases as an unavailable value to avoid producing an empty table column. All other columns and their ordering will remain unchanged. The implementation will use the existing StreamsGroupMemberDescription#instanceId() and StreamsGroupMemberDescription#rackId() methods. No Admin API or protocol changes are required.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
This change does not affect the Admin API, network protocol, broker or client configurations, or persisted data formats. No broker or Kafka Streams client migration is required.
The only user-visible impact is the addition of columns to the human-readable member output:
--describe --members adds GROUP-INSTANCE-ID.
--describe --members --verbose adds GROUP-INSTANCE-ID and RACK-ID.
Users or scripts that rely on fixed column positions may need to update their parsing logic after upgrading the command-line tool. No deprecation period or special migration tool is required. The new output format will take effect when the updated kafka-streams-groups.sh is used; older versions of the tool will continue to produce the previous format. The previous output layout will not be retained as a separate mode.
Test Plan
The existing kafka-streams-groups.sh tests will be extended to verify that:
--describe --members includes GROUP-INSTANCE-ID only when at least one member has instance ID information, and does not include RACK-ID.
--describe --members --verbose includes GROUP-INSTANCE-ID under the same condition and includes RACK-ID.
GROUP-INSTANCE-ID is omitted when none of the group members has instance ID information.
Non-empty instance IDs and rack IDs match the corresponding Streams group member metadata.
Both null values, represented as Optional.empty(), and empty strings ("") are rendered as -. (If it is possible for empty strings)
Existing columns, assignments, and other describe modes remain unchanged.
The existing Streams group command test suite will continue to validate that listing, state, offsets, topology, and other member output behavior is not affected.
Integration tests will verify the command output with actual group metadata, while command-level unit tests will cover absent and empty-string values.
Rejected Alternatives

Include both IDs only in verbose output
This was rejected because the instance ID represents the stable identity of a static member and should be available in the regular member view.
Include the rack ID in non-verbose output
This was rejected because rack information is optional and primarily useful for detailed assignment diagnostics. Including it by default would unnecessarily widen the regular member output.

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1370: Include Instance and Rack IDs in kafka-streams-groups.sh Member Output
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1370: Include Instance and Rack IDs in kafka-streams-groups.sh Member Output
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20888, ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20883
Motivation
KIP-1071 (https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=393677857) introduced Streams groups, the StreamsGroupDescribe API, and the  kafka-streams-groups.sh command-line tool.
The StreamsGroupDescribe response and the corresponding Admin API representation already expose the optional instance ID and rack ID of each Streams group member. However, kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --members does not currently display either field.
The instance ID identifies a static group member and remains stable when the member restarts. Displaying it is useful for mapping dynamically generated member IDs to application instances and for diagnosing static membership issues. The rack ID is primarily useful when investigating rack-aware task placement. Since it is optional and is generally needed only for detailed diagnostics, it should be included only in verbose member output.
This KIP proposes the following behavior:
The GROUP-INSTANCE-ID column will be displayed when --members is specified only if at least one group member has instance ID.
The rack ID is displayed only when --members and --verbose are specified together.
  This also makes verbose member output an additive extension of the regular member output: information available in the regular output, including the instance ID, is not omitted when verbose output is requested.
Public Interfaces
This KIP introduces no new command-line options and does not change any public Java API, network protocol, configuration, metric,  or persisted data format.
It changes the human-readable output of the existing kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --members command by adding member instance and rack information. Although console tool output is not considered a formal public interface under the Kafka KIP process, the output changes are documented in this KIP because they are user-visible and may affect scripts that parse the command output.
Proposed Changes
The member output of kafka-streams-groups.sh will expose the instance ID and rack ID already available in StreamsGroupMemberDescription.
CommandGROUP-INSTANCE-IDRACK-ID
--describe --membersIncludedNot included
--describe --members --verboseIncludedIncluded
The column order will change as follows:
CommandFromTo
--describe --members
(at least one group member has instance Id. non-empty string)
GROUP → MEMBER → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
GROUP → MEMBER → GROUP-INSTANCE-ID → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
--describe --members
GROUP → MEMBER → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
--describe --members --verbose
(at least one group member has instance Id. non-empty string)
GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 
MEMBER → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH → PROCESS →
CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 
MEMBER → GROUP-INSTANCE-ID → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH 
→ PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → RACK-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
--describe --members --verbose
GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 
MEMBER → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH → PROCESS 
→ CLIENT-ID → RACK-ID → ASSIGNMENTS
The instance ID will be displayed whenever --members is specified. The rack ID will only be displayed when --members and --verbose are specified together.
Instance IDs and rack IDs will be rendered as follows:
Source ValueConsole output
null or Optional.empty()-
Empty String ("")-
Non-empty stringThe value as reported
Although a null protocol value is converted to Optional.empty() by the Admin client, an empty string may be represented as a present optional value. The command will treat both cases as an unavailable value to avoid producing an empty table column. All other columns and their ordering will remain unchanged. The implementation will use the existing StreamsGroupMemberDescription#instanceId() and StreamsGroupMemberDescription#rackId() methods. No Admin API or protocol changes are required.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
This change does not affect the Admin API, network protocol, broker or client configurations, or persisted data formats. No broker or Kafka Streams client migration is required.
The only user-visible impact is the addition of columns to the human-readable member output:
--describe --members adds GROUP-INSTANCE-ID.
--describe --members --verbose adds GROUP-INSTANCE-ID and RACK-ID.
Users or scripts that rely on fixed column positions may need to update their parsing logic after upgrading the command-line tool. No deprecation period or special migration tool is required. The new output format will take effect when the updated kafka-streams-groups.sh is used; older versions of the tool will continue to produce the previous format. The previous output layout will not be retained as a separate mode.
Test Plan
The existing kafka-streams-groups.sh tests will be extended to verify that:
--describe --members includes GROUP-INSTANCE-ID only when at least one member has instance ID information, and does not include RACK-ID.
--describe --members --verbose includes GROUP-INSTANCE-ID under the same condition and includes RACK-ID.
GROUP-INSTANCE-ID is omitted when none of the group members has instance ID information.
Non-empty instance IDs and rack IDs match the corresponding Streams group member metadata.
Both null values, represented as Optional.empty(), and empty strings ("") are rendered as -. (If it is possible for empty strings)
Existing columns, assignments, and other describe modes remain unchanged.
The existing Streams group command test suite will continue to validate that listing, state, offsets, topology, and other member output behavior is not affected.
Integration tests will verify the command output with actual group metadata, while command-level unit tests will cover absent and empty-string values.
Rejected Alternatives

Include both IDs only in verbose output

[S1] Page: Design notes
This document contains some rough design notes about how to support transactional acknowledgements for share groups.
Application programming interface
Prior to KIP-1289, applications chose how to acknowledge record delivery using the share.acknowledgement.mode consumer configuration. It seems to me that neither implicit  nor explicit  is really ideal. I propose that we introduce a third acknowledgement mode transactional . This gives a nice clean way to enforce correct API usage in the application.
Transactional acknowledgement mode has the following features:
Acknowledgements are explicit, meaning that every record received from poll(Duration)  must be acknowledged using ShareConsumer.acknowledge(...)  before the next call to poll(Duration) .
ShareConsumer.commitSync(...)  and ShareConsumer.commitAsync(...)  are not permitted. The acknowledgements are committed as part of a transaction so these specific methods are not appropriate.
ShareConsumer.setAcknowledgementCommitCallback(...)  is likewise not permitted. The acknowledgements will be completed once the transaction commits so the callback is not as useful as it is with asynchronous, non-transactional acknowledgements.
AcknowledgeMode.RENEW  is not permitted. It is incompatible with transactions.
The following code snippet shows how the application code might look.java

This document contains some rough design notes about how to support transactional acknowledgements for share groups.

Prior to KIP-1289, applications chose how to acknowledge record delivery using the share.acknowledgement.mode consumer configuration. massive lag spikes and abnormal latency. Messages are essentially "living"
inside this specific service for up to 2.5 minutes before being processed,

For Kafka Streams I recall that increasing the partitions (and therefore having sufficient clients and cluster resources) is the only real scalability knob?

And for Kafka Streams, windowing size and state store may impact scalability.

We tried Kafka Streams a few years internally for aggregating performance data and found resource usage too high and scalability poor, and resorted to custom Kafka clients. Motivation
Today Kafka Streams use a single-thread per task architecture to achieve embarrassing parallelism and good isolation. However there are a couple scenarios where async processing may be preferable:
1) External resource access or heavy IOs with high-latency. Suppose you need to access a remote REST api, read / write to an external store, or do a heavy disk IO operation that may result in high latency. Current threading model would block any other records before this record's done, waiting on the remote call / IO to finish.
2) Robust failure handling with retries. Imagine the app-level processing of a (non-corrupted) record fails (e.g. the user attempted to do a RPC to an external system, and this call failed), and failed records are moved into a separate "retry" topic. How can you process such failed records in a scalable way? For example, imagine you need to implement a retry policy such as "retry with exponential backoff". Here, you have the problem that 1. you can't really pause processing a single record because this will pause the processing of the full stream (bottleneck!) and 2. there is no straight-forward way to "sort" failed records based on their "next retry time" (think: priority queue).

One use case is delaying re-processing (e.g. "delay re-processing this event for 5 minutes") as mentioned in 2), another is for implementing a scheduler: e.g. do some additional operations later based on this processed record. based on Zalando Dublin, for example, are implementing a distributed web crawler. This is the proposal for entry into the Apache Incubator, formatted for the Incubator cwiki. Aegis is a working codename; a name search will be run and the ASF trademark process followed if the project is accepted. Proposal metadata

Proposal dateto be set at submission
SponsorApache Incubator PMC

Reference repositoryhttps://github.com/vaquarkhan/aegis-mcp-gateway (public, Apache-2.0)
LicenseApache License 2.0
Discussion listgeneral at incubator.apache.org
Abstract
Aegis MCP Governance Gateway is a vendor-neutral, secure-by-default Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway that puts one governed, auditable control plane in front of many Apache data and streaming engines, so an AI agent never talks to Flink, Kafka, Spark, or Iceberg directly. Every agent action passes one fail-closed governance chain: secure-by-default tool exposure, per-caller authentication and scope, a policy decision point, approval for destructive operations, egress and server-side request forgery defense, rate limiting, circuit breaking, prompt-injection screening, output bounding and redaction, tool-catalog integrity, and a tamper-evident hash-chained audit trail. Engines plug in through a small service provider interface and contribute only tool definitions and backend calls.
Proposal
We propose to develop, under Apache governance, a Layer 7 policy MCP gateway plus a family of engine adapters. A proxy forwards bytes and a router dispatches by capability, but neither is a trust boundary. A gateway is: it knows the tool, the principal, the budget, and the policy for every call, and it can deny, redact, gate, and record. The gateway core is stateless at the protocol edge so it can scale behind an ordinary load balancer once shared governance state is externalized. It aligns with OAuth 2.1 and OpenTelemetry today, and treats SPIFFE, SLSA, and the AI-governance frameworks (NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001) as alignment goals to reach as the roadmap items land, not as claims of current compliance. The initial contribution is a working Java reference implementation: a reusable gateway core, four in-depth engine adapters (Flink, Kafka, Spark, Iceberg), and a further set of thinner adapters for the wider Apache data platform. During incubation the priorities are community building, IP clearance, and promoting the roadmap items to full implementations.
Background
The Model Context Protocol has become a common way for AI agents to reach tools and data. As organizations connect agents to distributed Apache data estates, an agent that needs Flink, Kafka, Spark, and Iceberg must either drive each engine control plane directly or connect to a sprawl of independent, mostly read-only MCP servers, each with its own security posture, no shared audit, and no unified policy. An MCP server that can reach a control plane (a JobManager REST API, a Kafka AdminClient, a SQL gateway, an Iceberg catalog) is a privileged client. Shipping one safely is effectively shipping an access-control product: authentication, authorization, approval for destructive actions, redaction of secrets and personal data, rate and cost limits, and forensic audit. Many existing options lack these controls and carry single-maintainer sustainability risk. A single governed gateway, developed in the open under neutral governance, gives the ecosystem a shared standard for how agents operate Apache systems safely.
Rationale
A single governed gateway resolves the problems of the decentralized approach:
Security. One place enforces identity, authorization, approval, redaction, egress, and audit, instead of each server reimplementing or omitting them.
Maintainability. Adding an engine is a small adapter, not a new security model. There is one chain to review and harden, so the security review surface stays flat as engines are added.
Governance. One control plane for policy, budget, and provenance, with a stable deny taxonomy so operators can alert on codes such as POLICY_DENIED or APPROVAL_REQUIRED across every engine with one rule.
Doing this under Apache governance keeps it neutral across vendors and engines rather than leaving agent access to fragmented single-vendor servers.
Initial goals
Establish the project and practice the Apache Way: transparency, consensus, meritocracy, and community over code.
Complete IP clearance for the existing code and land it under Apache-2.0 with correct LICENSE and NOTICE files.
Publish and stabilize the adapter service provider interface so per-engine adapters are small, reviewable contributions.
Promote the roadmap items to full implementations: externalized high-availability state, CIMD and SPIFFE identity, a full Cedar runtime, vault-backed credential exchange, and an OpenTelemetry SDK bridge.
Produce the first Apache source releases and grow a diverse, multi-organization contributor base.
Current status
Aegis is a new codebase with a working multi-module reference implementation. The design, threat model, low-level design, and standards research are complete and public. The code builds green and is tested. A published design-conformance matrix maps every design claim to Done or Roadmap, so the maturity line is explicit.
Verified build and test state
36 Maven modules: a gateway core, adapters for 33 Apache engines (four in-depth today, Flink, Kafka, Spark, and Iceberg, and 29 thinner integrations covering Cassandra, HBase, Hive, Pulsar, Airflow, NiFi, Druid, Pinot, Doris, Impala, Calcite, Hudi, Paimon, Kudu, Ignite, BookKeeper, Ozone, Hadoop, ZooKeeper, Solr, Superset, Arrow Flight, Beam, Storm, Flume, ActiveMQ, CouchDB, Ranger, and Atlas), and a shaded runnable distribution. These are engine adapters the gateway supports, which is distinct from external adopters.
Builds with JDK 21 and runs on JDK 17 or newer with Maven 3.9 or newer.
347 unit and integration tests across all modules, all passing, zero failures and zero errors on a clean build.
Implemented in 0.1.0
The governance chain with ordered steps and first-denial-wins semantics.
Identity: shared bearer and a hashed multi-caller token file with per-caller scope, and an OAuth 2.1 resource-server mode with JWKS validation. Constant-time secret comparison and fail-closed startup validation.
Approvals: HMAC-SHA256 signed, TTL-bounded, single-use, tool-and-scope-bound tokens with replay rejection.
Policy: a builtin decision point, a live fail-closed OPA HTTP decision point, and a Cedar-style deny-file or HTTP delegate.
Per-caller outbound credential pass-through so a downstream engine can see a per-caller Authorization value when one was bound at admission.
Egress and server-side request forgery defense: allow list plus unconditional deny of cloud metadata and non-routable ranges, including numeric IP encodings and resolved addresses, with redirects disabled on outbound clients.
Rate limiting, circuit breaking, per-tool timeout, read-only SQL guard, identifier validation, output bounding, and data-loss-prevention redaction.
Tool-catalog integrity with durable pins and a fail-closed switch, a tamper-evident hash-chained audit, Prometheus metrics, and GenAI-shaped span log lines.
Two transports: stdio and authenticated Streamable HTTP with TLS, plus health, readiness, and metrics endpoints. A CycloneDX software bill of materials is produced at build time.
Deferred to the roadmap (honestly labeled, not sold as implemented)
A full Cedar policy runtime, and vault-backed or token-exchange credential resolution.
Externalized high-availability state (shared nonce, rate, and audit stores). Until then, run a single replica; multi-replica replay protection and rate limits require the shared store.
The MCP Tasks extension for long-running jobs, an OpenTelemetry SDK bridge, a full Merkle and signature-based reconciliation proof, and true semantic routing and caching.
These are tracked in the roadmap and the design-conformance matrix that ship with the code.
Community
The repository is public and is no longer a single-author project. As of this writing it has four contributors with merged code: the initial author plus three others, including PJ Fanning, an established contributor active across multiple Apache projects. There are merged pull requests from several external contributors and further open pull requests under review (adapter tests and an SPI extension), alongside forks and open issues. Governance oversight is forming: Greg Stein (Champion) and Larry McCay (mentor) join the initial author to form a PPMC of three, which already meets the …

In general, Kafka has a 1-year support window, so currently we are 
supporting 4.3, 4.2, and 4.1 release: 
https://kafka.apache.org/community/downloads/#supported-releases

With the upcoming 4.4.0 release, 4.1 will drop out of the support window.

So it's very unlikely that we would ship another 3.9.x bug-fix release. 
Given that 3.9 is the last release with ZK support, and upgrading to 4.x 
requires to migrate to KRaft, there is a possibility that we might 
maintain 3.9.x for a little longer than usual. However, officially 3.9 
is not supported any longer, and the 3.9 and 4.0 release got archived 
already: https://kafka.apache.org/community/downloads/#archived-releases

-Matthias

[S3] Comment by KAI-JAY TU (2026-07-23)
Hi, I'd like to take a crack at this one.

I spent some time tracing through the code and the production evidence in the ticket, and here's what I found:

What's going wrong:

StateUpdaterThread.run() only catches RuntimeException. When something like OutOfMemoryError hits (as the reporter confirmed), it blows straight through to the finally block. The thread logs "State updater thread stopped" and cleans up queues, but nobody ever completes or fails the pending CompletableFutures sitting in those queues.

On the other side, DefaultStateUpdater.remove() happily enqueues new work with a fresh CompletableFuture — it never checks whether the thread is actually alive. So when TaskManager.waitForFuture() calls future.get(5, MINUTES) on trunk (or the unbounded future.get() on 3.9.x), it's waiting on a future that will never complete.

Agreed with Guang's point — the trunk's 5-minute timeout mitigates the infinite hang, but the underlying issue (silent StateUpdater death, undetected by remove()/add()) still leads to the obscure IllegalStateException on task not found. The root cause is the same.

[S1] Page: KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: [DISCUSS] KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers
JIRA: KAFKA-20995
Release: TBD
Summary
The async consumer has repeatedly entered busy loops when a timer reaches zero while another state blocks the related work. The current numeric wait says when to poll again, but it cannot say whether time can make the work eligible or another event must occur first. Existing fixes replace the zero with another duration, which can make correctness depend on that duration's configuration.
This KIP introduces the internal ManagerPollCondition type with ready(), after(...), and idle(). Each request-manager poll() returns its outgoing requests and the condition for the next manager pass. The same manager decision can govern request admission and network scheduling. The network thread combines all manager conditions and applies the existing network-poll bounds. Public APIs, protocols, and thread topology remain unchanged. The internal per-manager RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long) method becomes applicationPollCondition(long); the application-facing ApplicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait() path remains unchanged.
Motivation
The async consumer has repeatedly entered a busy loop when a timer reaches zero while another state prevents the related work from continuing. The loop polls the same request managers, gets the same zero wait, and immediately starts again.
Today, each request manager returns outgoing requests and one numeric wait. The network thread uses the minimum:java
0 starts another iteration immediately, a finite value schedules a timed iteration, and Long.MAX_VALUE adds no earlier deadline.
The application wait follows the same numeric model. Each manager returns a duration from RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long). The network thread publishes the minimum as cachedMaximumTimeToWait, and the application thread uses it to limit its wait.
Evidence from existing busy-loop fixes
The following issues share the same pattern: work is blocked, but its timer still contributes zero.
EvidenceStatus as of 2026-09-21Affected waitWork blocked bySource of zeroLocal repair
PR #22836 — KAFKA-20253: Heartbeat CPU spin fix for Consumer protocolMergedNetwork scheduling for in-flight coordinator discovery; application wait for heartbeat and auto-commit.Coordinator discovery or heartbeat progress is waiting on coordinator/request state.An elapsed retry or heartbeat timer remains urgent while the related operation cannot advance.Withdraw the in-flight coordinator deadline; use heartbeat or auto-commit intervals on affected application-wait paths.
PR #23227 — KAFKA-20970: Another busy loop happens if auto.commit.interval.ms is less than bootstrap.resolve.timeout.ms MergedApplication waitAuto-commit is waiting for coordinator discovery during bootstrap DNS resolution.The auto-commit timer has expired, so the application wait remains zero.Use the auto-commit interval while the coordinator is unavailable; apply a similar heartbeat-interval guard to Streams.
PR #23348 — KAFKA-21010: Another busy loop happens if the member is in JOINING state and bootstrap DNS resolution is not finishedMergedApplication waitHeartbeat is waiting for coordinator discovery.The initial heartbeat interval is zero while the coordinator remains unknown.Replace zero-capable heartbeat and auto-commit interval substitutes with the retry backoff and refine terminal-state guards.
PR #23357 — KAFKA-21031: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expiredOpenNetwork scheduling and application waitA heartbeat response is still in flight.The expired heartbeat timer contributes zero even though another heartbeat cannot be sent.Use the configured retry backoff while the heartbeat request is in flight.
Why the current timeout substitutions are incomplete
The fixes repair their reported paths by replacing one zero wait with another duration. PR #22836 and PR #23227 used heartbeat or auto-commit intervals. PR #23348 later used retry backoff because the heartbeat interval starts at zero and auto-commit may be configured as zero. PR #23357 also uses the configured retry backoff while a heartbeat request is in flight.
This approach has three drawbacks:
Correctness becomes configuration-dependent. A setting intended to control retry timing also decides whether blocked work enters a busy loop; configuring the replacement timer as zero restores the zero-wait loop.
A positive delay only postpones the next poll. Some prerequisites change when an event arrives: a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout resolves an in-flight request, while discovery supplies an unavailable coordinator. If none of these events has occurred, the next poll finds the manager still blocked.
A duration does not explain why the manager should run again. When backoff expires, the manager may send a request. When a request is in flight, the same elapsed time changes nothing; the manager still needs a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout.
The fixes remain correct for their reported cases, but they do not define one rule for future request-manager states.
Public Interfaces
Public consumer classes, metrics, configuration, wire protocols, persisted data, and broker behavior remain unchanged. ManagerPollCondition and the changes to PollResult remain internal to org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.
Proposed Changes

1. Introduce ManagerPollCondition
This KIP introduces the following internal type for request-manager scheduling:java
The three factories describe when another manager pass can be useful:
FormMeaningWait returned by remainingMs(...)
ready()Another pass can perform work immediately.Zero
after(now, delayMs)Time can make another pass useful.Time remaining to the retained deadline
idle()This work has no local deadline.Long.MAX_VALUE
The implementation represents ready() and idle() as enum singletons:java
either(first, second) is ready when either input is ready and retains the earlier wait. Therefore, either(ready(), x) is ready(), either(idle(), x) is x, and two timed conditions retain the earlier deadline instance. The implementation may return that instance directly to avoid allocating a composite.
after(...) rejects negative delays and retains one saturating absolute deadline. Zero delay is valid.
isReady(...) authorizes only the action whose condition was checked. A combined condition may be ready because another action expired while request sending remains blocked.
idle() removes only the deadline for this work. Other manager work, independent deadlines, network completions, application events, cancellation, and shutdown can still start another pass. For example, an in-flight heartbeat includes an idle() send condition and its independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry through either(...).
2. A request manager selects and returns its next poll condition
For the condition returned in PollResult, a request manager first checks whether its work can proceed:text
For request sources using RequestState, one method supplies both request admission and network scheduling:java
A manager checks sendCondition(now).isReady(now) before creating a request. When no request is created, it returns that condition. After a send, onSendAttempt(...) changes the condition to idle() until a response or failure clears the in-flight state.
Each call to RequestManager.poll(now) answers two questions:
What requests did this manager create in this pass?
When can polling this manager again be useful?
PollResult carries both answers:java
The condition describes the manager state after producing the requests. For example, after a request is created and marked in flight, its next condition is normally idle() until the network response changes that state.
3. Apply the rule to current request managers
Manager stateReturned condition
A request is in flight.idle() for sending; keep independent operation expiry with either(...).
Retry backoff remains.after(now, remainingBackoffMs)
Local work can proceed now.ready()
Several requests have different deadlines.Combine their conditions with either(...).
Coordinator discovery, offset commit, topic metadata, and share acknowledgements use RequestState.sendCondition(...). Heartbeat managers use the same rule with their membership state, heartbeat interval, and independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry. Fetch, queued offset work, and membership transitions derive their condition from their existing pending future, queue, or local state.
Correctness still depends on each manager choosing the condition that matches its state. A wrong ready(), a missing prerequisite, or an expired operation left in the manager can still cause repeated immediate passes. Focused tests cover these state transitions.

<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: [DISCUSS] KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers
JIRA: KAFKA-20995
Release: TBD
Summary
The async consumer has repeatedly entered busy loops when a timer reaches zero while another state blocks the related work. The current numeric wait says when to poll again, but it cannot say whether time can make the work eligible or another event must occur first. Existing fixes replace the zero with another duration, which can make correctness depend on that duration's configuration.
This KIP introduces the internal ManagerPollCondition type with ready(), after(...), and idle(). Each request-manager poll() returns its outgoing requests and the condition for the next manager pass. The same manager decision can govern request admission and network scheduling. The network thread combines all manager conditions and applies the existing network-poll bounds. Public APIs, protocols, and thread topology remain unchanged. The internal per-manager RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long) method becomes applicationPollCondition(long); the application-facing ApplicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait() path remains unchanged.
Motivation
The async consumer has repeatedly entered a busy loop when a timer reaches zero while another state prevents the related work from continuing. The loop polls the same request managers, gets the same zero wait, and immediately starts again.
Today, each request manager returns outgoing requests and one numeric wait. The network thread uses the minimum:java
0 starts another iteration immediately, a finite value schedules a timed iteration, and Long.MAX_VALUE adds no earlier deadline.
The application wait follows the same numeric model. Each manager returns a duration from RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long). The network thread publishes the minimum as cachedMaximumTimeToWait, and the application thread uses it to limit its wait.
Evidence from existing busy-loop fixes
The following issues share the same pattern: work is blocked, but its timer still contributes zero.
EvidenceStatus as of 2026-09-21Affected waitWork blocked bySource of zeroLocal repair
PR #22836 — KAFKA-20253: Heartbeat CPU spin fix for Consumer protocolMergedNetwork scheduling for in-flight coordinator discovery; application wait for heartbeat and auto-commit.Coordinator discovery or heartbeat progress is waiting on coordinator/request state.An elapsed retry or heartbeat timer remains urgent while the related operation cannot advance.Withdraw the in-flight coordinator deadline; use heartbeat or auto-commit intervals on affected application-wait paths.
PR #23227 — KAFKA-20970: Another busy loop happens if auto.commit.interval.ms is less than bootstrap.resolve.timeout.ms MergedApplication waitAuto-commit is waiting for coordinator discovery during bootstrap DNS resolution.The auto-commit timer has expired, so the application wait remains zero.Use the auto-commit interval while the coordinator is unavailable; apply a similar heartbeat-interval guard to Streams.
PR #23348 — KAFKA-21010: Another busy loop happens if the member is in JOINING state and bootstrap DNS resolution is not finishedMergedApplication waitHeartbeat is waiting for coordinator discovery.The initial heartbeat interval is zero while the coordinator remains unknown.Replace zero-capable heartbeat and auto-commit interval substitutes with the retry backoff and refine terminal-state guards.
PR #23357 — KAFKA-21031: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expiredOpenNetwork scheduling and application waitA heartbeat response is still in flight.The expired heartbeat timer contributes zero even though another heartbeat cannot be sent.Use the configured retry backoff while the heartbeat request is in flight.
Why the current timeout substitutions are incomplete
The fixes repair their reported paths by replacing one zero wait with another duration. PR #22836 and PR #23227 used heartbeat or auto-commit intervals. PR #23348 later used retry backoff because the heartbeat interval starts at zero and auto-commit may be configured as zero. PR #23357 also uses the configured retry backoff while a heartbeat request is in flight.
This approach has three drawbacks:
Correctness becomes configuration-dependent. A setting intended to control retry timing also decides whether blocked work enters a busy loop; configuring the replacement timer as zero restores the zero-wait loop.
A positive delay only postpones the next poll. Some prerequisites change when an event arrives: a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout resolves an in-flight request, while discovery supplies an unavailable coordinator. If none of these events has occurred, the next poll finds the manager still blocked.
A duration does not explain why the manager should run again. When backoff expires, the manager may send a request. When a request is in flight, the same elapsed time changes nothing; the manager still needs a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout.
The fixes remain correct for their reported cases, but they do not define one rule for future request-manager states.
Public Interfaces
Public consumer classes, metrics, configuration, wire protocols, persisted data, and broker behavior remain unchanged. ManagerPollCondition and the changes to PollResult remain internal to org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.
Proposed Changes

1. Introduce ManagerPollCondition
This KIP introduces the following internal type for request-manager scheduling:java
The three factories describe when another manager pass can be useful:
FormMeaningWait returned by remainingMs(...)
ready()Another pass can perform work immediately.Zero
after(now, delayMs)Time can make another pass useful.Time remaining to the retained deadline
idle()This work has no local deadline.Long.MAX_VALUE
The implementation represents ready() and idle() as enum singletons:java
either(first, second) is ready when either input is ready and retains the earlier wait. Therefore, either(ready(), x) is ready(), either(idle(), x) is x, and two timed conditions retain the earlier deadline instance. The implementation may return that instance directly to avoid allocating a composite.
after(...) rejects negative delays and retains one saturating absolute deadline. Zero delay is valid.
isReady(...) authorizes only the action whose condition was checked. A combined condition may be ready because another action expired while request sending remains blocked.
idle() removes only the deadline for this work. Other manager work, independent deadlines, network completions, application events, cancellation, and shutdown can still start another pass. For example, an in-flight heartbeat includes an idle() send condition and its independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry through either(...).
2. A request manager selects and returns its next poll condition
For the condition returned in PollResult, a request manager first checks whether its work can proceed:text
For request sources using RequestState, one method supplies both request admission and network scheduling:java
A manager checks sendCondition(now).isReady(now) before creating a request. When no request is created, it returns that condition. After a send, onSendAttempt(...) changes the condition to idle() until a response or failure clears the in-flight state.
Each call to RequestManager.poll(now) answers two questions:
What requests did this manager create in this pass?
When can polling this manager again be useful?
PollResult carries both answers:java
The condition describes the manager state after producing the requests. For example, after a request is created and marked in flight, its next condition is normally idle() until the network response changes that state.
3. Apply the rule to current request managers
Manager stateReturned condition
A request is in flight.idle() for sending; keep independent operation expiry with either(...).
Retry backoff remains.after(now, remainingBackoffMs)
Local work can proceed now.ready()
Several requests have different deadlines.Combine their conditions with either(...).
Coordinator discovery, offset commit, topic metadata, and share acknowledgements use RequestState.sendCondition(...). Heartbeat managers use the same rule with their membership state, heartbeat interval, and independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry. Fetch, queued offset work, and membership transitions derive their condition from their existing pending future, queue, or local state.
Correctness still depends on each manager choosing the condition that matches its state. A wrong ready(), a missing prerequisite, or an expired operation left in the manager can still cause repeated immediate passes. Focused tests cover these state transitions.

<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1372: Reject topic configurations where min.insync.replicas exceeds the replication factor
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here [Change the link from the KIP proposal email archive to your own email thread]
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka currently accepts any min.insync.replicas value of 1 or more, with no relation to the replication factor of the topics it applies to. A topic can be created with --replication-factor 1 --config min.insync.replicas=2 and the request succeeds, even though the configuration is contradictory: the topic can never have enough in-sync replicas to satisfy the configured minimum.
This misconfiguration is not hypothetical. It has been reported since 2017 (KAFKA-4680), where producing with acks=all to such a topic fails with the retriable NotEnoughReplicasException (retries that can never succeed), and the resulting error-log flood filled a broker's disk in a production cluster. Replication tooling that creates topics on a destination cluster whose default min.insync.replicas exceeds the source topic's replication factor hits the same trap, and the failure surfaces far from its cause.
KIP-966 (Eligible Leader Replicas) has already settled the semantic question: the effective minimum ISR of a partition is defined as min(min.insync.replicas, replication factor), and both the controller and the broker silently clamp to that value (ReplicationControlManager#getTopicEffectiveMinIsr, Partition#effectiveMinIsr). In other words, a min.insync.replicas above the replication factor already has no effect: the configured value is simply ignored beyond the clamp. Accepting a value the cluster will never honor is a silent footgun: the user believes they have configured a durability guarantee that does not exist.
This KIP proposes to reject such configurations at the API boundary, where the mistake is made: topic creation and topic-level configuration changes.
Public Interfaces
No new configurations, request/response schema fields, error codes, or APIs are introduced. The change is new validation behavior on two existing request types, using the existing INVALID_CONFIG (40) error code:
APIScenarioCurrent behaviorProposed behavior
CreateTopicsThe topic's resolved replication factor is lower than its effective min.insync.replicasTopic is created; the configured min ISR is silently clamped to the replication factorRequest fails with INVALID_CONFIG
IncrementalAlterConfigs / AlterConfigs (TOPIC resource)min.insync.replicas is set to a value higher than the topic's replication factorChange is accepted and silently clampedRequest fails with INVALID_CONFIG
CreatePartitions, AlterPartitionReassignments, broker-, cluster-, and controller-level configuration changesn/an/aUnchanged (see Proposed Changes for rationale)
For CreateTopics, the resolved replication factor is the request's value, the size of the manual replica assignment if one is given, or the cluster default (default.replication.factor) when the request passes -1. The effective min.insync.replicas is the value that would govern the new topic: the topic-level override in the request if present, otherwise the cluster-level dynamic default, otherwise the static broker/controller configuration.
Example error messages:
Proposed Changes

Validation at topic creation
In the KRaft controller (ReplicationControlManager#createTopic), after the replication factor has been resolved (from the request, the manual assignment, or the cluster default) and before any records are generated, the controller computes the effective min.insync.replicas for the new topic and rejects the creation with INVALID_CONFIG if it exceeds the replication factor.
The check must live here rather than in the existing topic-config validation path (ControllerConfigurationValidator / LogConfig.validate), because that path runs before the replication factor is resolved and receives only the topic name; the replication factor is structurally unavailable to it.
Internal topics (__consumer_offsets, __transaction_state, the share-group and remote-log-metadata state topics) are created through the same path and are validated identically. A rejection there can only occur when the broker's own settings are contradictory (e.g. offsets.topic.replication.factor below the cluster's min.insync.replicas); failing the creation with a clear message surfaces that operator misconfiguration instead of leaving an internal topic that cannot accept acks=all writes. Internal topic creation is retried by brokers, so fixing the configuration heals the cluster without manual intervention.
Validation at topic-level configuration changes
In the controller's configuration handling (ConfigurationControlManager, alongside the ELR-related min.insync.replicas checks introduced by KIP-966), a SET or legacy-alter of min.insync.replicas on a TOPIC resource is rejected with INVALID_CONFIG when the new value exceeds the topic's current replication factor. Both IncrementalAlterConfigs and the deprecated AlterConfigs funnel through the same validation and are covered.
A DELETE of a topic-level min.insync.replicas override remains allowed, even when the topic then falls back to a cluster-level or static default that exceeds its replication factor. The fallback value is not chosen by the caller, and rejecting the delete would prevent returning a topic to defaults; a topic in that state is governed by the effective min ISR clamp, like other grandfathered configurations. (APPEND and SUBTRACT do not arise, since min.insync.replicas is not a list-type config.)
What is deliberately not validated
Existing topics are grandfathered. No existing topic is touched, invalidated, or mutated by this KIP. Topics that already carry min.insync.replicas above their replication factor continue to work exactly as today, governed by the KIP-966 clamp. Only new requests that would create or change into a contradictory state are rejected.
Deletes of topic-level min.insync.replicas overrides, which fall back to a default that may exceed the replication factor. See "Validation at topic-level configuration changes" above for the rationale.
Cluster-level min.insync.replicas changes. Raising the cluster-wide default may put existing low-replication topics above the threshold, but validating it would require scanning every topic on the controller and would block a legitimate operation (hardening the default for future topics). Existing topics remain protected by the clamp; the recommended operator workflow is unchanged.
Partition reassignments that lower the replication factor below a topic's min.insync.replicas. Reassignment is an operator-driven surface with its own safeguard (allowReplicationFactorChange, KIP-860), and the clamp keeps the partition writable throughout. Extending validation there can be a follow-up if the community wants it.
Upgrade behavior
The validation is request-time logic on the active controller and requires no new metadata records, so it is not gated on a metadata version or feature flag. In a cluster with mixed controller versions during a rolling upgrade, enforcement begins when an upgraded controller becomes active.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
This is a backward-incompatible behavior change by design: requests that previously succeeded (and produced a configuration the cluster silently ignores) will now fail. We believe the break is acceptable because:
The rejected configurations have no effect today: since KIP-966 the effective min ISR is clamped to the replication factor, no working setup can depend on the accepted-but-ignored value.
The failure is immediate, at the API call that introduces the contradiction, with a message naming both values, as opposed to today's failure modes (producer retry storms, silent clamping) that surface later and elsewhere.
There is precedent for tightening configuration constraints in a major/minor release when the old values were harmful (e.g. KIP-1030).
One workflow requires reordering: increasing durability on an existing topic by setting min.insync.replicas above the current replication factor before adding replicas. After this KIP, the replication factor must be increased first (via reassignment), then min.insync.replicas. Topic-creation workflows are unaffected as long as the requested configuration is self-consistent.
Known deployment patterns affected:
Kafka Connect accepts topic-level settings for its internal topics (for example config.storage.min.insync.replicas together with config.storage.replication.factor=-1 to use the broker default; likewise for the offset and status topics, and for source-connector auto-created topics via topic.creation.<alias>.*). Where the resulting min.insync.replicas exceeds the resolved replication factor, internal-topic creation now fails at worker startup with an explicit error, instead of silently creating a topic with a weaker guarantee than the one requested. <<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1372: Reject topic configurations where min.insync.replicas exceeds the replication factor
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here [Change the link from the KIP proposal email archive to your own email thread]
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka currently accepts any min.insync.replicas value of 1 or more, with no relation to the replication factor of the topics it applies to. A topic can be created with --replication-factor 1 --config min.insync.replicas=2 and the request succeeds, even though the configuration is contradictory: the topic can never have enough in-sync replicas to satisfy the configured minimum.
This misconfiguration is not hypothetical. It has been reported since 2017 (KAFKA-4680), where producing with acks=all to such a topic fails with the retriable NotEnoughReplicasException (retries that can never succeed), and the resulting error-log flood filled a broker's disk in a production cluster. Replication tooling that creates topics on a destination cluster whose default min.insync.replicas exceeds the source topic's replication factor hits the same trap, and the failure surfaces far from its cause.
KIP-966 (Eligible Leader Replicas) has already settled the semantic question: the effective minimum ISR of a partition is defined as min(min.insync.replicas, replication factor), and both the controller and the broker silently clamp to that value (ReplicationControlManager#getTopicEffectiveMinIsr, Partition#effectiveMinIsr). In other words, a min.insync.replicas above the replication factor already has no effect: the configured value is simply ignored beyond the clamp. Accepting a value the cluster will never honor is a silent footgun: the user believes they have configured a durability guarantee that does not exist.
This KIP proposes to reject such configurations at the API boundary, where the mistake is made: topic creation and topic-level configuration changes.
Public Interfaces
No new configurations, request/response schema fields, error codes, or APIs are introduced. The change is new validation behavior on two existing request types, using the existing INVALID_CONFIG (40) error code:
APIScenarioCurrent behaviorProposed behavior
CreateTopicsThe topic's resolved replication factor is lower than its effective min.insync.replicasTopic is created; the configured min ISR is silently clamped to the replication factorRequest fails with INVALID_CONFIG
IncrementalAlterConfigs / AlterConfigs (TOPIC resource)min.insync.replicas is set to a value higher than the topic's replication factorChange is accepted and silently clampedRequest fails with INVALID_CONFIG
CreatePartitions, AlterPartitionReassignments, broker-, cluster-, and controller-level configuration changesn/an/aUnchanged (see Proposed Changes for rationale)
For CreateTopics, the resolved replication factor is the request's value, the size of the manual replica assignment if one is given, or the cluster default (default.replication.factor) when the request passes -1. The effective min.insync.replicas is the value that would govern the new topic: the topic-level override in the request if present, otherwise the cluster-level dynamic default, otherwise the static broker/controller configuration.
Example error messages:
Proposed Changes

Validation at topic creation
In the KRaft controller (ReplicationControlManager#createTopic), after the replication factor has been resolved (from the request, the manual assignment, or the cluster default) and before any records are generated, the controller computes the effective min.insync.replicas for the new topic and rejects the creation with INVALID_CONFIG if it exceeds the replication factor.
The check must live here rather than in the existing topic-config validation path (ControllerConfigurationValidator / LogConfig.validate), because that path runs before the replication factor is resolved and receives only the topic name; the replication factor is structurally unavailable to it.
Internal topics (__consumer_offsets, __transaction_state, the share-group and remote-log-metadata state topics) are created through the same path and are validated identically. A rejection there can only occur when the broker's own settings are contradictory (e.g. offsets.topic.replication.factor below the cluster's min.insync.replicas); failing the creation with a clear message surfaces that operator misconfiguration instead of leaving an internal topic that cannot accept acks=all writes. Internal topic creation is retried by brokers, so fixing the configuration heals the cluster without manual intervention.
Validation at topic-level configuration changes
In the controller's configuration handling (ConfigurationControlManager, alongside the ELR-related min.insync.replicas checks introduced by KIP-966), a SET or legacy-alter of min.insync.replicas on a TOPIC resource is rejected with INVALID_CONFIG when the new value exceeds the topic's current replication factor. Both IncrementalAlterConfigs and the deprecated AlterConfigs funnel through the same validation and are covered.
A DELETE of a topic-level min.insync.replicas override remains allowed, even when the topic then falls back to a cluster-level or static default that exceeds its replication factor. The fallback value is not chosen by the caller, and rejecting the delete would prevent returning a topic to defaults; a topic in that state is governed by the effective min ISR clamp, like other grandfathered configurations. (APPEND and SUBTRACT do not arise, since min.insync.replicas is not a list-type config.)
What is deliberately not validated
Existing topics are grandfathered. No existing topic is touched, invalidated, or mutated by this KIP. Topics that already carry min.insync.replicas above their replication factor continue to work exactly as today, governed by the KIP-966 clamp. Only new requests that would create or change into a contradictory state are rejected.
Deletes of topic-level min.insync.replicas overrides, which fall back to a default that may exceed the replication factor. See "Validation at topic-level configuration changes" above for the rationale.
Cluster-level min.insync.replicas changes. Raising the cluster-wide default may put existing low-replication topics above the threshold, but validating it would require scanning every topic on the controller and would block a legitimate operation (hardening the default for future topics). Existing topics remain protected by the clamp; the recommended operator workflow is unchanged.
Partition reassignments that lower the replication factor below a topic's min.insync.replicas. Reassignment is an operator-driven surface with its own safeguard (allowReplicationFactorChange, KIP-860), and the clamp keeps the partition writable throughout. Extending validation there can be a follow-up if the community wants it.
Upgrade behavior
The validation is request-time logic on the active controller and requires no new metadata records, so it is not gated on a metadata version or feature flag. In a cluster with mixed controller versions during a rolling upgrade, enforcement begins when an upgraded controller becomes active.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
This is a backward-incompatible behavior change by design: requests that previously succeeded (and produced a configuration the cluster silently ignores) will now fail. We believe the break is acceptable because:
The rejected configurations have no effect today: since KIP-966 the effective min ISR is clamped to the replication factor, no working setup can depend on the accepted-but-ignored value.
The failure is immediate, at the API call that introduces the contradiction, with a message naming both values, as opposed to today's failure modes (producer retry storms, silent clamping) that surface later and elsewhere.
There is precedent for tightening configuration constraints in a major/minor release when the old values were harmful (e.g. KIP-1030).
One workflow requires reordering: increasing durability on an existing topic by setting min.insync.replicas above the current replication factor before adding replicas. After this KIP, the replication factor must be increased first (via reassignment), then min.insync.replicas. Topic-creation workflows are unaffected as long as the requested configuration is self-consistent.
Known deployment patterns affected:
Kafka Connect accepts topic-level settings for its internal topics (for example config.storage.min.insync.replicas together with config.storage.replication.factor=-1 to use the broker default; likewise for the offset and status topics, and for source-connector auto-created topics via topic.creation.<alias>.*). Where the resulting min.insync.replicas exceeds the resolved replication factor, internal-topic creation now fails at worker startup with an explicit error, instead of silently creating a topic with a weaker guarantee than the one requested. [S3] EmailMessage by Gaurav Narula (2026-07-18)
Hi Matthias,

Thank you for your reply.

Consider a scenario where a KIP author wants to propose a change which involves
new Request/Response types and a new Metadata Record type. As you rightly
mentioned, the author doesn't need to pick specific values in the KIP but if
they are to prototype their work in their fork they do need to pick one.

This is where the prototyper has to make a careful choice. If they pick the next
available apiKey, they run the risk of running into issues when the value they
picked is claimed by another implementation that's merged first upstream,
specially when the prototype is deployed. Even if they bump the apiKey after a
rebase, safely rolling out changes in such a scenario would be hard as existing
brokers/controllers would have a different mapping for the apiKeys compared to
the new ones.

A workaround for this is selecting a high enough apiKey value that is unlikely
to be used in the foreseeable future. My proposal formalises that to reserve
some values for private use. This also ensures that future KIPs that propose any
changes to how apiKeys are used take that into account.

Regards,
Gaurav

Hi Matthias,

Thank you for your reply.

Consider a scenario where a KIP author wants to propose a change which involves
new Request/Response types and a new Metadata Record type. As you rightly
mentioned, the author doesn't need to pick specific values in the KIP but if
they are to prototype their work in their fork they do need to pick one.

This is where the prototyper has to make a careful choice. If they pick the next
available apiKey, they run the risk of running into issues when the value they
picked is claimed by another implementation that's merged first upstream,
specially when the prototype is deployed. Even if they bump the apiKey after a
rebase, safely rolling out changes in such a scenario would be hard as existing
brokers/controllers would have a different mapping for the apiKeys compared to
the new ones.

A workaround for this is selecting a high enough apiKey value that is unlikely
to be used in the foreseeable future. My proposal formalises that to reserve
some values for private use. This also ensures that future KIPs that propose any
changes to how apiKeys are used take that into account.

QUESTION: What status does this page give the proposal 'KIP-335: Consider configurations for KafkaStreams'?
ACCEPT ONLY IF: the page states the status (a 'Current state' line, a vote result, 'accepted', 'adopted', 'under discussion', 'superseded by' ...). If the page says rejected, discarded, withdrawn or dormant, or says nothing, reject: the schema has no value for those.

<<<TEXT
SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-335: Consider configurations for KafkaStreams
Status
Current state: Discarded
Discussion thread:  here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Eversince KIP-266 was concluded, several new versions of KafkaConsumer's methods has been introduced. Meanwhile, older versions has been deprecated in favor of these newer methods which allows us to control how much time each individual method blocks. Therefore, there has been a pressing need to migrate Kafka Streams from these old API to newer ones. It has also been noted that some of the older methods which Kafka Streams call blocks infinitely, migrating Kafka Streams will help solve that issue.
Public Interfaces
Currently, there are a couple of options that are available to us:
A couple of old configurations were related with blocking in Streams: RETRIES_CONFIG and RETRY_BACKOFF_MS_CONFIG. However, it has been noted that the application of these two configs has been relatively restricted, mainly being used in global consumer's methods (per current design).  We might remove these configs in favor of a larger timeout.
Another concern is the introduction of another config for blocking. We might use a global configuration (similar to request.timeout.ms) or allow a user-specified timeout which is passed in via methods (the latter option was favored over the former in KIP-266).
Proposed Changes
We will change the KafkaConsumer methods used in Kafka Streams to the newer methods created in KIP-266.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The older methods will be deprecated in favor of the newer ones found in Kafka Streams if  the user-specified timeout approach is found to be more applicable to this KIP.
Rejected Alternatives
If there are alternative ways of accomplishing the same thing, what were they? The purpose of this section is to motivate why the design is the way it is and not some other way.
TEXT>>>

Reply with one JSON object: {"verdict": "accept" or "reject", "choice": one of the values proposed, accepted, superseded, reversed, reinstated, disputed or "none", "quote": "...", "cue": "...", "reason": "..."}
- accept: the text settles the question; choice is that answer.
- reject: nothing fits, or the text does not settle it; choice is "none".
- quote: copy word for word the shortest passage (under 200 characters) of the text that shows the answer. Empty when you reject.
- cue: the writing habit that gave it away, as a general pattern a parser could look for (e.g. 'Fixed in <branch> at <sha>', 'ticket key in the branch name'). Empty when you reject.
- reason: one short sentence.

response.reason: The page explicitly states the proposal's status as 'Discarded', which does not meet the acceptance criteria.

CONVERSATION: Ticket KAFKA-20848: Consider to surface group-level misconfigurations client side
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by 이선민 (2026-10-22)
[^analyze.py]  [^run.sh]  [^summary.txt] [~mjsax] [~chia7712] I reproduced the situation this ticket describes, and wanted to check how it relates to KAFKA-20835 before going further.

On trunk (a3444d8b32, single KRaft node), I set consumer.session.timeout.ms=60000 and consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms=12000 on a consumer group, then restarted the broker with group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms=30000 and group.consumer.max.heartbeat.interval.ms=6000:

* At startup, the broker logs a WARN that both values are capped, to 30000 and 6000.
* kafka-configs.sh --describe still returns 60000 and 12000. The describe path builds the GroupConfig from the stored overrides, without the evaluation step that caps them.
* The consumer logs the heartbeat interval it receives (6000ms), but nothing indicates that a value was capped, and the session timeout is not sent to the client.
* After I killed the consumer, the member was fenced 30.0s after the broker processed its last heartbeat, so 30000 is the value in effect.

In this reproduction, the broker log shows the effective session timeout, while the client does not receive it and describe still reports the stored value. The reproduction script, analysis script, and result summary are attached.

KAFKA-20835 discusses adding a warning to the alter-config response when a stored value differs from the effective one, with a KIP planned. This ticket covers the same mismatch from the client side, through the heartbeat response, and the …
[S2] Comment by Matthias J. Sax (2026-10-22)
Thanks [~sunm2n] – I think both are related but independent. This ticket is about logging relevant config client side, while Kafka-20835 is a problem on the broker, and both ticket would update different RPCs, so I think it's better to do two KIPs? Feel free to pick it up either one.

Not 100% sure about the issue with kafka-configs.sh, but again, it might be another related but independent bug. In doubt, it's related to KAFKA-20848, but not this ticket.

The fact that a client is not updated w/o a client restart is interesting, but make sense to me. From my understanding, it would be more complex to allow the client to auto-update. \cc [~dajac] [~lianetm] – I believe, if we would want to support client auto-update, we should track it with it's own ticket, and it might also require a KIP.
[S3] Comment by 이선민 (2026-10-26)
Thanks [~mjsax]. That makes sense, so I'll keep them as two KIPs and pick up this one.

The scope I have in mind for this KIP:
* The consumer, share, and streams group heartbeat responses carry the effective values of the group configs that are relevant to the client, and the client logs them when it first receives them and whenever they change.
* When a stored group config is clamped to the broker bounds, the response indicates it, so the client can log a warning with both the configured and the effective value.

Out of scope: the describe output, the alter-config validation (KAFKA-20835), and updating client behavior automatically. If it's useful, I can file a separate ticket for the describe output.

I'll share the KIP on the dev list once the draft is ready.
[S4] Comment by 이선민 (2026-10-28)
I have written KIP-1389 for this issue:
https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/462815689/KIP-1389+Surface+effective+group+configurations+to+clients

Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/gctkxrg2y664jt4sq18znrgl0omd93tp
