CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1373: Client Quota Utilization Metrics
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1373: Client Quota Utilization Metrics
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Brokers already expose per-client quota usage byte-rate , request-time  and throttle time throttle-time . They do not expose how that usage compares to the effective quota applied to the same quota sensor.
That join is left to operators: scrape the rate, then independently resolve user, client-id, and default overrides (or a custom ClientQuotaCallback)  from a different path. Limits can differ by orders of magnitude and can change dynamically, so absolute-rate alerts do not transfer across clients.
throttle-time  only changes after throttling has occurred. Operators need a normalized rate signal that identifies clients whose recent usage is approaching or exceeding the quota actually applied on that broker, without requiring the monitoring stack to resolve the quota independently.
KIP-1257: Partition Size Percentage Metrics for Storage Monitoring established the precedent of shipping a normalized percentage from Kafka rather than requiring operators to compute it externally. The analogy is only partial: retention.bytes  is a topic configuration, while client quotas are resolved per quota entity through the existing quota hierarchy and optional callbacks. This KIP preserves the existing quota-resolution and enforcement behavior.
Proposed Changes
Add quota-utilization as an additional attribute on the existing client-quota MBeans. No new MBean type, ObjectName, sensor, or quota entity is introduced.   
existingnew
byte-rate | request-time ,  throttle-timequota-utilization
Definition
quota-utilization is the recent quota-measured rate expressed as a percentage of the effective quota applied to the same quota sensor.calculation
Measured rate is the value of the existing quota rate metric on that sensor (byte-rate or request-time).
Effective quota is the quota currently associated with that rate metric's MetricConfig, after callback resolution and default/override resolution, and is the same bound used for enforcement on that sensor.
The metric is a rate-utilization signal. It is not a representation of throttle state or of remaining headroom before the next request is delayed.
Value and meaning
Less than 100: recent rate is below the effective quota.
Equal to 100: recent rate equals the effective quota.
Greater than 100: recent rate exceeds the effective quota; not capped.
throttle-time: actual throttling that already occurred.
The result is always a percentage of the applicable quota, regardless of the physical unit of the numerator.
Quotanumeratordenominator
Producebyte-rate (bytes/sec)producer_byte_rate
Fetchbyte-rate (bytes/sec)consumer_byte_rate
Requestrequest-timerequest_percentage
Request units are the easiest to misread. request-time is already a percentage of broker network and I/O thread time, and request_percentage caps that quantity. Utilization is a percentage of that cap, not request-time / 100. Exempt request time is not included in the numerator.
Examples
QuotaInputQuota-utilization
Producebyte-rate = 800 KiB/s, producer_byte_rate = 1 MiB/s80
Requestrequest-time = 40, request_percentage = 5080 (40 percent of the pool, 80 percent of the client quota)
Unlimitedbyte-rate = 800 KiB/s, quota = Long.MaxValueNaN
Effective quota
The denominator is not re-resolved by calling ClientQuotaCallback.quotaLimit() during metric collection.
Kafka already writes the resolved bound onto the quota rate metric when the sensor is created and when quota configuration is updated (MetricConfig.quota). Utilization uses that cached bound.
Consequences:
JMX and reporter scrapes do not execute custom callback code.
ClientQuotaCallback invocation frequency is unchanged.
If a custom callback changes limits only through the existing update paths (updateQuota, or quotaResetRequired triggering a metric config refresh), utilization stays aligned with enforcement.
This KIP does not add a requirement that callbacks be safe to run on the scrape path.
Resolution of user, client-id, and default quotas is unchanged. It follows the existing documented client-quota precedence; this KIP does not restate or alter that hierarchy.
A missing, non-positive, or unlimited bound (greater than or equal to Long.MaxValue, Kafka's unlimited sentinel) is not a meaningful denominator, and yields NaN.
Scope
Produce, Fetch, and Request quotas are enforced independently on each broker. The metric on broker A is the client's usage on broker A divided by the quota applied on broker A. It is not cluster-wide quota headroom.
Operators should therefore scrape every broker and should not average the metric across brokers and interpret the result as cluster-wide utilization.
Controller Mutation
ControllerMutation quotas are not included in version 1.
Controller mutation quotas are enforced using a token bucket (tokens), while this KIP defines quota-utilization as a windowed rate divided by the configured rate. A windowed mutation-rate ratio would therefore not represent how much of the resource that actually controls throttling is currently available.
For example, a burst can exhaust tokens and cause throttle-time while the windowed mutation rate is still below 100%. Conversely, the windowed mutation rate can remain above 100% after the token bucket has begun to refill.
A future KIP can define an appropriate ControllerMutation metric, either as explicit rate utilization or as a token-bucket/remaining-token metric.
This KIP does not cover:
Replica and replication quotas LeaderReplication, FollowerReplication, AlterLogDirsReplication
Remote-log copy or fetch quotas
Connection-rate quotas
Max-connections quotas
These quotas use different managers, units, or MBeans and can be addressed separately.
Presence, NaN, and sensor lifecycle
The attribute is present exactly when the existing quota sensor exists. Presence is not a function of whether the current bound is finite.
That distinguishes the following cases:
Finite quota, from an override or a matching default: sensor and attribute are present; value is measured-rate / effective-quota * 100.
Quotas of this type never configured (quotasEnabled == false): sensor and attribute are absent, same as byte-rate today.
Sensor exists, bound is unlimited, missing, or non-positive: sensor and attribute are present; value is NaN.
Quotas configured, then all removed, quotasEnabled becomes false immediately. Sensors created before removal remain until the existing inactive-sensor expiry; quota-utilization is NaN because the bound is the unlimited sentinel. New sensors are not created until a quota is configured again.
Inactive client, sensor expired after the existing one hour expiry: sensor and attribute are absent until traffic resumes.
NaN means there is no finite quota to divide by. It does not mean 0 percent used. The attribute is kept on the MBean so that "sensor exists, no finite denominator" stays distinguishable from "quotas were never enabled, no MBean". Returning 0 for an unlimited quota would look like an idle, well-behaved client.
The metric is a double, as the neighbouring attributes already are. Exporter handling of JMX NaN is implementation dependent, so operators should verify their collector. Aggregations that require finite input should exclude NaN samples.
Fetch may unrecord bytes that were not returned after throttling. Utilization can therefore fall back below 100 percent on the same request that recorded throttle-time. This is existing rate-metric behaviour rather than something introduced here. Produce does not unrecord.
Public Interfaces
JMX
QuotaProduced onMBeanAttributes after this KIP
​Produce​Every broker​kafka.server:type=Produce,user=...,client-id=...​byte-rate, throttle-time, quota-utilization
FetchEvery brokerkafka.server:type=Fetch,user=...,client-id=...​byte-rate, throttle-time, quota-utilization
RequestEvery brokerkafka.server:type=Request,user=...,client-id=...​request-time, throttle-time, quota-utilization
There are no new broker configurations, request APIs, or Admin APIs.
Tags
quota-utilization uses exactly the same metric tags as the existing quota rate metric.
With the default quota callback, these are user and client-id. Either tag may be empty:
Per-client-id quotas have an empty user tag.
Per-user quotas have an empty client-id tag.
User plus client-id quotas have both tags populated.
A custom ClientQuotaCallback may provide additional metric tags. quota-utilization uses those same tags and does not introduce a second tag namespace.
The metric is an additional attribute on the same sensor and ObjectName as byte-rate or request-time.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The change is additive: an attribute is added to existing MBeans.
Existing MBean ObjectNames are unchanged.
Scrapers that ignore unknown attributes continue to work.
Scrapers that allowlist attributes by name must add …

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1373: Client Quota Utilization Metrics
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1373: Client Quota Utilization Metrics
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Brokers already expose per-client quota usage byte-rate , request-time  and throttle time throttle-time . They do not expose how that usage compares to the effective quota applied to the same quota sensor.
That join is left to operators: scrape the rate, then independently resolve user, client-id, and default overrides (or a custom ClientQuotaCallback)  from a different path. Limits can differ by orders of magnitude and can change dynamically, so absolute-rate alerts do not transfer across clients.
throttle-time  only changes after throttling has occurred. Operators need a normalized rate signal that identifies clients whose recent usage is approaching or exceeding the quota actually applied on that broker, without requiring the monitoring stack to resolve the quota independently.
KIP-1257: Partition Size Percentage Metrics for Storage Monitoring established the precedent of shipping a normalized percentage from Kafka rather than requiring operators to compute it externally. The analogy is only partial: retention.bytes  is a topic configuration, while client quotas are resolved per quota entity through the existing quota hierarchy and optional callbacks. This KIP preserves the existing quota-resolution and enforcement behavior.
Proposed Changes
Add quota-utilization as an additional attribute on the existing client-quota MBeans. No new MBean type, ObjectName, sensor, or quota entity is introduced.   
existingnew
byte-rate | request-time ,  throttle-timequota-utilization
Definition
quota-utilization is the recent quota-measured rate expressed as a percentage of the effective quota applied to the same quota sensor.calculation
Measured rate is the value of the existing quota rate metric on that sensor (byte-rate or request-time).
Effective quota is the quota currently associated with that rate metric's MetricConfig, after callback resolution and default/override resolution, and is the same bound used for enforcement on that sensor.
The metric is a rate-utilization signal. It is not a representation of throttle state or of remaining headroom before the next request is delayed.
Value and meaning
Less than 100: recent rate is below the effective quota.
Equal to 100: recent rate equals the effective quota.
Greater than 100: recent rate exceeds the effective quota; not capped.
throttle-time: actual throttling that already occurred.
The result is always a percentage of the applicable quota, regardless of the physical unit of the numerator.
Quotanumeratordenominator
Producebyte-rate (bytes/sec)producer_byte_rate
Fetchbyte-rate (bytes/sec)consumer_byte_rate
Requestrequest-timerequest_percentage
Request units are the easiest to misread. request-time is already a percentage of broker network and I/O thread time, and request_percentage caps that quantity. Utilization is a percentage of that cap, not request-time / 100. Exempt request time is not included in the numerator.
Examples
QuotaInputQuota-utilization
Producebyte-rate = 800 KiB/s, producer_byte_rate = 1 MiB/s80
Requestrequest-time = 40, request_percentage = 5080 (40 percent of the pool, 80 percent of the client quota)
Unlimitedbyte-rate = 800 KiB/s, quota = Long.MaxValueNaN
Effective quota
The denominator is not re-resolved by calling ClientQuotaCallback.quotaLimit() during metric collection.
Kafka already writes the resolved bound onto the quota rate metric when the sensor is created and when quota configuration is updated (MetricConfig.quota). Utilization uses that cached bound.
Consequences:
JMX and reporter scrapes do not execute custom callback code.
ClientQuotaCallback invocation frequency is unchanged.
If a custom callback changes limits only through the existing update paths (updateQuota, or quotaResetRequired triggering a metric config refresh), utilization stays aligned with enforcement.
This KIP does not add a requirement that callbacks be safe to run on the scrape path.
Resolution of user, client-id, and default quotas is unchanged. It follows the existing documented client-quota precedence; this KIP does not restate or alter that hierarchy.
A missing, non-positive, or unlimited bound (greater than or equal to Long.MaxValue, Kafka's unlimited sentinel) is not a meaningful denominator, and yields NaN.
Scope
Produce, Fetch, and Request quotas are enforced independently on each broker. The metric on broker A is the client's usage on broker A divided by the quota applied on broker A. It is not cluster-wide quota headroom.
Operators should therefore scrape every broker and should not average the metric across brokers and interpret the result as cluster-wide utilization.
Controller Mutation
ControllerMutation quotas are not included in version 1.
Controller mutation quotas are enforced using a token bucket (tokens), while this KIP defines quota-utilization as a windowed rate divided by the configured rate. A windowed mutation-rate ratio would therefore not represent how much of the resource that actually controls throttling is currently available.
For example, a burst can exhaust tokens and cause throttle-time while the windowed mutation rate is still below 100%. Conversely, the windowed mutation rate can remain above 100% after the token bucket has begun to refill.
A future KIP can define an appropriate ControllerMutation metric, either as explicit rate utilization or as a token-bucket/remaining-token metric.
This KIP does not cover:
Replica and replication quotas LeaderReplication, FollowerReplication, AlterLogDirsReplication
Remote-log copy or fetch quotas
Connection-rate quotas
Max-connections quotas
These quotas use different managers, units, or MBeans and can be addressed separately.
Presence, NaN, and sensor lifecycle
The attribute is present exactly when the existing quota sensor exists. Presence is not a function of whether the current bound is finite.
That distinguishes the following cases:
Finite quota, from an override or a matching default: sensor and attribute are present; value is measured-rate / effective-quota * 100.
Quotas of this type never configured (quotasEnabled == false): sensor and attribute are absent, same as byte-rate today.
Sensor exists, bound is unlimited, missing, or non-positive: sensor and attribute are present; value is NaN.
Quotas configured, then all removed, quotasEnabled becomes false immediately. Sensors created before removal remain until the existing inactive-sensor expiry; quota-utilization is NaN because the bound is the unlimited sentinel. New sensors are not created until a quota is configured again.
Inactive client, sensor expired after the existing one hour expiry: sensor and attribute are absent until traffic resumes.
NaN means there is no finite quota to divide by. It does not mean 0 percent used. The attribute is kept on the MBean so that "sensor exists, no finite denominator" stays distinguishable from "quotas were never enabled, no MBean". Returning 0 for an unlimited quota would look like an idle, well-behaved client.
The metric is a double, as the neighbouring attributes already are. Exporter handling of JMX NaN is implementation dependent, so operators should verify their collector. Aggregations that require finite input should exclude NaN samples.
Fetch may unrecord bytes that were not returned after throttling. Utilization can therefore fall back below 100 percent on the same request that recorded throttle-time. This is existing rate-metric behaviour rather than something introduced here. Produce does not unrecord.
Public Interfaces
JMX
QuotaProduced onMBeanAttributes after this KIP
​Produce​Every broker​kafka.server:type=Produce,user=...,client-id=...​byte-rate, throttle-time, quota-utilization

RequestEvery brokerkafka.server:type=Request,user=...,client-id=...​request-time, throttle-time, quota-utilization

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1374: Allow StreamsBuilder.globalTable to Rekey
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1374: Allow StreamsBuilder.globalTable to Rekey
Status
Current state: "Under Discussion"
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
StreamsBuilder.globalTable()  currently lags behind the functionality of StreamsBuilder.addGlobalStore() which lets users rekey data from a topic before populating the GlobalStateStore.  StreamsBuilder.globalTable  currently does not  let a client remap keys when building a GlobalKTable  from a topic. It would be useful to let clients remap when reading from a topic to build a global store.
Public Interfaces

Changes to StreamsBuilder
four new overrides will be added to StreamsBuilder.globalTable. They will mirror the existing methods but have a KeyValueMapper as an argument and more generic type parameters relevant for mapping.
java
Proposed Changes
This KIP introduces 4 new overloads to globalTable  that lets clients remap keys when building a GlobalKTable . The current overrides of globalTable  source their GlobalKTable  with an internal KTableSource  . KTableSource  provides no callback to remap keys so we will create the following new internal classes.
java
The behavior of these classes is similar to the existing KTableSource  and KTableSourceProcessor  classes. The difference is that a KeyValueMapper  is run at the start of KTableSourceWithRemappingProcessor.process. The mapper is a data member of KTableSourceWithRemapping  and is injectable via a constructor.
To avoid code duplication, the implementation of KTableSource  will be changed to compose a dlegate KTableSourceWithRemapping with an identity KeyValueMapper which it will delegate its logic to. KTableSourceProcessor will be deleted.
The table semantics of converting values to Change<V>  objects will be now owned by KTableSourceWithRemappingProcessor  instead of KTableSourceProcessor .
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
This change is fully backwards compatable. Existing users should not be affected. No externally facing classes, methods, or interfaces will be deleted. The internals of the existing globalTable  methods will be changed but this should not be observable by a Kafka user.
Test Plan
We will add unit tests for the "WithRemapping"  classes and integration tests for the new overrides of globalTable. We will use existing unit and integration tests to confirm there are no regressions in the behavior KTableSource  and the existing globalTable  overrides.
We may need to add more unit and integration tests for the existing components to cover scenarios that may differ when run through a unit remapper (i.g. null keys).
Rejected Alternatives

Use a ProcessorSupplier instead of a KeyValueMapper as an argument for globalTable
This would let a user supply a ProcessorSupplier  instead of a KeyValueMapper, letting them perform arbitrary stateless processing steps from the topic instead of just remapping. The problem is that a GlobalStateStore  is associated with only one state updater ProcessorSupplier . KTableSource is the currently used as the processor supplier, but letting a user inject their own processor supplier means that the user must have their ProcessorSupplier  implement table semantics. Using a KeyValueMapper abstracts the table semantics change away from the user. Changing GlobalStateStore  to use more than one ProcessorSupplier  to update its state seems like a nontrivial change that may have unforseen consequences.
TEXT>>>

Status
Current state: "Under Discussion"

Motivation
The interface StateRestoreListener has a method onRestoreSuspended  which lets a client observe the restoration of a StateStore  when that StateStore's restoration is suspended before it is finished.
StateRestoreListener.onRestoreSuspended  currently does not provide the reason for the restoration being suspended. The suspension can happen for one of three reasons:
the task was assigned to another instance
the task was demoted to a standby task on this instance
the instance is shutting down
A StateRestoreListener  is currently unable to differentiate between these reasons even though these reasons may be useful for a Kafka user who, for example, wants to emit observability to diagnose their application.
The analagous listener for standby tasks StateUpdateListener does provide the suspension reason for its analagous method, StateUpdateListener.onUpdateSuspended . Adding the suspension reason to the StateRestoreListener 
would fix this mismatch in the listener API.
Public Interfaces
Briefly list any new interfaces that will be introduced as part of this proposal or any existing interfaces that will be removed or changed. The purpose of this section is to concisely call out the public contract that will come along with this feature.
A public interface is any change to the following:
Binary log format
The network protocol and api behavior
Any class in the public packages under clientsConfiguration, especially client configuration
org/apache/kafka/common/serialization
org/apache/kafka/common
org/apache/kafka/common/errors
org/apache/kafka/clients/producer
org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer (eventually, once stable)
Monitoring
Command line tools and arguments
Anything else that will likely break existing users in some way when they upgrade
Changes to StateUpdateListener
StateUpdateListener  will add a new overload of .onUpdateSuspend  that has the suspension reason as an argument. the old. The new overload will have a default implementation to call the old .onUpdateSuspend  while dropping the suspension reason.
java
Proposed Changes
Swap KafkaStreams.DelegatingStateRestoreListener.OnRestoreSuspended  to use the new four argument overload
note that DelegatingStateRestoreListener is package private, so this is a backwards compatible change
Modify StateChangelogReader.unregister to pass the reason it calculates into its call to StateRestoreListener.OnRestoreSuspended  (effectively replacing the call to existing .OnRestoreSuspended  with a call to its overload
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

Kafka 4.X
The existing method will be deprecated but its observable behavior will remain the same to a caller. Existing implementations of StateRestoreListener  will remain implementations due to the use of a default method.
This ensures that backwards compatibility will remain during 4.X releases.
Kafka 5.0
When Kafka 5.0 releases, we can remove the deprecated original overload of StateRestoreListener.OnRestoreSuspended . This is a backwards breaking change.
Test Plan
Unit tests for new method overload
Enforce that an implementation that does not explicitly define the new overload of OnRestoresSuspended  is still able to implement StateRestoreListener (likely through an anonymous implementation in a unit test)
Rejected Alternatives

Defining a new interface that extends from StateRestoreListener that adds this overload
this was rejected because using a default method for the new overload provided a cleaner way of adding the change without breaking backwards compatability

Status

JIRA: KAFKA-7206
Motivation
Today each FindCoordinatorRequest only contains a single consumer id at a time. That means if we have N number of groupIds that need to find their coordinator, we would have to send out N number of requests. This can be optimized by batching up the groupIds and send out fewer requests. Therefore we want to extend FindCoordinatorRequest to have multiple consumer ids. 
Furthermore, this is the foundation of some later possible optimizations(enable batching in describeConsumerGroups, batching in deleteConsumerGroups). For example, now in KafkaAdmin, we are sending  describeConsumerGroups and deleteConsumerGroups with one pair of coordinatorId and groupId at a time. If we enable batching in FindCoordinatorRequest,  we can group all the groupId with the same coordinatorId, and only need to send out one request for those with the same coordinatorId.
Proposed Changes
Send a single FindCoordinatorRequest to a broker asking for coordinators of all consumer groups. These are the changes that need to be made:
Update the Schema in FindCoordinatorRequest to store an array of groupID (with a new FIND_COORDINATOR_REQUEST_V3); modify the class structure to take more than one coordinatorKey (List<String> groupIds). 
Update FindCoordinatorResponse 's class to have a map structure (now it only has Node to support one result, we need to support multiple results so something like <GroupId, CoordinatorNodeMetadata>)
Update handleFindCoordinatorRequest to correctly parse the new FindCoordinatorRequest and map the result to the new FindCoordinatorResponse.
Public Interfaces
API Changes

FindCoordinatorRequest.java
I suggest that we modify FindCoordinatorRequest.java to support multiple coordinator keys by adding a new FIND_COORDINATOR_REQUEST_V3:java
FindCoordinatorResponse.java
We also want to modify FindCoordinatorResponse.java to support multiple coordinator keys by adding a new FIND_COORDINATOR_REQUEST_V3:java
KafkaApis.scala/handleFindCoordinatorRequest
scala
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
FindCoordinatorResponse and FindCoordinatorRequests need to update to V3.
Requests that contains a single groupID still can be supported.
Compatibility issues between old and new versions need to be considered, we should think about how to convert requests from a newer version to a old …

CONVERSATION: Ticket KAFKA-16768: SocketServer leaks accepted SocketChannel instances due to race condition
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Muralidhar Basani (2024-05-15)
To fix this, when Processor#closeAll() is called, should we close all the acceptors in dataPlaneAcceptors, so that no new connections are accepted ?
[S2] Comment by Greg Harris (2024-05-15)
[~muralibasani] Do you mean call Acceptor#close? That might cause an infinite loop (because Acceptor#close calls Processor#close which calls Processor#closeAll).
I think if the Processor closeAll (where newConnections is drained) could call just the acceptor thread `join` and get the same effect, but without the infinite loop.
[S3] Comment by Chang-Yu Huang (2025-07-15)
Hi,

I would like to work on this issue. I have been analyzing the race condition between the Acceptor and Processor during shutdown.

My proposed solution is to make Processor#accept aware of the shutdown state. The method could return false if {{{}!shouldRun{}}}. Consequently, the calling Acceptor would be responsible for closing the SocketChannel upon receiving a false return. This approach maintains a clear separation of concerns, as the Processor doesn't manage the lifecycle of a channel it never queued.

An alternative I considered was modifying Processor#close to call closeAll() unconditionally. However, I noticed the if (!started.get) check seems to handle the specific case of a processor that failed to start. I'm hesitant to remove it as it might have unintended side effects.

I would appreciate your thoughts on this direction. If this approach seems reasonable, could you please assign this ticket to me?
[S4] Comment by Chang-Yu Huang (2025-08-05)
Hello [~gharris1727] may you review my PR?
[S5] Comment by Jainam Shah (2025-12-20)
Hi [~showuon] / [~gharris1727], I’ve been looking into this issue and would be happy to pick it up if that’s okay.
[S6] Comment by Chang-Yu Huang (2025-12-20)
Hello [~jainamshah102]. I've already created a PR that is waiting for review. Maybe we can share some idea on how to solve the issue and merge our commits first?
[S7] Comment by Jainam Shah (2025-12-20)
Hey [~cyh2012aa], Sounds good, I’ll share my approach as well so we can align on a starting point and converge on a single solution.

Fix implemented: the Processor’s accept(...) path now checks shouldRun and returns false when the processor is shutting down; on a false return the Acceptor immediately closes the SocketChannel and calls connectionQuotas.closeChannel(...) to update bookkeeping.

Why this resolves the race: by making acceptance conditional on the Processor still being alive, we ensure the _hand-off_ is fail-fast and the Acceptor never leaves a channel queued to a Processor that has already drained and terminated. If the Processor is shutting down, the Acceptor becomes responsible for cleanup, so there is no window where an accepted channel remains unclosed in {{{}newConnections{}}}.
[S8] Comment by Jainam Shah (2025-12-22)
[~gharris1727] / [~showuon] can you please review [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/21197] ?

<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1376: Support setting TLS named groups
Status
Current state: In Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: KAFKA-20728 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Named groups are how the JVM describes TLS key exchange schemes. APIs to use named groups have been added in Java 20.
Via JEP 527: Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3, new key exchange schemes resistant to quantum attacks, usually referred to as Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC), are being introduced. This JEP was initially delivered in Java 27. It's being backported by several implementations to earlier Java versions. Note that the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() API is available from Java 20, but the PQC named groups themselves (e.g. x25519_mlkem768) require Java 27 or a vendor backport that includes JEP 527.
Due to threats like "harvest now, decrypt later", many organizations are now actively considering PQC TLS. It is also mandated by several governments and industries such as finance, healthcare and defense.
Public Interfaces
All communication channels that are encrypted via TLS need to support PQC. This includes:
Client to broker/controller
Broker/controller to client
Broker/controller to broker/controller
Connect workers accepting REST traffic
Connect worker to Connect worker
OAuth token retrieval (client)
OAuth JWKS retrieval (server)
To cover all these scenarios, a single configuration can be used:
Name: ssl.named.groups
Type: List
Default: Empty, the default JVM named groups are used
Description: An ordered list of key exchange named groups to use for SSL connections, with the most preferred group first. The supported values depend on the SSL provider and Java runtime.
It can be set in clients, servers, Streams instances and Connect worker configurations. For example:
On servers, it can also be set per listener, for example:
For OAuth it must be set via sasl.jaas.config or a JAAS file, for example:
If the configuration is set and the JVM does not support the named groups APIs, a ConfigException will be thrown at startup.
If the configuration is set to unknown named groups, the failure happens when the TLS connection is established. This is the same behavior as with ssl.cipher.suites.
If the configuration is set, like with ssl.cipher.suites, a TLS connection can only be established when the client and server share at least one named group.
The TLS version (set via ssl.protocol) gates what named groups are valid and automatically drops entries not compatible (like for ciphers).
Proposed Changes
The named groups APIs are only available in Java 20+. Because the Kafka modules still support Java 11 (clients) and Java 17 (servers), logic trying to set named groups will use reflection so it compiles with the currently supported Java versions.
Clients/Servers
The DefaultSslEngineFactory class handles the TLS logic for clients and brokers. If ssl.named.groups is set, the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() method will be called via reflection.
OAuth
The OAuth/OIDC implementation makes two types of outbound HTTPS connections to the identity provider:
Token retrieval (client-side): OAuthBearerLoginCallbackHandler uses HttpJwtRetriever to fetch JWT access tokens from the token endpoint. Every Kafka client (producer, consumer, admin) and broker (for inter-broker OAuth) makes this call on each token refresh.
JWKS key retrieval (broker-side): OAuthBearerValidatorCallbackHandler uses VerificationKeyResolverFactory to periodically fetch the identity provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint, which are used to verify JWT signatures.
The JaasOptionsUtils.createSSLSocketFactory() method will be updated to wrap the returned SSLSocketFactory so that SSLParameters (including named groups, cipher suites, and enabled protocols) are applied to each socket after creation, mirroring what DefaultSslEngineFactory does for clients and servers.
Connect REST API
Connect uses Jetty to expose its REST API for users and for worker-to-worker communications.
Server-side: This handles REST API traffic from users and other Connect workers.
Client-side: This is used to forward requests to other Connect workers.
Both paths go through SSLUtils.configureSslContextFactoryAlgorithms(), which currently configures protocols, cipher suites, SSL provider, and algorithm settings. It will be updated to also set named groups if the configuration is set.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The ssl.named.groups configuration is new and optional. When not set, the JVM's default named groups are used so existing behavior is unchanged.
The SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() API is required for this feature. The implementation uses reflection so it compiles with older Java versions. If ssl.named.groups is set when the Java runtime lacks the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() then a ConfigException is thrown with a clear error message at startup.
The ssl.named.groups configuration is not dynamically reconfigurable. Changing it requires a restart. A phased PQC rollout can be achieved via rolling restarts across the cluster.
Since Java 8, users can set the jdk.tls.namedGroups system property to set named groups at the JVM level. The table below details the interaction between the system property and the new configuration:
ssl.named.groupsjdk.tls.namedGroupsBehavior
not setnot setJVM built-in defaults
not setsetSystem property applies
setnot setKafka config applies
setsetKafka config takes precedence:
If ssl.named.groups is set all connections use the specified named groups.
If only listener.name.internal.ssl.named.groups is set, the internal listener uses the specified named groups. If there are other listeners, they use the system property if it's set, otherwise the JVM built-in defaults.Effectively the precedence chain is:
  1. listener.name.<name>.ssl.named.groups (per-listener override when available)
  2. ssl.named.groups (global Kafka config)
  3. jdk.tls.namedGroups (JVM system property)
  4. JVM built-in defaults
The behavior is consistent with how the cipher suites work (via ssl.cipher.suites and jdk.tls.client.cipherSuites).
Test Plan
Unit tests covering the changes for all components.
Integration tests verify end-to-end TLS connections with named groups configured for client-broker, inter-broker, and Connect REST scenarios. 
These tests will be skipped when run on a JVM that does not support named groups. The CI already runs with Java 25, so this will be effectively tested.
Tests that exercise the error handling in case of lack of support for named groups will run in the CI with Java 17.
Rejected Alternatives
Rely on the JVM jdk.tls.namedGroups system property: This property applies to the whole JVM, so it prevents using different named groups for different components/listeners.
Distinguish between null and empty for ssl.named.groups: This only enables very niche scenarios (for example resetting named groups for a specific listener). I favored aligning the behavior with the ssl.cipher.suites configuration.
Do a multi-release JAR: A multi-release JAR could be used instead of relying on reflection. Overall using reflection is simpler and does not require making build changes.

<<<TEXT
SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-364: Remove implicit Materialized, Consumed and Produced
Status
Current state: Subsumed by KIP-365
Discussion thread: here
Github PR: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
I've proposed when Kafka Stream's Scala API was not released yet to solve the serdes issue on functions that takes a materialized (count, reduce and aggregate) to just make the materialized implicit and have a default implicit in ImplicitConversions that had the serdes filled in.
Given the following definitions:
def count()(implicit materialized: Materialized[K, Long, ByteArrayKeyValueStore])
def reduce(reducer: (V, V) => V)(implicit materialized: Materialized[K, V, ByteArrayKeyValueStore])
def aggregate[VR](initializer: => VR)(aggregator: (K, V, VR) => VR)(implicit materialized: Materialized[K, VR, ByteArrayKeyValueStore])
We can call them without Materialized:
groupedStream.count()
Or with a materialized:
groupedStream.count()(Materialized.as("store-name"))
By doing that we solved the case when no Materialized is given, setting implicitly the serdes to avoid runtime errors but still allowing the ability to give explicitly our own Materialized.
The issue with this solution are the followings:
Making Materialized implicit suggests that a Materialized is a context object whereas it's not.
The user of the API will by default just not care about implicit parameters and assume that they are provided.
The user of the API might declare it's own Materialized in an implicit val since the parameter is implicit and then be caught by other unwanted functions that also takes Materialized as implicit.
This a long shot view but in Scala 3 giving implicits explicitly looks like:
groupedStream.count().explicitly(Materialized.as("store-name"))
So it's clear that implicits should not be used as a defaulting system.
All of that applies to Consumed and Produced too.

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1376: Support setting TLS named groups
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1376: Support setting TLS named groups
Status
Current state: In Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: KAFKA-20728 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Named groups are how the JVM describes TLS key exchange schemes. APIs to use named groups have been added in Java 20.
Via JEP 527: Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3, new key exchange schemes resistant to quantum attacks, usually referred to as Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC), are being introduced. This JEP was initially delivered in Java 27. It's being backported by several implementations to earlier Java versions. Note that the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() API is available from Java 20, but the PQC named groups themselves (e.g. x25519_mlkem768) require Java 27 or a vendor backport that includes JEP 527.
Due to threats like "harvest now, decrypt later", many organizations are now actively considering PQC TLS. It is also mandated by several governments and industries such as finance, healthcare and defense.
Public Interfaces
All communication channels that are encrypted via TLS need to support PQC. This includes:
Client to broker/controller
Broker/controller to client
Broker/controller to broker/controller
Connect workers accepting REST traffic
Connect worker to Connect worker
OAuth token retrieval (client)
OAuth JWKS retrieval (server)
To cover all these scenarios, a single configuration can be used:
Name: ssl.named.groups
Type: List
Default: Empty, the default JVM named groups are used
Description: An ordered list of key exchange named groups to use for SSL connections, with the most preferred group first. The supported values depend on the SSL provider and Java runtime.
It can be set in clients, servers, Streams instances and Connect worker configurations. For example:
On servers, it can also be set per listener, for example:
For OAuth it must be set via sasl.jaas.config or a JAAS file, for example:
If the configuration is set and the JVM does not support the named groups APIs, a ConfigException will be thrown at startup.
If the configuration is set to unknown named groups, the failure happens when the TLS connection is established. This is the same behavior as with ssl.cipher.suites.
If the configuration is set, like with ssl.cipher.suites, a TLS connection can only be established when the client and server share at least one named group.
The TLS version (set via ssl.protocol) gates what named groups are valid and automatically drops entries not compatible (like for ciphers).
Proposed Changes
The named groups APIs are only available in Java 20+. Because the Kafka modules still support Java 11 (clients) and Java 17 (servers), logic trying to set named groups will use reflection so it compiles with the currently supported Java versions.
Clients/Servers
The DefaultSslEngineFactory class handles the TLS logic for clients and brokers. If ssl.named.groups is set, the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() method will be called via reflection.
OAuth
The OAuth/OIDC implementation makes two types of outbound HTTPS connections to the identity provider:
Token retrieval (client-side): OAuthBearerLoginCallbackHandler uses HttpJwtRetriever to fetch JWT access tokens from the token endpoint. Every Kafka client (producer, consumer, admin) and broker (for inter-broker OAuth) makes this call on each token refresh.
JWKS key retrieval (broker-side): OAuthBearerValidatorCallbackHandler uses VerificationKeyResolverFactory to periodically fetch the identity provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint, which are used to verify JWT signatures.
The JaasOptionsUtils.createSSLSocketFactory() method will be updated to wrap the returned SSLSocketFactory so that SSLParameters (including named groups, cipher suites, and enabled protocols) are applied to each socket after creation, mirroring what DefaultSslEngineFactory does for clients and servers.
Connect REST API
Connect uses Jetty to expose its REST API for users and for worker-to-worker communications.
Server-side: This handles REST API traffic from users and other Connect workers.
Client-side: This is used to forward requests to other Connect workers.
Both paths go through SSLUtils.configureSslContextFactoryAlgorithms(), which currently configures protocols, cipher suites, SSL provider, and algorithm settings. It will be updated to also set named groups if the configuration is set.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The ssl.named.groups configuration is new and optional. When not set, the JVM's default named groups are used so existing behavior is unchanged.
The SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() API is required for this feature. The implementation uses reflection so it compiles with older Java versions. If ssl.named.groups is set when the Java runtime lacks the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() then a ConfigException is thrown with a clear error message at startup.
The ssl.named.groups configuration is not dynamically reconfigurable. Changing it requires a restart. A phased PQC rollout can be achieved via rolling restarts across the cluster.
Since Java 8, users can set the jdk.tls.namedGroups system property to set named groups at the JVM level. The table below details the interaction between the system property and the new configuration:
ssl.named.groupsjdk.tls.namedGroupsBehavior
not setnot setJVM built-in defaults
not setsetSystem property applies
setnot setKafka config applies
setsetKafka config takes precedence:
If ssl.named.groups is set all connections use the specified named groups.
If only listener.name.internal.ssl.named.groups is set, the internal listener uses the specified named groups. If there are other listeners, they use the system property if it's set, otherwise the JVM built-in defaults.Effectively the precedence chain is:
  1. listener.name.<name>.ssl.named.groups (per-listener override when available)
  2. ssl.named.groups (global Kafka config)
  3. jdk.tls.namedGroups (JVM system property)
  4. JVM built-in defaults
The behavior is consistent with how the cipher suites work (via ssl.cipher.suites and jdk.tls.client.cipherSuites).
Test Plan
Unit tests covering the changes for all components.
Integration tests verify end-to-end TLS connections with named groups configured for client-broker, inter-broker, and Connect REST scenarios. 
These tests will be skipped when run on a JVM that does not support named groups. The CI already runs with Java 25, so this will be effectively tested.
Tests that exercise the error handling in case of lack of support for named groups will run in the CI with Java 17.
Rejected Alternatives
Rely on the JVM jdk.tls.namedGroups system property: This property applies to the whole JVM, so it prevents using different named groups for different components/listeners.
Distinguish between null and empty for ssl.named.groups: This only enables very niche scenarios (for example resetting named groups for a specific listener). I favored aligning the behavior with the ssl.cipher.suites configuration.
Do a multi-release JAR: A multi-release JAR could be used instead of relying on reflection. Overall using reflection is simpler and does not require making build changes.

JIRA: KAFKA-3333 Alternative Partitioner to Support "Always Round-Robin" Selection
Motivation
In my organisation, we have been using kafka as the basic publish-subscribe messaging system provider. Our goal is to send event-based (secure, encrypted) SQL messages reliably, and process them accordingly. For us, the message keys represent some metadata which we use to either ignore messages (if a loop-back to the sender), or log some information. We have the following use case for messaging:
1) A business object transaction occurs at SQL server/HANA Database.
2) The event is captured at the ORM layer, and messaged across multiple data centres around the world.
3) A group of consumers (for each data centre with a unique consumer-group ID) will process messages from their respective partitions. 1 consumer per partition.
Under the circumstances, we only need a guarantee that same message won't be sent to multiple partitions. In other words, 1 partition will never be sought by multiple consumers.
 Using DefaultPartitioner, we can achieve this only with NULL keys. But since we need keys for metadata, we cannot maintain "Round-robin" selection of partitions because a key hash will determine which partition to choose. We need to have round-robin style selection regardless of key type (NULL or not-NULL).

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1377: ByteBuffer serialize method for Serializer
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1377: ByteBuffer serialize method for Serializer
This page is meant as a template for writing a . To create a KIP choose Tools->Copy on this page and modify with your content and replace the heading with the next KIP number and a description of your issue. Replace anything in italics with your own description.
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here [Change the link from the KIP proposal email archive to your own email thread]
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21122
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The consumer read path avoids a per-record copy for the record value. KIP-863 added a ByteBuffer method to Deserializer so that CompletedFetch#parseRecord can hand the deserializer the record value straight from the fetch buffer:javaDeserializer.java
The default falls back to the byte[] method, so existing deserializers are unaffected, and ByteBufferDeserializer overrides it to skip the copy.
The producer has no matching method. Serializer only returns byte[]:
javaSerializer.java
So a producer whose record value is already in a ByteBuffer has to copy it into a byte[] for every record. This is the case for a caller that holds data off the Java heap or in a reused buffer, for example a Netty ByteBuf exposed through nioBuffer(), or a service that forwards a payload it does not read.
This KIP adds the missing method so the write side matches the read side that KIP-863 already added. It is opt-in, so a serializer that returns byte[] keeps working with no change.
Public Interfaces

Serializer.serializeToBuffer
A new default method on org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.Serializer<T>:
javaSerializer.java
A separate name is used because Java cannot overload on the return type alone.
ByteBufferSerializer
org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.ByteBufferSerializer overrides the method to return the buffer without copying:
javaByteBufferSerializer.java
duplicate() gives the producer its own position and limit. The caller's buffer is left unchanged and can be refilled and reused for the next record.
Partitioner.partition with a ByteBuffer key
A new default method on org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner, so that choosing the partition from the key does not force a byte[] copy of the key:javaPartitioner.java
A custom Partitioner that implements only the byte[] method keeps working. It receives a copied key, the same as today. Only the built-in partitioner skips the copy.
Proposed Changes
KafkaProducer.doSend calls serializeToBuffer in place of serialize. For the default serializers this wraps the byte[] and behaves as before. For ByteBufferSerializer it passes the caller's buffer through with no copy.
The producer already copies the payload into the record batch once, when it writes the record. This only change removes the extra per-record byte[] that the serializer uses to allocate. The producer reads the returned buffer without moving its position, so a caller can hand in the same ByteBuffer on every send and refill it in place.
Currently, Utils#murmur2 hash operates on byte[] array and we would provide bit identical version backed by a ByteBuffer.
All references from MemoryRecordsBuilder -> DefaultRecord operate on ByteBuffers. However, there is an implementation cost associated with the Utils#writeTo method that currently does a array copy directly since the backing store for the ByteBuffer is a byte array. For uncompressed payloads, we can write the ByteBufferDataOutputStream directly into the appendStream of MemoryRecordsBuilder.
Extension Considerations
This method is the serializer step of the send path. It removes the copy where the value enters the producer. It does not by itself, keep the value off the heap all the way to the socket in the current flow. A caller who wants that should know the points where the value still touches the heap today. Each is a separate concern and is not part of this KIP.
Batch memory: The producer copies each record into a batch buffer before it is sent, and that buffer is on the heap today. This is the only point that grows with the record size, but can be capped with the batch.size config today. An offheap version of this bufferpool can be a follow-up KIP.
Compression: The compression codecs take byte[] input, so a ByteBuffer value is copied through a small heap buffer, reused across records, before it reaches the codec. A ByteBuffer codec input path would be a separate change.
TLS: With the built-in JDK TLS provider the plaintext is copied to the heap inside the SSLEngine. Keeping it off-heap through TLS needs a native provider, which is already pluggable through ssl.engine.factory.class. For instance, Netty's SSLEngine provides this capability and users can configure a custom netty SSLEngine Factory.
Of these, only the batch buffer grows with the record size. The compression and TLS buffers are fixed and reused, so are not affected by the payload size.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
serializeToBuffer is a default method, so every existing Serializer compiles and runs unchanged. The new Partitioner.partition overload is also a default method, so existing partitioners are unaffected. A custom partitioner that implements only the byte[] method receives a copied key, the same as today.
There is no wire protocol change, no broker change, and no required configuration. A producer configured with ByteBufferSerializer and passing ByteBuffer values stops allocating a byte[] per record with no application code change.
Test Plan
A Serializer that implements only serialize returns the same bytes through the default serializeToBuffer.
ByteBufferSerializer.serializeToBuffer returns the data without moving the caller's position, and returns null for a null value.
KafkaProducer.doSend produces byte-identical records through the byte[] and ByteBuffer paths, for heap and direct input buffers.
The built-in partitioner chooses the same partition for a ByteBuffer key and the equal byte[] key.
Rejected Alternatives
Change the return type of Serializer.serialize, or add a required method. This would break every existing serializer. A default method keeps the change opt-in and source-compatible, the same way KIP-863 added the ByteBuffer deserialize method.
Add the ByteBuffer key method to the Partitioner contract as a required method. Every custom partitioner would have to implement it. The default method keeps them working and copies the key for them, the same as today.
TEXT>>>

This page is meant as a template for writing a . To create a KIP choose Tools->Copy on this page and modify with your content and replace the heading with the next KIP number and a description of your issue. Replace anything in italics with your own description.
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here [Change the link from the KIP proposal email archive to your own email thread]
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21122
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The consumer read path avoids a per-record copy for the record value. KIP-863 added a ByteBuffer method to Deserializer so that CompletedFetch#parseRecord can hand the deserializer the record value straight from the fetch buffer:javaDeserializer.java
The default falls back to the byte[] method, so existing deserializers are unaffected, and ByteBufferDeserializer overrides it to skip the copy.
The producer has no matching method. Serializer only returns byte[]:
javaSerializer.java
So a producer whose record value is already in a ByteBuffer has to copy it into a byte[] for every record. This is the case for a caller that holds data off the Java heap or in a reused buffer, for example a Netty ByteBuf exposed through nioBuffer(), or a service that forwards a payload it does not read.
This KIP adds the missing method so the write side matches the read side that KIP-863 already added. It is opt-in, so a serializer that returns byte[] keeps working with no change.
Public Interfaces

Serializer.serializeToBuffer
A new default method on org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.Serializer<T>:
javaSerializer.java
A separate name is used because Java cannot overload on the return type alone.
ByteBufferSerializer
org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.ByteBufferSerializer overrides the method to return the buffer without copying:
javaByteBufferSerializer.java
duplicate() gives the producer its own position and limit. The caller's buffer is left unchanged and can be refilled and reused for the next record.
Partitioner.partition with a ByteBuffer key
A new default method on org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner, so that choosing the partition from the key does not force a byte[] copy of the key:javaPartitioner.java
A custom Partitioner that implements only the byte[] method keeps working. It receives a copied key, the same as today. Only the built-in partitioner skips the copy.
Proposed Changes
KafkaProducer.doSend calls serializeToBuffer in place of serialize. For the default serializers this wraps the byte[] and behaves as before. For ByteBufferSerializer it passes the caller's buffer through with no copy.
The producer already copies the payload into the record batch once, when it writes the record. This only change removes the extra per-record byte[] that the serializer uses to allocate. The producer reads the returned buffer without moving its position, so a caller can hand in the same ByteBuffer on every send and refill it in place.
Currently, Utils#murmur2 hash operates on byte[] array and we would provide bit identical version backed by a ByteBuffer.
All references from MemoryRecordsBuilder -> DefaultRecord operate on ByteBuffers. However, there is an implementation cost associated with the Utils#writeTo method that currently does a array copy directly since the backing store for the ByteBuffer is a byte array. For uncompressed payloads, we can write the ByteBufferDataOutputStream directly into the appendStream of MemoryRecordsBuilder.
Extension Considerations
This method is the serializer step of the send path. It removes the copy where the value enters the producer. It does not by itself, keep the value off the heap all the way to the socket in the current flow. A caller who wants that should know the points where the value still touches the heap today. Each is a separate concern and is not part of this KIP.
Batch memory: The producer copies each record into a batch buffer before it is sent, and that buffer is on the heap today. This is the only point that grows with the record size, but can be capped with the batch.size config today. An offheap version of this bufferpool can be a follow-up KIP.
Compression: The compression codecs take byte[] input, so a ByteBuffer value is copied through a small heap buffer, reused across records, before it reaches the codec. A ByteBuffer codec input path would be a separate change.
TLS: With the built-in JDK TLS provider the plaintext is copied to the heap inside the SSLEngine. Keeping it off-heap through TLS needs a native provider, which is already pluggable through ssl.engine.factory.class. For instance, Netty's SSLEngine provides this capability and users can configure a custom netty SSLEngine Factory.
Of these, only the batch buffer grows with the record size. The compression and TLS buffers are fixed and reused, so are not affected by the payload size.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
serializeToBuffer is a default method, so every existing Serializer compiles and runs unchanged. The new Partitioner.partition overload is also a default method, so existing partitioners are unaffected. A custom partitioner that implements only the byte[] method receives a copied key, the same as today.
There is no wire protocol change, no broker change, and no required configuration. A producer configured with ByteBufferSerializer and passing ByteBuffer values stops allocating a byte[] per record with no application code change.
Test Plan
A Serializer that implements only serialize returns the same bytes through the default serializeToBuffer.
ByteBufferSerializer.serializeToBuffer returns the data without moving the caller's position, and returns null for a null value.
KafkaProducer.doSend produces byte-identical records through the byte[] and ByteBuffer paths, for heap and direct input buffers.
The built-in partitioner chooses the same partition for a ByteBuffer key and the equal byte[] key.
Rejected Alternatives
Change the return type of Serializer.serialize, or add a required method. This would break every existing serializer. A default method keeps the change opt-in and source-compatible, the same way KIP-863 added the ByteBuffer deserialize method.
Add the ByteBuffer key method to the Partitioner contract as a required method. Every custom partitioner would have to implement it. The default method keeps them working and copies the key for them, the same as today.
TEXT>>>

Whenever there is a need to introduce dependencies for handlers into a Kafka Streams project, additional steps used to be required to ensure this process. One possibility was to provide dependencies inside a Map for a configure method during application configuration process and another one was to create your own StreamsConfig class implementation with one method being overridden.

Registration of an exception handler class in Kafka Streams configuration

[S1] Page: KIP-1378: Allow Consumer Group Renaming in MirrorMaker 2 Checkpoint Connector
Status
Current state: "Under Discussion"
Discussion thread: DISCUSS: KIP-1378: Allow Consumer Group Renaming in MirrorMaker 2 Checkpoint Connector
JIRA: KAFKA-21127 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
MirrorMaker 2 (MM2) provides pluggable topic renaming across clusters via the `ReplicationPolicy` interface (e.g., `DefaultReplicationPolicy` prefixes topic names with the source cluster alias `<source>.<topic>`, while `IdentityReplicationPolicy` keeps them identical).
However, consumer groups do not have an equivalent pluggable naming mechanism. Today, `MirrorCheckpointConnector` and `MirrorCheckpointTask` mirror consumer group offsets to the target cluster preserving the exact source consumer group ID (`group.id`).
When multiple primary clusters replicate into a single disaster recovery (DR) or analytical target cluster, consumer group names from different source clusters can easily collide if identical group IDs were used independently on each source.
This KIP proposes introducing a pluggable `GroupMirroringPolicy` interface (analogous to `ReplicationPolicy`) to allow operators to customize consumer group names created and tracked on the target cluster.
Public Interfaces
New Interface: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.GroupMirroringPolicy`
```
package org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror;
/**
 * An interface used by MirrorMaker connectors to rename consumer groups between source and target clusters.
 * Analogous to ReplicationPolicy for topics, this allows operators to define a custom naming
 * convention for consumer groups on the target cluster.
 */@InterfaceAudience.Publicpublic interface GroupMirroringPolicy extends Configurable {
 /**
 * Returns the name that the given source consumer group should use on the target cluster.
 * This name is used when emitting checkpoints and syncing consumer group offsets to the target.
 *
 * @param sourceClusterAlias the alias of the source cluster
 * @param group the consumer group ID on the source cluster
 * @return the consumer group ID to use on the target cluster
 */
 String targetGroupId(String sourceClusterAlias, String group);
 /**
 * Returns the source consumer group ID for a given group on the target cluster.
 * This is the inverse of targetGroupId(String, String).
 *
 * @param sourceClusterAlias the alias of the source cluster
 * @param targetGroup the consumer group ID on the target cluster
 * @return the original consumer group ID on the source cluster, or null if not determinable
 */
 String sourceGroupId(String sourceClusterAlias, String targetGroup);
 @Override
 default void configure(Map<String, ?> configs) {
 // no-op by default
 }
}
```
Default Implementation: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.DefaultGroupMirroringPolicy`
An identity implementation providing backward-compatible default behavior:
3. New Configuration Property
The following configuration property is added to `MirrorCheckpointConfig` and `MirrorClientConfig`:
 `group.mirroring.policy.class` 
Type: `Class` 
Deafult: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.DefaultGroupMirroringPolicy` 
Importance : `LOW` 
Description: Class which defines the consumer group naming convention on the target cluster.
Proposed Changes
Describe the new thing you want to do in appropriate detail. This may be fairly extensive and have large subsections of its own. Or it may be a few sentences. Use judgement based on the scope of the change.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Fully backward compatible. Existing setups without this configuration will use `DefaultGroupMirroringPolicy`, which preserves existing consumer group IDs verbatim.
Test Plan
Junit-driven integration test, that includes stopping and restarting the connector to exercise CheckpointStore initialisation

JIRA: KAFKA-21127 
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
MirrorMaker 2 (MM2) provides pluggable topic renaming across clusters via the `ReplicationPolicy` interface (e.g., `DefaultReplicationPolicy` prefixes topic names with the source cluster alias `<source>.<topic>`, while `IdentityReplicationPolicy` keeps them identical).
However, consumer groups do not have an equivalent pluggable naming mechanism. Today, `MirrorCheckpointConnector` and `MirrorCheckpointTask` mirror consumer group offsets to the target cluster preserving the exact source consumer group ID (`group.id`).
When multiple primary clusters replicate into a single disaster recovery (DR) or analytical target cluster, consumer group names from different source clusters can easily collide if identical group IDs were used independently on each source.
This KIP proposes introducing a pluggable `GroupMirroringPolicy` interface (analogous to `ReplicationPolicy`) to allow operators to customize consumer group names created and tracked on the target cluster.
Public Interfaces
New Interface: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.GroupMirroringPolicy`
```
package org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror;
/**
 * An interface used by MirrorMaker connectors to rename consumer groups between source and target clusters.
 * Analogous to ReplicationPolicy for topics, this allows operators to define a custom naming
 * convention for consumer groups on the target cluster.
 */@InterfaceAudience.Publicpublic interface GroupMirroringPolicy extends Configurable {
 /**
 * Returns the name that the given source consumer group should use on the target cluster.
 * This name is used when emitting checkpoints and syncing consumer group offsets to the target.
 *
 * @param sourceClusterAlias the alias of the source cluster
 * @param group the consumer group ID on the source cluster
 * @return the consumer group ID to use on the target cluster
 */
 String targetGroupId(String sourceClusterAlias, String group);
 /**
 * Returns the source consumer group ID for a given group on the target cluster.
 * This is the inverse of targetGroupId(String, String).
 *
 * @param sourceClusterAlias the alias of the source cluster
 * @param targetGroup the consumer group ID on the target cluster
 * @return the original consumer group ID on the source cluster, or null if not determinable
 */
 String sourceGroupId(String sourceClusterAlias, String targetGroup);
 @Override
 default void configure(Map<String, ?> configs) {
 // no-op by default
 }
}
```

[S1] Page: KIP-383:  Pluggable interface for SSL Factory
Status
Current state: Discarded, replaced by 
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
It has been a common request to be able to customize SslFactory beyond the existing configuration options. For example, users want encrypted passwords, an alias to choose a certificate, OCSP support, etc. For these, alternative config options make the most sense because these are generic config options that are useful in many environments, so we should support these without having to write Java code.
There are situations where adding configuration options will never be able to satisfy the requirement. For example, the user may need to reuse an existing SSL implementation or share an implementation across multiple applications. For those cases, the simplest approach would be to support the customization of the SslFactory implementation.
A custom SslFactory implementation might also serve as a stop gap measure when a user needs an SSL feature immediately but the necessary configuration option is not yet available.
Of course it would be easy to simply change the Kafka source code and ship a customized distribution. The idea is you should be able to replace the implementation through configuration, without rebuilding a custom Kafka distribution or resorting to classpath tricks to shadow Kafka classes.
SslFactory handles two different tasks: creating the SSLContext and reconfiguration. There is no need to make reconfiguration pluggable. This functionality should remain in SslFactory to be shared by all pluggable implementations. SslFactory only needs to delegate the creation of the SSLContext to the pluggable interface.
Since SslFactory will handle reconfiguration, the idea is to make the configuration immutable in the pluggable factory. SslFactory would create a new pluggable factory every time the configuration changes. The pluggable factory creates its SSLContext when it is configured and never changes it. It turns out SslFactory does not really need the SSLContext, so it can use the new pluggable factory as an SSLEngine factory instead.
Public Interfaces
This KIP will introduce a new configuration option ssl.sslengine.factory.class to be added to SslConfigs. This will automatically add the new option to AdminClientConfig, ConsumerConfig and ProducerConfig.

Thanks for letting me know!
I'll wait for the discussion. 
Please let me know once the direction is agreed upon, I'd be happy to help with the implementation then!
[S4] Comment by chomingi (2026-08-03)
I may be missing a path, but I couldn't reconcile sections 2 and 3 with the request validation in GroupCoordinatorService.

The broker's public StreamsGroupHeartbeat path goes through GroupCoordinatorService#streamsGroupHeartbeat, which calls throwIfStreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestIsInvalid before scheduling the coordinator operation. If any of ActiveTasks, StandbyTasks, or WarmupTasks is non-null, the validation requires all three to be non-null. A partial report therefore returns INVALID_REQUEST ("If one task-type is non-null, all must be non-null.") before reaching GroupMetadataManager. This check has been present since 4.1.0, the first release with this RPC, and is also present in 4.2.0, 4.3.0, and trunk.

The GroupMetadataManager behavior described in section 2 does exist, but I couldn't find a current production path that allows a partial public request to reach it without going through the service-level validation. Unless I missed one, the no-error stall described in section 3 does not appear reachable through the public RPC on these versions. A third-party client following the per-field "Null if unchanged since last heartbeat" wording would receive an explicit INVALID_REQUEST instead.

If that is correct, it changes the current failure mode but not the design choice: should the existing all-or-none contract be documented in KIP-1071 and the schema, as in Option C, or should the broker support per-role partial reports as the current wording suggests? PR #23002 …

[S6] Comment by Matthias J. Sax (2026-08-03)

GroupMetadataManager:1872-1882, the stale-epoch branch whose own comment says "we accept it because the response with the bumped epoch may have been lost":

  || !areOwnedTasksContainedInAssignedTasksWithEpochs(ownedActiveTasks, ...)
  || !areOwnedTasksContainedInAssignedTasks(ownedStandbyTasks, ...)

and both helpers open with if (ownedTasks == null) return false; (:1539, :1565). So null → false → negated → fenced. A member retrying with its previous epoch and "nothing changed" gets FencedMemberEpochException instead of the acceptance that branch exists to provide.

One distinction may matter: all three lists being null is valid for an ordinary heartbeat, but KIP-1071 appears to require more information after an error.

Replicating topic data across multiple Kafka clusters is a very common scenario and there are many tools that provide this functionality. However simply copying topic records (key/value/headers/timestamp) may not be enough in many use cases.

The Record Accumulator yields batches that only contain records with consecutive offsets.
The Sender sends ProduceRequests with a "use_offset" flag.

it checks against a new required permission (ReplicatorWrite) in the ACL. This operation is checked against the ClusterResource.
it uses the provided offsets instead of generating new incremental ones.
The broker still ensures offsets are monotonically increasing. 
If a batch violates this requirement, an InvalidProducerOffset Error is returned.
The broker ensures batches only contain records with sequential offsets. 
If a batch violates this requirement, a CorruptRecord Error is returned.
Batches are required to only contain sequential offsets because the last offset is used to compute the last sequence for Idempotent Producers.
