<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1379: Make server-side rack-aware assignment opt-in
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Rack-aware assignment is costly and, in the common case, changes nothing. Yet the group coordinator pays for it for every group.
Rack-aware assignment gives each member partitions with a replica in its rack, so that the member can fetch from that replica instead of crossing racks (KIP-392). It changes nothing in two common cases:
Fetch from follower is not used, so the members fetch from the leader. It is off by default for consumers, and share consumers do not support it.
The replicas of every partition already cover all racks, as with three availability zones and a replication factor of three.
Neither the coordinator nor the assignor can tell which case applies without doing the work that would be wasted.
The assignor. Rack awareness is planned for the built-in consumer assignors (KAFKA-19387). A rack-aware assignor has to read the racks of the replicas of every subscribed partition on every assignment. Finding out whether the racks matter costs as much as using them. So every consumer group would pay this cost on every assignment, including in the two cases above.
The metadata hash. The coordinator already pays for the racks today. Since KIP-1101, the metadata hash of every group covers the racks of the replicas of every subscribed partition. Computing it looks up the rack of every replica, and it is recomputed after every change to a subscribed topic, including leader and ISR changes. A rack change also bumps the group epoch, even though no built-in assignor uses racks today.
The classic protocol makes rack awareness opt-in: a consumer only considers racks when client.rack is set (KIP-881). This KIP does the same on the server for consumer groups, with a broker configuration that is off by default. Share and streams groups cannot use the racks today, so they stop paying for them.
Public Interfaces

Broker configuration
NameTypeDefaultImportanceUpdate mode
group.consumer.rack.aware.assignment.enablebooleanfalsemediumread-only
Documentation: Whether rack-aware assignment is enabled for consumer groups. When enabled, the assignor is given the rack ids of the members and the racks of the partition replicas, and a change of the racks of a subscribed partition triggers a new assignment. It is only useful when both of the following hold: the consumers use fetch-from-follower (replica.selector.class on the brokers and client.rack on the consumers), and the partitions do not have a replica in every rack (or availability zone). Otherwise, rack-aware assignment changes nothing and only adds cost.
Assignor interface
A new default method on org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.api.assignor.GroupSpec:javaThe coordinator's implementation returns the value of the configuration for consumer groups and false for share groups. When it returns false, MemberSubscription#rackId() is empty and SubscribedTopicDescriber#racksForPartition(Uuid, int) returns an empty set.
There are no RPC or record changes. Describe APIs still return the rack ids of the members.
Proposed Changes

Metadata hash
The topic hash comes in two forms:
With racks: the topic hash defined by KIP-1101, unchanged.
Without racks: it only covers the topic id, name and number of partitions.0x00 | topic id | topic name | number of partitions
This is the KIP-1101 format, with the same magic byte, without the per-partition section. Without racks, that section only listed the partition ids, which added nothing: they are always 0 to the number of partitions minus one. When present, the section has an entry for every partition, so the two forms never produce the same input for different topics.
The group hash, computed from the topic hashes, is unchanged. The form a group uses, and the rack information its assignor gets, depend on its type and on group.consumer.rack.aware.assignment.enable:
Group typeConfigurationTopic hashRack information given to the assignor
Consumerdisabled (default)without racksnone; GroupSpec#isRackAware() is false
Consumerenabledwith racksmember and partition racks; GroupSpec#isRackAware() is true
Sharenonewithout racksnone; GroupSpec#isRackAware() is false
Streamsnonewithout racksunchanged
The following sections explain each row.
Consumer groups
When the configuration is disabled, the assignor gets no member racks and no partition racks, and GroupSpec#isRackAware() is false. The flag lets an assignor skip its rack-aware logic without looking at the partitions. Hiding the racks guarantees that an assignor cannot base the assignment on racks that the metadata hash does not track.
When the configuration is enabled, GroupSpec#isRackAware() is true and the assignor gets the rack ids of the members and the racks of the partition replicas, so it can make rack-aware decisions. The metadata hash covers the racks, so a change of the racks of a subscribed partition triggers a new assignment.
Share groups
Share groups do not support rack-aware assignment yet, so it is left for a future KIP. They always use the topic hash without racks. Share assignors receive the same GroupSpec as consumer assignors, so they inherit GroupSpec#isRackAware(). The coordinator always sets it to false for share groups, so share assignors get no rack information.
Streams groups
Streams groups do not support rack-aware assignment yet, so it is left for a future KIP. They always use the topic hash without racks.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Upgrade. When a broker with this change loads a group, it recomputes the metadata hash on the group's first heartbeat, as the coordinator already does after loading a group. If the group now uses the topic hash without racks, the hash differs from the one stored by the previous version, so a rebalance is triggered. This is the case for every group, except consumer groups when the configuration is enabled. The assignment does not change: the built-in assignors do not use partition racks, and they are sticky or deterministic.
Downgrade. When a broker without this change loads a group that used the topic hash without racks, it recomputes the hash with racks. The hash differs from the stored one, so a rebalance is triggered as well. Again, the assignment does not change.
Rolling upgrade or downgrade. A group may move between brokers with and without this change several times, and a rebalance is triggered on each move.
Custom assignors. Custom consumer assignors (group.consumer.assignors) only receive rack information when the configuration is enabled. Custom share assignors (group.share.assignors) no longer receive it. We believe this is acceptable given the current adoption of custom server-side assignors: they are very likely not used, let alone rack-aware ones. A custom consumer assignor that uses racks keeps working once the configuration is enabled. The upgrade notes will say so.
Implementations of GroupSpec outside Kafka, such as test doubles for custom assignors, keep working, because isRackAware() is a default method.
Test Plan
The existing unit and integration tests will be extended to cover the change.
Rejected Alternatives
Detecting automatically whether racks matter. None of the candidates can tell without doing the work this KIP avoids, or at all:
The assignor would have to read the racks of every partition to find out. It cannot tell whether the members fetch from the closest replica. Being inside the assignor, the check would also leave the racks in the metadata hash, which the coordinator computes.
client.rack is set by consumers that fetch from the closest replica, including with three racks and a replication factor of three, where rack-aware assignment changes nothing. The mode would also change for the whole group whenever a member without a rack joins or leaves.
replica.selector.class enables fetch-from-follower on the brokers, but that does not mean rack-aware assignment is needed. Whether it is depends on how the replicas are placed across racks, that is on the topology of the cluster and the replication factor. With three racks and a replication factor of three, for example, fetch-from-follower is useful but rack-aware assignment changes nothing.
Keeping the partition ids in the topic hash without racks. The hash would then equal the previous one when no broker has a rack, and those clusters would see no epoch bump on upgrade. Clusters with racks, which this KIP targets, see one bump either way. In exchange, the hash would stay linear in the number of partitions, for ids that are always 0 to the number of partitions minus one.
A coordinator-wide configuration for all group types. Share and streams groups do not support rack-aware assignment. A switch that covers them would suggest that they do.
A dynamic configuration. Replica placement and fetching from followers are cluster-level choices that rarely change. A read-only …

A rack-aware assignor has to read the racks of the replicas of every subscribed partition on every assignment. Finding out whether the racks matter costs as much as using them. So every consumer group would pay this cost on every assignment, including in the two cases above.
The metadata hash. The coordinator already pays for the racks today. Since KIP-1101, the metadata hash of every group covers the racks of the replicas of every subscribed partition. Computing it looks up the rack of every replica, and it is recomputed after every change to a subscribed topic, including leader and ISR changes. A rack change also bumps the group epoch, even though no built-in assignor uses racks today.
The classic protocol makes rack awareness opt-in: a consumer only considers racks when client.rack is set (KIP-881). This KIP does the same on the server for consumer groups, with a broker configuration that is off by default. Share and streams groups cannot use the racks today, so they stop paying for them.
Public Interfaces

Broker configuration
NameTypeDefaultImportanceUpdate mode
group.consumer.rack.aware.assignment.enablebooleanfalsemediumread-only
Documentation: Whether rack-aware assignment is enabled for consumer groups. When enabled, the assignor is given the rack ids of the members and the racks of the partition replicas, and a change of the racks of a subscribed partition triggers a new assignment. It is only useful when both of the following hold: the consumers use fetch-from-follower (replica.selector.class on the brokers and client.rack on the consumers), and the partitions do not have a replica in every rack (or availability zone). Otherwise, rack-aware assignment changes nothing and only adds cost.
Assignor interface
A new default method on org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.api.assignor.GroupSpec:javaThe coordinator's implementation returns the value of the configuration for consumer groups and false for share groups. When it returns false, MemberSubscription#rackId() is empty and SubscribedTopicDescriber#racksForPartition(Uuid, int) returns an empty set.
There are no RPC or record changes. Describe APIs still return the rack ids of the members.
Proposed Changes

Metadata hash
The topic hash comes in two forms:
With racks: the topic hash defined by KIP-1101, unchanged.
Without racks: it only covers the topic id, name and number of partitions.0x00 | topic id | topic name | number of partitions
This is the KIP-1101 format, with the same magic byte, without the per-partition section. Without racks, that section only listed the partition ids, which added nothing: they are always 0 to the number of partitions minus one. When present, the section has an entry for every partition, so the two forms never produce the same input for different topics.
The group hash, computed from the topic hashes, is unchanged. The form a group uses, and the rack information its assignor gets, depend on its type and on group.consumer.rack.aware.assignment.enable:
Group typeConfigurationTopic hashRack information given to the assignor
Consumerdisabled (default)without racksnone; GroupSpec#isRackAware() is false
Consumerenabledwith racksmember and partition racks; GroupSpec#isRackAware() is true
Sharenonewithout racksnone; GroupSpec#isRackAware() is false
Streamsnonewithout racksunchanged
The following sections explain each row.
Consumer groups
When the configuration is disabled, the assignor gets no member racks and no partition racks, and GroupSpec#isRackAware() is false. The flag lets an assignor skip its rack-aware logic without looking at the partitions. Hiding the racks guarantees that an assignor cannot base the assignment on racks that the metadata hash does not track.
When the configuration is enabled, GroupSpec#isRackAware() is true and the assignor gets the rack ids of the members and the racks of the partition replicas, so it can make rack-aware decisions. The metadata hash covers the racks, so a change of the racks of a subscribed partition triggers a new assignment.
Share groups
Share groups do not support rack-aware assignment yet, so it is left for a future KIP. They always use the topic hash without racks. Share assignors receive the same GroupSpec as consumer assignors, so they inherit GroupSpec#isRackAware(). The coordinator always sets it to false for share groups, so share assignors get no rack information.
Streams groups
Streams groups do not support rack-aware assignment yet, so it is left for a future KIP. They always use the topic hash without racks.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Upgrade. When a broker with this change loads a group, it recomputes the metadata hash on the group's first heartbeat, as the coordinator already does after loading a group. If the group now uses the topic hash without racks, the hash differs from the one stored by the previous version, so a rebalance is triggered. This is the case for every group, except consumer groups when the configuration is enabled. The assignment does not change: the built-in assignors do not use partition racks, and they are sticky or deterministic.
Downgrade. When a broker without this change loads a group that used the topic hash without racks, it recomputes the hash with racks. The hash differs from the stored one, so a rebalance is triggered as well. Again, the assignment does not change.
Rolling upgrade or downgrade. A group may move between brokers with and without this change several times, and a rebalance is triggered on each move.
Custom assignors. Custom consumer assignors (group.consumer.assignors) only receive rack information when the configuration is enabled. Custom share assignors (group.share.assignors) no longer receive it. We believe this is acceptable given the current adoption of custom server-side assignors: they are very likely not used, let alone rack-aware ones. A custom consumer assignor that uses racks keeps working once the configuration is enabled. The upgrade notes will say so.
Implementations of GroupSpec outside Kafka, such as test doubles for custom assignors, keep working, because isRackAware() is a default method.
Test Plan
The existing unit and integration tests will be extended to cover the change.
Rejected Alternatives
Detecting automatically whether racks matter. None of the candidates can tell without doing the work this KIP avoids, or at all:
The assignor would have to read the racks of every partition to find out. It cannot tell whether the members fetch from the closest replica. Being inside the assignor, the check would also leave the racks in the metadata hash, which the coordinator computes.
client.rack is set by consumers that fetch from the closest replica, including with three racks and a replication factor of three, where rack-aware assignment changes nothing. The mode would also change for the whole group whenever a member without a rack joins or leaves.
replica.selector.class enables fetch-from-follower on the brokers, but that does not mean rack-aware assignment is needed. Whether it is depends on how the replicas are placed across racks, that is on the topology of the cluster and the replication factor. With three racks and a replication factor of three, for example, fetch-from-follower is useful but rack-aware assignment changes nothing.
Keeping the partition ids in the topic hash without racks. The hash would then equal the previous one when no broker has a rack, and those clusters would see no epoch bump on upgrade. Clusters with racks, which this KIP targets, see one bump either way. In exchange, the hash would stay linear in the number of partitions, for ids that are always 0 to the number of partitions minus one.
A coordinator-wide configuration for all group types. Share and streams groups do not support rack-aware assignment. A switch that covers them would suggest that they do.

Status

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
In the current consumer protocol, the field `member.id` is assigned by broker to track group member status. A new consumer joins the group with `member.id` field set as UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID (empty string), since it needs to receive the identity assignment from broker first. For request with unknown member id, broker will blindly accept the new join group request, store the member metadata and return a UUID to consumer. The edge case is that if initial join group request keeps failing due to connection timeout, or the consumer keeps restarting, or the max.poll.interval.ms configured on client is set to infinite (no rebalance timeout kicking in to clean up the member metadata map), there will be accumulated MemberMetadata info within group metadata cache which will eventually burst broker memory. The detection and fencing of invalid join group request is crucial for broker stability.
This KIP is a parallel work with KIP-389 which tries to enforce hard cap on the group metadata size, and an important complement for KIP-345 which introduces static membership.
Public Interfaces
We will introduce a new join group error type called MEMBER_ID_REQUIRED which will be triggered when broker meets join group request with unknown member id:javaErrors.java
We shall also bump join group protocol version so that broker knows whether the consumer could safely handle this type of error. For example if we bump protocol version from m to m+1, all the request with version >= m+1 will be returned with MEMBER_ID_REQUIRED error, while version <= m will still be blindly accepted for backward compatibility.
Proposed Changes
When encountering MEMBER_ID_REQUIRED exception, the client will use the given member id in the join group response to retry the join, which is expected to be accepted by the broker if id matches. If we encounter UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID exception with the second join attempt, client handling logic will be the same, which is reseting the generation and ask a new member id from broker by sending anonymous join group request. Status
Current state: "Under Discussion"
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: here 
Related: KAFKA-20609 / PR #22873 (the current last-modified fallback; design discussion in that PR's review thread), [KAFKA-21158](documents and warns about raising `message.timestamp.after.max.ms`)
Motivation
In a tiered topic, a local segment is deleted by time, once it has been uploaded to remote storage and condition 'now - largestRecordTimestamp > local.retention.ms' succeeds. The age is measured from record timestamps, which producers set. This causes two problems:
1. Old timestamps
For records produced with timestamps older than local.retention.ms, the local copy is deleted as soon as the segment is uploaded to remote storage. The configured local window is zero for this data, for example during backfills or replays.
Example: local.retention.ms is 1 hour. At 10:00, a backfill writes records stamped 07:00 the same day. The segment is uploaded at 10:05. At the next retention check, the records are already about 3 hours old, so the local copy is deleted right away. Consumers reading this data in the next hour must fetch it from remote storage.
2. Future timestamps
Records produced with future timestamps would block deletion: such a segment can't be deleted by time until its timestamp plus local.retention.ms has passed, and it blocks deletion of every later segment.
KAFKA-20609 works around this by using the segment file's last-modified time instead. But a disk replacement or a partition move resets that time, so the segment's age restarts from zero and its deletion is delayed again.
Example: 
`message.timestamp.after.max.ms` has been raised, so a record stamped one year ahead is accepted at 10:00. The segment is uploaded at 10:05.
- Without the fallback, the local copy stays on disk for a year, and so does every later segment.
- With the fallback, the local copy is deleted around 11:05. But if the partition is moved to another broker at 10:30, the file gets a new last-modified time, and deletion moves to around 11:30.
The change
This KIP changes local.retention.ms (and log.local.retention.ms) for tiered topics to mean: keep the local copy of a segment for local.retention.ms after it was uploaded to remote storage.
No new data has to be stored for this. When an upload finishes, the broker already records the upload time in the segment's remote log metadata. With the default metadata manager (`TopicBasedRemoteLogMetadataManager`), this is stored in the internal `__remote_log_metadata` topic, which other brokers read.
Public Interfaces
There are no new configs, except changes to existing configs. The meaning of one existing config changes, and one javadoc rule is added.
1. The meaning of `local.retention.ms` and `log.local.retention.ms`
This applies to tiered topics with remote copy enabled.
- Currently the local copy is deleted once the newest record timestamp in the segment is older than `local.retention.ms`. For future timestamps, the file's last-modified time is used instead.
- With this KIP - the local copy is deleted once `local.retention.ms` has passed since the segment was uploaded to remote storage.
New doc text for `local.retention.ms` (`TopicConfig.LOCAL_LOG_RETENTION_MS_DOC`):
> The number of milliseconds to keep a local log segment after it has been copied to remote storage. The time is counted from when the copy finished, not from the record timestamps in the segment. Default value is -2, which means the `retention.ms` value is used. The effective value should always be less than or equal to `retention.ms`.
Unaffected : Topics without tiered storage and configs - local.retention.bytes and log.local.retention.bytes
2. A clarified rule for `RemoteLogMetadataManager` plugins
The broker calls this method RemoteLogMetadataManager#remoteLogSegmentMetadata(....) , to look up a segment's upload time. This gets a javadoc addition. For a segment in state `COPY_SEGMENT_FINISHED`, the returned `eventTimestampMs()` must be the time the copy to remote storage finished. This is a new documented expectation for custom plugins.
If a custom plugin doesn't follow it:  the broker can't tell, so it uses whatever time the plugin returns.
For example, if a plugin returns the copy-started time, the local copy is deleted earlier by the time the copy took. If the plugin returns no metadata/upload time for the segment, local retention for that segment falls back to record timestamps and a warning is logged.

Change to the local retention check
Currently the local copy is deleted when `now - newest record timestamp > local.retention.ms`. If the record timestamp is in the future, the segment file's last-modified time is used instead.
With this kip, the local copy should be deleted when `now - upload time > local.retention.ms`. The upload time is the time the segment's copy to remote storage finished.
The broker reads the upload time from remote metadata and keeps it in memory. After a restart or a leadership change, a segment is not deleted by time until its upload time has been read again.
Where the upload time comes from? - There is no dedicated upload-time method. The broker uses `RemoteLogSegmentMetadata#eventTimestampMs()` from `RemoteLogMetadataManager#remoteLogSegmentMetadata(topicIdPartition, epoch, offset)` for a segment in state `COPY_SEGMENT_FINISHED`.  - `RemoteLogManager` sets the `COPY_SEGMENT_FINISHED` update's `eventTimestampMs` when the copy finishes.

The javadoc is added to `remoteLogSegmentMetadata(...)` in `storage/api/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/server/log/remote/storage/RemoteLogMetadataManager.java`.
Current javadoc:java
New javadoc (the added paragraph is the second one):java

All settings are defaults except for local retention. The broker accepts any past timestamp and future timestamps up to 1 hour ahead.java
The current time is 10:00. Each segment finishes uploading at 10:05.

Records are stamped 10:00, and the broker accepts them.
- Today: the local copy is deleted around 11:00, because the records are now more than 1 hour old.
- With this KIP: the local copy is deleted around 11:05, 1 hour after the upload.
Case B: future timestamps within the 1-hour limit.
Records are stamped 10:50, and the broker accepts them.
- Today: the local copy is deleted around 11:50. The last-modified fallback only applies while the timestamp is still in the future. After 10:50 the normal rule applies, so the data is deleted 1 hour after 10:50.
- With this KIP: the local copy is deleted around 11:05, 1 hour after the upload.
Case B': future timestamps beyond the 1-hour limit.
Records are stamped one year ahead.
- With the default limit, the broker rejects them with `INVALID_TIMESTAMP`. Nothing is written, so retention is not involved, today or with this KIP.

If the partition is moved to another broker at 10:30, the file gets a new last-modified time, and the deletion moves to around 11:30. With this KIP it is deleted around 11:05, even if the partition is moved.
Case C: old timestamps within `retention.ms`
. A backfill writes records stamped 07:00 today, and the broker accepts them.
- Today: the local copy is deleted around 10:05, right after the upload, because the records are already 3 hours old. The data gets no time on local disk.
- With this KIP: the local copy is deleted around 11:05, 1 hour after the upload.
Case D: old timestamps, beyond `retention.ms`
Records are stamped 30 days ago, and the broker accepts them.
- Today and with this KIP: the data is deleted around 10:05. It is past `retention.ms` (7 days), so it expires from remote storage right after the upload, and the local copy is deleted with it. This KIP does not change this case.
With this KIP, every accepted segment stays local until `upload time + local.retention.ms`, or until it expires under `retention.ms`, whichever comes first. The record timestamp no longer affects local …

Proposed Changes

rest.wadl.enable with the default value of 'true', and with the importance of 'low'.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

[S1] Comment by kirktrue (2026-03-20)
cc @lianetm @mjsax—This looks to be partly related to heartbeat interval timing.
[S2] Comment by mvanhorn (2026-03-31)
Right, the heartbeat interval timing is central to the bug. When re-auth fails, the heartbeat timer is left expired, so `timeToNextHeartbeat()` returns 0 and the poll loop spins.

The fix adds `heartbeat.failHeartbeat()` in both auth exception handlers (classic consumer) to reset the timer with backoff. For the async path, `maximumTimeToWait()` now checks `canSendRequest()` before returning 0 when `shouldHeartbeatNow()` is true, so the backoff is respected instead of busy-waiting.

Both paths are covered by new tests. CI is green.
[S3] Comment by lianetm (2026-06-30)
Hey @mvanhorn, sorry for the delays on this one. Could you please rebase? We'll be taking a look soon. Thanks!
[S4] Comment by mvanhorn (2026-07-06)
Rebased onto trunk. Two small conflicts:

In `maximumTimeToWait`, trunk added an UNSUBSCRIBED early-return and kept the combined `pollTimer.isExpired() || shouldHeartbeatNow()` condition. I kept trunk's UNSUBSCRIBED guard but used the split form this fix introduces (`pollTimer.isExpired()` alone returns 0, then the `shouldHeartbeatNow` branch checks `canSendRequest` before returning 0), since folding `shouldHeartbeatNow` back into the first condition would short-circuit and defeat the backoff fix.

The test conflict was just placement of the two new tests. `ConsumerHeartbeatRequestManagerTest` passes (66/66) and `:clients` checkstyle is clean, on JDK 17.
[S5] Comment by mvanhorn (2026-10-27)
Rebased onto trunk again (9f27eb6), and the PR is now smaller. #22836 fixed KAFKA-20253 for the consumer protocol in July, and trunk's `maximumTimeToWait` now waits a retry backoff while the coordinator is unknown. So I dropped this branch's changes to the async heartbeat managers and their test. On current trunk they also made a joining member wait out its first heartbeat interval, which broke trunk's own `testInitialHeartbeatIntervalUsesRequestTimeout`.

What's left is the classic protocol side, which #22836 didn't touch. `AbstractCoordinator`'s heartbeat thread now calls `heartbeat.failHeartbeat()` in its `AuthenticationException` and `GroupAuthorizationException` handlers. Without it the heartbeat timer stays expired after the failure, so `timeToNextHeartbeat()` returns 0 and the thread spins. `HeartbeatTest.testFailHeartbeatResetsTimerWithBackoff` covers that. HeartbeatTest, AbstractCoordinatorTest, ConsumerHeartbeatRequestManagerTest and StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestManagerTest pass on JDK 21 (402 tests), and `:clients` checkstyle is clean.

@lianetm, this is ready whenever you have time.

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1382: Expose Explicit Configuration Deletions to AlterConfigPolicy
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1382: Expose Explicit Configuration Deletions to AlterConfigPolicy
Expose Explicit Configuration Deletions to AlterConfigPolicy

Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: link
JIRA: KAFKA-21147
Released: TBD
Motivation
AlterConfigPolicy implementations receive an AlterConfigPolicy.RequestMetadata instance when a configuration change is validated. Its configs() method does not consistently identify explicit DELETE operations made through the Incremental Alter Configs API.
For a topic configuration, deleting an unset override is a no-op and does not generate a ConfigRecord. Consequently, the key is absent from configs(). For a broker configuration, Kafka generates a record even when the configuration is unset, so the key is present in configs() with a null value. A policy therefore cannot reliably determine whether a key was explicitly deleted by inspecting configs().
Changing configs() so every explicit deletion appears as a key mapped to null would resolve this inconsistency, but it would also change the behavior observed by existing policy implementations. In particular, KIP-1252 introduced alter.config.policy.kraft.compatibility.enable in Kafka 3.9.2 so ZooKeeper-based clusters could opt into the existing KRaft policy behavior before migrating. Changing that KRaft behavior in a later release would undermine the compatibility guarantee for users who enabled the setting.
This KIP proposes an additive API that exposes explicit deletions consistently while preserving the existing configs() contract and behavior. Existing policies continue to receive the same map, while policies that need operation-level deletion information can opt into the new method.
Public Interfaces
This KIP adds the following constructor and methods to the public AlterConfigPolicy.RequestMetadata class:public RequestMetadata(
    ConfigResource resource,
    Map<String, String> configs,
    Set<String> deletedConfigs
)
public Set<String> deletedConfigs()
public Map<String, String> configsWithoutNullValues()
The existing constructor remains unchanged:public RequestMetadata(ConfigResource resource, Map<String, String> configs)
Instances created with the existing constructor return an empty set from deletedConfigs().
deletedConfigs()
deletedConfigs() returns the names of configurations explicitly targeted by DELETE operations in an Incremental Alter Configs request. It includes deletions that do not generate metadata records, such as deleting an unset topic configuration.
The returned set is empty for legacy Alter Configs requests. It does not include configurations implicitly removed because they were omitted from a legacy full-replacement request.
The returned set is immutable and does not contain null.
configsWithoutNullValues()
configsWithoutNullValues() returns the entries from configs() whose values are non-null. This gives policy implementations a direct way to consume the existing configuration representation without interpreting null as either a value or an operation.
Calling this method does not change the meaning of configs() and does not replace deletedConfigs(): a no-op topic deletion may be absent from both maps but will still be present in deletedConfigs().
Proposed Changes
When processing an Incremental Alter Configs request, the controller will collect the key of every explicitly requested DELETE operation and pass those keys to RequestMetadata. Collection is based on the request operations rather than generated metadata records, so it is consistent across resource types and includes no-op deletions.
The behavior visible to a policy will be:
RequestExisting configs()New deletedConfigs()New configsWithoutNullValues()
Incremental SETExisting behavior: resulting key/valueEmptySame non-null entry
Incremental APPEND or SUBTRACTExisting behavior: resulting key/valueEmptySame non-null entry
Delete an existing topic overrideExisting behavior: key mapped to nullDeleted keyEntry omitted
Delete an unset topic overrideExisting behavior: key omittedDeleted keyEntry omitted
Delete a broker configurationExisting behavior: key mapped to null when a record is generatedDeleted keyEntry omitted
Legacy Alter Configs requestExisting behaviorEmptyNon-null entries from configs()
The existing two-argument constructor will delegate to the new constructor with an empty deletion set.
To avoid changing behavior unrelated to the new accessors, configs(), resource(), equals(Object), hashCode(), and toString() retain their existing semantics. In particular, the new deletion set will not alter equality or hash-code results for otherwise equivalent RequestMetadata instances.
No protocol, configuration, command-line, metric, or metadata-record changes are introduced.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The change is binary- and source-compatible for existing AlterConfigPolicy implementations. Existing implementations do not need to be rebuilt or modified.
configs() retains its current contents for every request. This preserves the KRaft behavior used as the compatibility target by KIP-1252 and avoids surprising users migrating from Kafka 3.9.2 with alter.config.policy.kraft.compatibility.enable=true.
Policies that need to validate explicit deletions can adopt deletedConfigs(). Policies that currently filter null values from configs() can optionally adopt configsWithoutNullValues().
There is no deprecation and no migration tool is required.
Test Plan
Unit tests will verify that:
deleting an unset topic configuration leaves configs() unchanged and exposes the key through deletedConfigs();
deleting an existing topic configuration exposes the key through deletedConfigs() while preserving the existing null entry in configs();
deleting an unset broker configuration exposes the key through deletedConfigs() while preserving existing configs() behavior;
non-delete incremental operations do not populate deletedConfigs();
legacy Alter Configs requests return an empty deletion set;
configsWithoutNullValues() excludes null-valued entries without changing configs();
the existing constructor continues to produce metadata with an empty deletion set; and
equality and hash-code behavior remain compatible with existing RequestMetadata instances.
No new system test is required because this proposal changes only the in-process arguments passed by the controller to the configured policy. Existing controller and policy unit tests exercise that boundary directly.
Documentation Plan
The Javadocs for RequestMetadata.configs() will document its existing record-derived behavior, including the differing representation of no-op topic deletions and broker deletions. The new constructor and accessors will document the explicit-deletion semantics and the behavior of legacy Alter Configs requests.
No user-facing broker configuration documentation changes are required.
Rejected Alternatives

Change configs() to include every explicit deletion as a null value
This was the approach taken by the original fix for KAFKA-19028. It is simple and makes topic and broker deletion behavior consistent inside the existing map. It also directly addresses the correctness concern that policies should be able to recognize every requested deletion.
However, it changes the input observed by existing policies. Users who enabled the KIP-1252 compatibility setting before migrating from ZooKeeper mode would no longer receive the KRaft behavior they explicitly selected. Because policy implementations may reject requests based on map membership or null values, the change could alter request outcomes after an upgrade. The additive API achieves the same validation capability without imposing that behavior change on existing policies.
Return effective values after deletions from configs()
Returning the default or inherited value after a deletion could make configs() look consistent with the effective-state representation used for some other incremental operations. It would not communicate that a deletion was explicitly requested, and a policy could not distinguish deletion from setting the same effective value. It would also change existing behavior.
Add only deletedConfigs()
This is sufficient to identify explicit deletions. Adding configsWithoutNullValues() as well provides an unambiguous non-null view for policies and avoids requiring every implementation to duplicate filtering logic. The two methods have distinct roles: one reports the requested operation, while the other provides a value-only view of the existing map.
Replace AlterConfigPolicy with a new policy interface
A new interface could model each incremental operation explicitly and address broader limitations of the existing policy API. That is substantially larger than the problem tracked by KAFKA-21147, would require a migration and deprecation plan, and would delay a narrowly scoped way to validate explicit deletions. Such a redesign can be proposed independently if broader policy requirements justify it.

[S1] Comment by kirktrue (2026-03-20)
cc @lianetm @mjsax—This looks to be partly related to heartbeat interval timing.
[S2] Comment by mvanhorn (2026-03-31)
Right, the heartbeat interval timing is central to the bug. When re-auth fails, the heartbeat timer is left expired, so `timeToNextHeartbeat()` returns 0 and the poll loop spins.

The fix adds `heartbeat.failHeartbeat()` in both auth exception handlers (classic consumer) to reset the timer with backoff. For the async path, `maximumTimeToWait()` now checks `canSendRequest()` before returning 0 when `shouldHeartbeatNow()` is true, so the backoff is respected instead of busy-waiting.

Both paths are covered by new tests. CI is green.
[S3] Comment by lianetm (2026-06-30)
Hey @mvanhorn, sorry for the delays on this one. Could you please rebase? We'll be taking a look soon. Thanks!
[S4] Comment by mvanhorn (2026-07-06)
Rebased onto trunk. Two small conflicts:

In `maximumTimeToWait`, trunk added an UNSUBSCRIBED early-return and kept the combined `pollTimer.isExpired() || shouldHeartbeatNow()` condition. I kept trunk's UNSUBSCRIBED guard but used the split form this fix introduces (`pollTimer.isExpired()` alone returns 0, then the `shouldHeartbeatNow` branch checks `canSendRequest` before returning 0), since folding `shouldHeartbeatNow` back into the first condition would short-circuit and defeat the backoff fix.

The test conflict was just placement of the two new tests. `ConsumerHeartbeatRequestManagerTest` passes (66/66) and `:clients` checkstyle is clean, on JDK 17.
[S5] Comment by mvanhorn (2026-10-27)
Rebased onto trunk again (9f27eb6), and the PR is now smaller. #22836 fixed KAFKA-20253 for the consumer protocol in July, and trunk's `maximumTimeToWait` now waits a retry backoff while the coordinator is unknown. So I dropped this branch's changes to the async heartbeat managers and their test. On current trunk they also made a joining member wait out its first heartbeat interval, which broke trunk's own `testInitialHeartbeatIntervalUsesRequestTimeout`.

What's left is the classic protocol side, which #22836 didn't touch. `AbstractCoordinator`'s heartbeat thread now calls `heartbeat.failHeartbeat()` in its `AuthenticationException` and `GroupAuthorizationException` handlers. Without it the heartbeat timer stays expired after the failure, so `timeToNextHeartbeat()` returns 0 and the thread spins. `HeartbeatTest.testFailHeartbeatResetsTimerWithBackoff` covers that. HeartbeatTest, AbstractCoordinatorTest, ConsumerHeartbeatRequestManagerTest and StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestManagerTest pass on JDK 21 (402 tests), and `:clients` checkstyle is clean.

@lianetm, this is ready whenever you have time.

Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: link
JIRA: KAFKA-21147
Released: TBD
Motivation
AlterConfigPolicy implementations receive an AlterConfigPolicy.RequestMetadata instance when a configuration change is validated. Its configs() method does not consistently identify explicit DELETE operations made through the Incremental Alter Configs API.
For a topic configuration, deleting an unset override is a no-op and does not generate a ConfigRecord. Consequently, the key is absent from configs(). For a broker configuration, Kafka generates a record even when the configuration is unset, so the key is present in configs() with a null value. A policy therefore cannot reliably determine whether a key was explicitly deleted by inspecting configs().
Changing configs() so every explicit deletion appears as a key mapped to null would resolve this inconsistency, but it would also change the behavior observed by existing policy implementations. In particular, KIP-1252 introduced alter.config.policy.kraft.compatibility.enable in Kafka 3.9.2 so ZooKeeper-based clusters could opt into the existing KRaft policy behavior before migrating. Changing that KRaft behavior in a later release would undermine the compatibility guarantee for users who enabled the setting.
This KIP proposes an additive API that exposes explicit deletions consistently while preserving the existing configs() contract and behavior. Existing policies continue to receive the same map, while policies that need operation-level deletion information can opt into the new method.
Public Interfaces
This KIP adds the following constructor and methods to the public AlterConfigPolicy.RequestMetadata class:public RequestMetadata(
    ConfigResource resource,
    Map<String, String> configs,
    Set<String> deletedConfigs
)
public Set<String> deletedConfigs()
public Map<String, String> configsWithoutNullValues()
The existing constructor remains unchanged:public RequestMetadata(ConfigResource resource, Map<String, String> configs)
Instances created with the existing constructor return an empty set from deletedConfigs().
deletedConfigs()
deletedConfigs() returns the names of configurations explicitly targeted by DELETE operations in an Incremental Alter Configs request. It includes deletions that do not generate metadata records, such as deleting an unset topic configuration.
The returned set is empty for legacy Alter Configs requests. It does not include configurations implicitly removed because they were omitted from a legacy full-replacement request.
The returned set is immutable and does not contain null.
configsWithoutNullValues()
configsWithoutNullValues() returns the entries from configs() whose values are non-null. This gives policy implementations a direct way to consume the existing configuration representation without interpreting null as either a value or an operation.
Calling this method does not change the meaning of configs() and does not replace deletedConfigs(): a no-op topic deletion may be absent from both maps but will still be present in deletedConfigs().
Proposed Changes
When processing an Incremental Alter Configs request, the controller will collect the key of every explicitly requested DELETE operation and pass those keys to RequestMetadata. Collection is based on the request operations rather than generated metadata records, so it is consistent across resource types and includes no-op deletions.
The behavior visible to a policy will be:
RequestExisting configs()New deletedConfigs()New configsWithoutNullValues()
Incremental SETExisting behavior: resulting key/valueEmptySame non-null entry
Incremental APPEND or SUBTRACTExisting behavior: resulting key/valueEmptySame non-null entry
Delete an existing topic overrideExisting behavior: key mapped to nullDeleted keyEntry omitted
Delete an unset topic overrideExisting behavior: key omittedDeleted keyEntry omitted
Delete a broker configurationExisting behavior: key mapped to null when a record is generatedDeleted keyEntry omitted
Legacy Alter Configs requestExisting behaviorEmptyNon-null entries from configs()
The existing two-argument constructor will delegate to the new constructor with an empty deletion set.
To avoid changing behavior unrelated to the new accessors, configs(), resource(), equals(Object), hashCode(), and toString() retain their existing semantics. In particular, the new deletion set will not alter equality or hash-code results for otherwise equivalent RequestMetadata instances.
No protocol, configuration, command-line, metric, or metadata-record changes are introduced.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The change is binary- and source-compatible for existing AlterConfigPolicy implementations. Existing implementations do not need to be rebuilt or modified.
configs() retains its current contents for every request. This preserves the KRaft behavior used as the compatibility target by KIP-1252 and avoids surprising users migrating from Kafka 3.9.2 with alter.config.policy.kraft.compatibility.enable=true.
Policies that need to validate explicit deletions can adopt deletedConfigs(). Policies that currently filter null values from configs() can optionally adopt configsWithoutNullValues().
There is no deprecation and no migration tool is required.
Test Plan
Unit tests will verify that:
deleting an unset topic configuration leaves configs() unchanged and exposes the key through deletedConfigs();
deleting an existing topic configuration exposes the key through deletedConfigs() while preserving the existing null entry in configs();
deleting an unset broker configuration exposes the key through deletedConfigs() while preserving existing configs() behavior;
non-delete incremental operations do not populate deletedConfigs();
legacy Alter Configs requests return an empty deletion set;
configsWithoutNullValues() excludes null-valued entries without changing configs();
the existing constructor continues to produce metadata with an empty deletion set; and
equality and hash-code behavior remain compatible with existing RequestMetadata instances.
No new system test is required because this proposal changes only the in-process arguments passed by the controller to the configured policy. Existing controller and policy unit tests exercise that boundary directly.
Documentation Plan
The Javadocs for RequestMetadata.configs() will document its existing record-derived behavior, including the differing representation of no-op topic deletions and broker deletions. The new constructor and accessors will document the explicit-deletion semantics and the behavior of legacy Alter Configs requests.
No user-facing broker configuration documentation changes are required.
Rejected Alternatives

Change configs() to include every explicit deletion as a null value
This was the approach taken by the original fix for KAFKA-19028. It is simple and makes topic and broker deletion behavior consistent inside the existing map. It also directly addresses the correctness concern that policies should be able to recognize every requested deletion.
However, it changes the input observed by existing policies. Users who enabled the KIP-1252 compatibility setting before migrating from ZooKeeper mode would no longer receive the KRaft behavior they explicitly selected. Because policy implementations may reject requests based on map membership or null values, the change could alter request outcomes after an upgrade. The additive API achieves the same validation capability without imposing that behavior change on existing policies.
Return effective values after deletions from configs()
Returning the default or inherited value after a deletion could make configs() look consistent with the effective-state representation used for some other incremental operations. It would not communicate that a deletion was explicitly requested, and a policy could not distinguish deletion from setting the same effective value. It would also change existing behavior.
Add only deletedConfigs()
This is sufficient to identify explicit deletions. Adding configsWithoutNullValues() as well provides an unambiguous non-null view for policies and avoids requiring every implementation to duplicate filtering logic. The two methods have distinct roles: one reports the requested operation, while the other provides a value-only view of the existing map.
Replace AlterConfigPolicy with a new policy interface
A new interface could model each incremental operation explicitly and address broader limitations of the existing policy API. That is substantially larger than the problem tracked by KAFKA-21147, would require a migration and deprecation plan, and would delay a narrowly scoped way to validate explicit deletions. Such a redesign can be proposed independently if broader policy requirements justify it.

Kafka is an important part of data infrastructure and is seeing significant adoption and growth. As the Kafka cluster size grows and more data is stored in Kafka for a longer duration, several issues related to scalability, efficiency, and operations become important to address.
Kafka stores the messages in append-only log segments on local disks on Kafka brokers. The retention period for the log is based on `log.retention` that can be set system-wide or per topic. This results in data consumers having to build different versions of applications to consume the data from different systems depending on the age of the data.

[S1] Page: KIP-1381: Allow Brokers to Disable Compression Types for Client Writes
Allow Brokers to Disable Compression Types for Client Writes

Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: link
JIRA: KAFKA-21178
Released: TBD
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki.
Motivation
Kafka supports gzip, Snappy, LZ4, and Zstandard compression for record batches. Brokers must retain support for decompressing every codec that may be present in existing log segments. Removing a codec implementation from Kafka would therefore prevent brokers from reading historical records that use that codec.
At the same time, operators may need to prevent new records from being written with a particular compression type. Reasons include a vulnerability in a compression library, a codec implementation becoming unmaintained, native-library compatibility problems, or an operational policy that prohibits a codec.
The existing compression.type broker and topic configuration does not provide this protection. When it is set to a specific codec, Kafka recompresses incoming records using that codec. However, Kafka must first decompress a producer-supplied batch. Consequently, forcing a different final compression type does not prevent a client from sending records encoded with an undesired codec.
This KIP proposes a broker-controlled denylist for compression types used by new client writes. The broker will reject a write before decompressing its records when either:
The producer supplied a disabled compression type; or
The broker would recompress the records using a disabled compression type.
The restriction will not apply when reading or replicating existing records. This preserves compatibility with historical log data and allows replicas to remain synchronized.
Public Interfaces

New broker configuration
A new broker configuration will be introduced:
PropertyValue
Namecompression.disabled.types
TypeList
DefaultEmpty list
Valid valuesgzip, snappy, lz4, zstd
Dynamic update modeCluster-wide
ImportanceHigh
Example:compression.disabled.types=snappy,lz4
The configuration contains a comma-separated list of compression types that brokers must reject for new client writes.
An empty list preserves the existing behavior and permits every compression type supported by Kafka.
none is not a valid entry because uncompressed records do not invoke an external compression implementation.
This is a broker-only configuration. It will not have a corresponding topic-level configuration and therefore cannot be overridden by a topic configuration.
Produce API behavior
No request or response schema changes are proposed.
When a client produce request uses a disabled compression type, the affected partition will return the existing UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE error.
The same error will be returned when the effective topic configuration would cause the broker to recompress the records using a disabled type.
For example, given:compression.disabled.types=snappy
the broker will reject both of the following cases:
A producer sends a Snappy-compressed record batch, regardless of the effective compression.type.
The effective topic configuration has compression.type=snappy, even when the producer sends an uncompressed batch or uses another compression type.
Other partitions in the same produce request will continue to be processed according to the existing produce-request behavior.
Dynamic configuration
compression.disabled.types will support cluster-wide dynamic updates through the existing broker configuration API.
For example:bin/kafka-configs.sh \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --entity-type brokers \
  --entity-default \
  --alter \
  --add-config compression.disabled.types=snappy,lz4
A dynamic update will be propagated to existing logs without requiring a broker restart.
As with other dynamic broker configurations, propagation is asynchronous. During propagation, brokers may temporarily observe different values. Enforcement for a partition is determined by the current configuration of its leader.
Proposed Changes

Configuration parsing and propagation
The broker configuration definition will declare compression.disabled.types as a list containing zero or more supported compressed record codecs.
Unknown values will cause configuration validation to fail. For example:compression.disabled.types=brotli
will be rejected because Brotli is not a Kafka record-batch compression type.
The parsed configuration will be represented internally as a set of compression types. It will be included in the broker’s default log configuration and propagated to existing logs when the dynamic broker configuration changes.
The value will be stored as an internal log property rather than exposed as a topic property. This prevents principals with topic-configuration privileges from overriding a restriction established by the cluster administrator.
Produce-path validation
Kafka currently determines two compression types while processing a client append:
The source compression type declared in the producer’s record-batch header.
The target compression type selected from the effective compression.type configuration.
For client-originated appends, Kafka will check both types against compression.disabled.types before record validation or decompression begins.
If either compression type is disabled, Kafka will throw UnsupportedCompressionTypeException. The existing exception-to-protocol mapping will return UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE in the produce response.
Checking the producer compression type before decompression is important because it avoids invoking the disabled codec while processing the rejected request.
Checking the target compression type prevents Kafka itself from writing data with a disabled codec.
Append origins
The restriction will apply only to appends with CLIENT origin.
It will not apply to:
REPLICATION appends
COORDINATOR appends
RAFT_LEADER appends
Replication must remain permitted so that followers can receive records already accepted by a leader and historical partitions can be reassigned or recovered.
Coordinator and Raft writes are trusted broker-internal operations and are not controlled by external producers. Compression used by internal topics continues to be governed by the existing internal-topic configurations.
Existing records
The proposed configuration does not disable decompression globally.
Existing records using a disabled compression type may still be:
Fetched by consumers
Replicated between brokers
Recovered during broker startup
Examined by broker log operations
Processed by log compaction
This distinction is required because Kafka cannot safely remove the ability to interpret codecs already present in log segments.
The configuration prevents additional client data using the codec from entering the log; it is not a mechanism for removing or rewriting historical data.
Interaction with compression.type
The existing compression.type setting continues to select the final on-disk compression type.
If its effective value selects a codec included in compression.disabled.types, new client writes will be rejected with UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE.
For example:compression.type=snappy
compression.disabled.types=snappy
is a valid configuration, but client writes governed by that effective compression configuration will be rejected. This permits administrators to disable a codec dynamically even when existing topics or broker defaults still select it. Administrators can subsequently change compression.type without making the denylist update dependent on simultaneous topic-configuration changes.
When compression.type=producer, the producer’s source compression type is also the target type, and the same validation applies.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The default value is an empty list, so upgrading Kafka will not change existing behavior.
No existing configuration, API, record format, or compression type is deprecated or removed.
Operators who enable the configuration must ensure that producers stop using the disabled codecs. Produce requests that continue to use them will fail with UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE.
A suggested migration sequence is:
Identify producers using the codec that will be disabled.
Reconfigure those producers to use another codec or no compression.
Confirm that the new producer configuration has taken effect.
Add the codec to compression.disabled.types.
Monitor produce errors for clients that still use the disabled codec.
Before enabling the setting during a rolling upgrade, every broker that may become a partition leader should run a Kafka version supporting this KIP. Otherwise, enforcement may depend on which broker is currently the leader.
Before downgrading to a version that does not support this KIP, operators should remove the dynamic configuration. Static configuration should also be removed from broker property files before starting an older broker version.
Disabling a codec does not rewrite existing segments. Operators must retain the corresponding codec library …

[S1] Page: KIP-1381: Allow Brokers to Disable Compression Types for Client Writes
Allow Brokers to Disable Compression Types for Client Writes

Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: link
JIRA: KAFKA-21178
Released: TBD
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki.
Motivation
Kafka supports gzip, Snappy, LZ4, and Zstandard compression for record batches. Brokers must retain support for decompressing every codec that may be present in existing log segments. Removing a codec implementation from Kafka would therefore prevent brokers from reading historical records that use that codec.
At the same time, operators may need to prevent new records from being written with a particular compression type. Reasons include a vulnerability in a compression library, a codec implementation becoming unmaintained, native-library compatibility problems, or an operational policy that prohibits a codec.
The existing compression.type broker and topic configuration does not provide this protection. When it is set to a specific codec, Kafka recompresses incoming records using that codec. However, Kafka must first decompress a producer-supplied batch. Consequently, forcing a different final compression type does not prevent a client from sending records encoded with an undesired codec.
This KIP proposes a broker-controlled denylist for compression types used by new client writes. The broker will reject a write before decompressing its records when either:
The producer supplied a disabled compression type; or
The broker would recompress the records using a disabled compression type.
The restriction will not apply when reading or replicating existing records. This preserves compatibility with historical log data and allows replicas to remain synchronized.
Public Interfaces

New broker configuration
A new broker configuration will be introduced:
PropertyValue
Namecompression.disabled.types
TypeList
DefaultEmpty list
Valid valuesgzip, snappy, lz4, zstd
Dynamic update modeCluster-wide
ImportanceHigh
Example:compression.disabled.types=snappy,lz4
The configuration contains a comma-separated list of compression types that brokers must reject for new client writes.
An empty list preserves the existing behavior and permits every compression type supported by Kafka.
none is not a valid entry because uncompressed records do not invoke an external compression implementation.
This is a broker-only configuration. It will not have a corresponding topic-level configuration and therefore cannot be overridden by a topic configuration.
Produce API behavior
No request or response schema changes are proposed.
When a client produce request uses a disabled compression type, the affected partition will return the existing UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE error.
The same error will be returned when the effective topic configuration would cause the broker to recompress the records using a disabled type.
For example, given:compression.disabled.types=snappy
the broker will reject both of the following cases:
A producer sends a Snappy-compressed record batch, regardless of the effective compression.type.
The effective topic configuration has compression.type=snappy, even when the producer sends an uncompressed batch or uses another compression type.
Other partitions in the same produce request will continue to be processed according to the existing produce-request behavior.
Dynamic configuration
compression.disabled.types will support cluster-wide dynamic updates through the existing broker configuration API.
For example:bin/kafka-configs.sh \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --entity-type brokers \
  --entity-default \
  --alter \
  --add-config compression.disabled.types=snappy,lz4
A dynamic update will be propagated to existing logs without requiring a broker restart.
As with other dynamic broker configurations, propagation is asynchronous. During propagation, brokers may temporarily observe different values. Enforcement for a partition is determined by the current configuration of its leader.
Proposed Changes

Configuration parsing and propagation
The broker configuration definition will declare compression.disabled.types as a list containing zero or more supported compressed record codecs.
Unknown values will cause configuration validation to fail. For example:compression.disabled.types=brotli
will be rejected because Brotli is not a Kafka record-batch compression type.
The parsed configuration will be represented internally as a set of compression types. It will be included in the broker’s default log configuration and propagated to existing logs when the dynamic broker configuration changes.
The value will be stored as an internal log property rather than exposed as a topic property. This prevents principals with topic-configuration privileges from overriding a restriction established by the cluster administrator.
Produce-path validation
Kafka currently determines two compression types while processing a client append:
The source compression type declared in the producer’s record-batch header.
The target compression type selected from the effective compression.type configuration.
For client-originated appends, Kafka will check both types against compression.disabled.types before record validation or decompression begins.
If either compression type is disabled, Kafka will throw UnsupportedCompressionTypeException. The existing exception-to-protocol mapping will return UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE in the produce response.
Checking the producer compression type before decompression is important because it avoids invoking the disabled codec while processing the rejected request.
Checking the target compression type prevents Kafka itself from writing data with a disabled codec.
Append origins
The restriction will apply only to appends with CLIENT origin.
It will not apply to:
REPLICATION appends
COORDINATOR appends
RAFT_LEADER appends
Replication must remain permitted so that followers can receive records already accepted by a leader and historical partitions can be reassigned or recovered.
Coordinator and Raft writes are trusted broker-internal operations and are not controlled by external producers. Compression used by internal topics continues to be governed by the existing internal-topic configurations.
Existing records
The proposed configuration does not disable decompression globally.
Existing records using a disabled compression type may still be:
Fetched by consumers
Replicated between brokers
Recovered during broker startup
Examined by broker log operations
Processed by log compaction
This distinction is required because Kafka cannot safely remove the ability to interpret codecs already present in log segments.
The configuration prevents additional client data using the codec from entering the log; it is not a mechanism for removing or rewriting historical data.
Interaction with compression.type
The existing compression.type setting continues to select the final on-disk compression type.
If its effective value selects a codec included in compression.disabled.types, new client writes will be rejected with UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE.
For example:compression.type=snappy
compression.disabled.types=snappy
is a valid configuration, but client writes governed by that effective compression configuration will be rejected. This permits administrators to disable a codec dynamically even when existing topics or broker defaults still select it. Administrators can subsequently change compression.type without making the denylist update dependent on simultaneous topic-configuration changes.
When compression.type=producer, the producer’s source compression type is also the target type, and the same validation applies.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
The default value is an empty list, so upgrading Kafka will not change existing behavior.
No existing configuration, API, record format, or compression type is deprecated or removed.
Operators who enable the configuration must ensure that producers stop using the disabled codecs. Produce requests that continue to use them will fail with UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE.
A suggested migration sequence is:
Identify producers using the codec that will be disabled.
Reconfigure those producers to use another codec or no compression.
Confirm that the new producer configuration has taken effect.
Add the codec to compression.disabled.types.
Monitor produce errors for clients that still use the disabled codec.
Before enabling the setting during a rolling upgrade, every broker that may become a partition leader should run a Kafka version supporting this KIP. Otherwise, enforcement may depend on which broker is currently the leader.
Before downgrading to a version that does not support this KIP, operators should remove the dynamic configuration. Static configuration should also be removed from broker property files before starting an older broker version.
Disabling a codec does not rewrite existing segments. Operators must retain the corresponding codec library …

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1383: Standard record headers for content type
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1383: Standard record headers for content type
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here [Ticket will be opened once the KIP is approved]
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
For many releases, Kafka records have been able to include additional information alongside the payload in the form of headers. Compared with other messaging technologies, Kafka has very little standard metadata which describes the records. One obvious kind of metadata which is would be helpful to carry is the “content type” of the records. In a future Kafka with schema support, the schema information would naturally live in the record headers. This KIP proposes using standard headers for carrying this kind of metadata.
The presence of this information makes many scenarios easier. For example, a UI for browsing the records on a topic has a much better chance of being able to render the records properly if it can tell what they are. An error topic used to accumulate records which could not be delivered can safely contain many different kinds of records if they have headers enabling them to be deserialized. Finally, people trying to write a "smart deserializer" no longer need to guess what the records are.
Proposed Changes
This KIP introduces the concept of standard record headers. A standard record header is a record header used by Kafka to annotate records with additional metadata. Kafka reserves headers with keys starting with the characters "__"  (double underscore). KIP-298 introduced headers starting with these characters for dead-letter queues in Kafka Connect, and KIP-1191 did a similar thing for dead-letter queues in share groups, so there is clear precedent.
The KIP defines the following standard record headers.
Header nameJava constantString valueMeaning
Key content typeHeader.CONTENT_TYPE_KEY "__ct.k" This header describes the content type of the record's key. The value of this header is one of the content types is defined in the table below.
Value content typeHeader.CONTENT_TYPE_VALUE "__ct.v" This header describes the content type of the record's value. The value of this header is one of the content types is defined in the table below.
Schema information would be another obvious candidate for standard record headers.
Content type
The KIP defines two standard record headers for describing the content type of a record. "__ct.k" describes the content type of the record's key, while "__ct.v" describes the content type of the record's value. These are the equivalent of the HTTP content-type header giving the consumers knowledge of the content they are about to receive.
The following table contains the values used for the content-type headers, "__ct.k" and "__ct.v":
Java constantByte valueMeaningAssociated serializer
Content.BYTES 0The content is an array of bytes.ByteArraySerializer, ByteBufferSerializer
Content.STRING_UTF8 1The content is a string in UTF8 encoding.StringSerializer
Content.BOOLEAN 2The content is a boolean.BooleanSerializer
Content.DOUBLE 3The content is a 64-bit floating-point number.DoubleSerializer
Content.FLOAT 4The content is a 32-bit floating-point number.FloatSerializer
Content.INTEGER 5The content is a 32-bit integer.IntegerSerializer
Content.LONG 6The content is a 64-bit integer.LongSerializer
Content.SHORT 7The content is a 16-bit integer.ShortSerializer
Content.UUID 8The content is a UUID expressed as a string in UTF8 format.UuidSerializer
Content.JSON 9The content is in JSON encoding.JsonSerializer
Content.MIME 255, followed by any MIME type in UTF8 encodingThe content is in the MIME type.
Additional Content  values can be added by future KIPs.
Handling by serializers and deserializers
The serializers mentioned in the table above can annotate the records they serialize with the content-type record headers. For compatibility reasons, this behavior is controlled by configuration, key.serializer.content.type.enable  and value.serializer.content.type.enable for key and value serializers respectively. In AK 4.x, these configurations default to false while in AK 5.0, they default to true . If true , the serializer adds the content-type header to the record headers. This means that an application using one of these serializers and not setting an explicit value for these configurations will have the content-type headers added to its records as it migrates to Apache Kafka 5.0 serializers.
The deserializers use the content-type header in the equivalent way with the new behaviour controlled by configuration, key.deserializer.content.type.enable  and value.deserializer.content.type.enable for key and value deserializers respectively. If the configuration is false , the deserializer does not look for or validate the content-type header. If the configuration is true , the deserializer deserializes the record if it does not have a content-type header or if the value of the header matches the content type it supports. If the content-type header is present and does not contain the expected value, the deserializer throws the new exception org.apache.kafka.common.errors.ContentTypeException  which is a subclass of SerializationException .

[S1] Page: KIP-1383: Standard record headers for content type
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here 
JIRA: here [Ticket will be opened once the KIP is approved]
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
For many releases, Kafka records have been able to include additional information alongside the payload in the form of headers. Compared with other messaging technologies, Kafka has very little standard metadata which describes the records. One obvious kind of metadata which is would be helpful to carry is the “content type” of the records. In a future Kafka with schema support, the schema information would naturally live in the record headers. This KIP proposes using standard headers for carrying this kind of metadata.
The presence of this information makes many scenarios easier. For example, a UI for browsing the records on a topic has a much better chance of being able to render the records properly if it can tell what they are. An error topic used to accumulate records which could not be delivered can safely contain many different kinds of records if they have headers enabling them to be deserialized. Finally, people trying to write a "smart deserializer" no longer need to guess what the records are.
Proposed Changes
This KIP introduces the concept of standard record headers. A standard record header is a record header used by Kafka to annotate records with additional metadata. Kafka reserves headers with keys starting with the characters "__"  (double underscore). KIP-298 introduced headers starting with these characters for dead-letter queues in Kafka Connect, and KIP-1191 did a similar thing for dead-letter queues in share groups, so there is clear precedent.
The KIP defines the following standard record headers.
Header nameJava constantString valueMeaning
Key content typeHeader.CONTENT_TYPE_KEY "__ct.k" This header describes the content type of the record's key. The value of this header is one of the content types is defined in the table below.
Value content typeHeader.CONTENT_TYPE_VALUE "__ct.v" This header describes the content type of the record's value. The value of this header is one of the content types is defined in the table below.
Schema information would be another obvious candidate for standard record headers.
Content type
The KIP defines two standard record headers for describing the content type of a record. "__ct.k" describes the content type of the record's key, while "__ct.v" describes the content type of the record's value. These are the equivalent of the HTTP content-type header giving the consumers knowledge of the content they are about to receive.
The following table contains the values used for the content-type headers, "__ct.k" and "__ct.v":
Java constantByte valueMeaningAssociated serializer
Content.BYTES 0The content is an array of bytes.ByteArraySerializer, ByteBufferSerializer
Content.STRING_UTF8 1The content is a string in UTF8 encoding.StringSerializer
Content.BOOLEAN 2The content is a boolean.BooleanSerializer
Content.DOUBLE 3The content is a 64-bit floating-point number.DoubleSerializer
Content.FLOAT 4The content is a 32-bit floating-point number.FloatSerializer
Content.INTEGER 5The content is a 32-bit integer.IntegerSerializer
Content.LONG 6The content is a 64-bit integer.LongSerializer
Content.SHORT 7The content is a 16-bit integer.ShortSerializer
Content.UUID 8The content is a UUID expressed as a string in UTF8 format.UuidSerializer
Content.JSON 9The content is in JSON encoding.JsonSerializer
Content.MIME 255, followed by any MIME type in UTF8 encodingThe content is in the MIME type.
Additional Content  values can be added by future KIPs.
Handling by serializers and deserializers
The serializers mentioned in the table above can annotate the records they serialize with the content-type record headers. For compatibility reasons, this behavior is controlled by configuration, key.serializer.content.type.enable  and value.serializer.content.type.enable for key and value serializers respectively. In AK 4.x, these configurations default to false while in AK 5.0, they default to true . If true , the serializer adds the content-type header to the record headers. This means that an application using one of these serializers and not setting an explicit value for these configurations will have the content-type headers added to its records as it migrates to Apache Kafka 5.0 serializers.
The deserializers use the content-type header in the equivalent way with the new behaviour controlled by configuration, key.deserializer.content.type.enable  and value.deserializer.content.type.enable for key and value deserializers respectively. If the configuration is false , the deserializer does not look for or validate the content-type header. If the configuration is true , the deserializer deserializes the record if it does not have a content-type header or if the value of the header matches the content type it supports. If the content-type header is present and does not contain the expected value, the deserializer throws the new exception org.apache.kafka.common.errors.ContentTypeException  which is a subclass of SerializationException .
