Typically, all test cases in benchmark_test.py are designed to wait until ProducerPerformance completes its execution[1]. However, it seems that the tests are not doing this correctly (or possibly ProducerPerformance crashes during the test). As a result, the tests may parse intermediate output instead of waiting for the final output, which leads to errors.

In a normal scenario, we should expect ProducerPerformance to output something like this:

7182435 records sent, 1436487.0 records/sec (13.70 MB/sec), 9.6 ms avg latency, 340.0 ms max latency.
1604593 records sent, 320918.6 records/sec (3.06 MB/sec), 0.7 ms avg latency, 18.0 ms max latency.
2251787 records sent, 448920.9 records/sec (4.28 MB/sec), 0.8 ms avg latency, 278.0 ms max latency.
13421772 records sent, 748439.859477 records/sec (7.14 MB/sec), 5.58 ms avg latency, 340.00 ms max latency, 1 ms 50th, 28 ms 95th, 117 ms 99th, 131 ms 99.9th.

The tests are expected to parse the last line of this output. However, if they parse intermediate results (i.e., any lines before the last one), it can cause errors.

[1]: [https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/0711d1558250c60807dfa815d46907eac8bb4b98/tests/kafkatest/services/performance/producer_performance.py#L140]
[S3] Comment by Chia-Ping Tsai (2024-08-14)
The root cause is the JVM process gets killed by OOM-killer, so the "final" metrics output is gone also. see following message

however, I'm not sure why PB runs out of memory so easy in the test.

Just as one data point, I ran this locally via ducker-ak, and it passed for me.

However, I can believe that the memory consumption might not be ideal. So if you want to get your change into 3.9, I think that's reasonable.

However, I'm not sure if this is a blocker. Nothing changed here between 3.8 and 3.9, did it?

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1384: Base image for system test dependencies
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1384: Base image for system test dependencies
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread.html/jqbjdxv1ormzcgbrfn5hk46mls8oh6tk
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21261
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Every release today ends with a manual upload to an S3 bucket that only Confluent can write to. The system tests then run against copies of the release that nobody verifies.
The compatibility and upgrade tests run older releases from /opt/kafka-<version>. The tests/docker/Dockerfile downloads them from https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/kafka-packages. Each release needs one line for its binary tarball and one for its kafka-streams-<version>-test.jar, which the streams upgrade tests load from libs/. The vagrant/base.sh keeps a second copy of the same list.
After a release, the Release Process asks the release manager to:
Update gradle/dependencies.gradle, tests/docker/Dockerfile, tests/kafkatest/version.py and vagrant/base.sh, as in #22373 and #23629.
Upload both tarballs and the test jar to kafka-packages. Confluent owns the bucket, so a release manager who does not work there has to ask a Confluent committer.
This causes three problems:
Uploads get missed. The upload is one of the After release steps in the Release Process, so a release manager may forget it. 
The copies are not the released artifacts. Nothing checks a checksum or a signature. The 2.4.1 and 4.2.2 test jars on S3 hold the same classes as Maven Central but were rebuilt later, so their bytes differ.
The test setup depends on a vendor's bucket. The project cannot fix a missing or broken file without asking Confluent.
Public Interfaces
This KIP changes no public interface: no protocol, client API, configuration, metric or command-line tool. Only the system test setup changes:
Item
Change
Details
ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps
New container image
Tagged with the 12-character tree hash of tests/docker/deps, plus latest from trunk. For testing only, not a release artifact
KAFKA_DEPS_IMAGE build arg of tests/docker/Dockerfile
New
Defaults to ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps:latest. Set it to use a local or pinned image
KAFKA_MIRROR build arg of tests/docker/Dockerfile
Removed
APACHE_DIST_URL and MAVEN_REPO_URL take over
APACHE_DIST_URL and MAVEN_REPO_URL build args of tests/docker/deps/Dockerfile
New
Default to https://archive.apache.org/dist and https://repo1.maven.org/maven2
Build System Test Dependencies Image workflow
New
Runs on trunk pushes that touch tests/docker/deps/**, or by hand
Proposed Changes
One image, ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps, holds every release the system tests need. A workflow builds it from the official artifacts, and the ducker image copies it instead of downloading from S3.
The deps image
A new directory, tests/docker/deps/, holds a Dockerfile and a fetch-kafka.sh script. The Dockerfile lists one line per release:RUN fetch-kafka 4.2.2 2.13
RUN fetch-kafka 4.3.1 2.13
fetch-kafka.sh <version> <scala version> does the following:
Downloads kafka_<scala>-<version>.tgz from https://archive.apache.org/dist/kafka/<version>/.
Downloads kafka-streams-<version>-test.jar from Maven Central.
Verifies both detached signatures against https://downloads.apache.org/kafka/KEYS, as docker/jvm/Dockerfile already does for the release image.
Installs the release into /opt/kafka-<version> and puts the test jar into its libs/.
The publishing workflow
A new workflow, .github/workflows/system_test_deps_image.yml, builds and pushes the image:
Setting
Value
Why
Trigger
A push to trunk that touches tests/docker/deps/**, or workflow_dispatch
The image is published as soon as the release PR merges
Tags
The git tree hash of tests/docker/deps (12 characters), plus latest from trunk
The hash names the content and never moves; latest follows trunk
Changes to tests/docker/Dockerfile
The curl lines become a stage and one COPY:ARG KAFKA_DEPS_IMAGE="ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps:latest"
FROM $KAFKA_DEPS_IMAGE AS kafka-deps

Status
Current state: Under Discussion

JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21261
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Every release today ends with a manual upload to an S3 bucket that only Confluent can write to. The system tests then run against copies of the release that nobody verifies.
The compatibility and upgrade tests run older releases from /opt/kafka-<version>. The tests/docker/Dockerfile downloads them from https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/kafka-packages. Each release needs one line for its binary tarball and one for its kafka-streams-<version>-test.jar, which the streams upgrade tests load from libs/. The vagrant/base.sh keeps a second copy of the same list.
After a release, the Release Process asks the release manager to:
Update gradle/dependencies.gradle, tests/docker/Dockerfile, tests/kafkatest/version.py and vagrant/base.sh, as in #22373 and #23629.
Upload both tarballs and the test jar to kafka-packages. Confluent owns the bucket, so a release manager who does not work there has to ask a Confluent committer.
This causes three problems:
Uploads get missed. The upload is one of the After release steps in the Release Process, so a release manager may forget it. 
The copies are not the released artifacts. Nothing checks a checksum or a signature. The 2.4.1 and 4.2.2 test jars on S3 hold the same classes as Maven Central but were rebuilt later, so their bytes differ.
The test setup depends on a vendor's bucket. The project cannot fix a missing or broken file without asking Confluent.
Public Interfaces
This KIP changes no public interface: no protocol, client API, configuration, metric or command-line tool. Only the system test setup changes:
Item
Change
Details
ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps
New container image
Tagged with the 12-character tree hash of tests/docker/deps, plus latest from trunk. For testing only, not a release artifact

New

KAFKA_MIRROR build arg of tests/docker/Dockerfile
Removed
APACHE_DIST_URL and MAVEN_REPO_URL take over
APACHE_DIST_URL and MAVEN_REPO_URL build args of tests/docker/deps/Dockerfile
New
Default to https://archive.apache.org/dist and https://repo1.maven.org/maven2
Build System Test Dependencies Image workflow
New
Runs on trunk pushes that touch tests/docker/deps/**, or by hand
Proposed Changes
One image, ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps, holds every release the system tests need. A workflow builds it from the official artifacts, and the ducker image copies it instead of downloading from S3.
The deps image
A new directory, tests/docker/deps/, holds a Dockerfile and a fetch-kafka.sh script. The Dockerfile lists one line per release:RUN fetch-kafka 4.2.2 2.13
RUN fetch-kafka 4.3.1 2.13

Downloads kafka_<scala>-<version>.tgz from https://archive.apache.org/dist/kafka/<version>/.

Installs the release into /opt/kafka-<version> and puts the test jar into its libs/.

Setting
Value
Why

The image is published as soon as the release PR merges

CONVERSATION: Ticket KAFKA-17464: Flaky test: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.AbstractCoordinatorTest.testWakeupAfterSyncGroupSentExternalCompletion
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Chu Cheng Li (2024-10-12)
I ran the tests for 100 times with

I=0; while ./gradlew clients:test -tests AbstractCoordinatorTest.testWakeupAfterSyncGroupSentExternalCompletion -rerun; do (( I=$I+1 )); echo "Completed run: $I"; sleep 1; done 
and it didn't fail
[^test_result]
[S2] Comment by Matthias J. Sax (2025-01-07)
Just failed two times in a row on [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/18402]
[S3] Comment by Szymon Blumczynski (2026-08-21)
Duplicate of KAFKA-18310, fixed by https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/18945 (commit 19d8a414ef (https://github.com/apache/kafka/commit/19d8a414ef6d86596d5f8d33828d8d7560cc8678), fix version 4.1.0). That ticket covered all three AbstractCoordinatorTest sync-group wakeup tests, including this one.

Cause: ensureActiveGroup() starts the real HeartbeatThread before joinGroupIfNeeded(). The heartbeat loop calls client.pollNoWakeup(), whose trySend() can transmit the queued SyncGroupRequest and MockClient.send() is where the test's RequestMatcher (and therefore consumerClient.wakeup()) runs. Because pollNoWakeup() passes disableWakeup=true, that thread sets the wakeup flag and completes the future without raising anything. The main thread sits in ConsumerNetworkClient.poll(future, timer), whose do/while only checks the flag inside poll(); seeing future.isDone() it exits without another iteration, so maybeTriggerWakeup() never runs and ensureActiveGroup() returns normally.

The fix extracted BaseHeartbeatThread and injects a Mockito mock in these tests, so the SyncGroup request is always sent by the main thread and the wakeup is observed deterministically. The test has carried no @Flaky annotation on trunk since then.

Hey [~apoorvmittal10], I believe we can close this one as it is a Duplicate of KAFKA-18310.

[S1] Comment by Chu Cheng Li (2024-10-12)
I ran the tests for 100 times with

[^test_result]
[S2] Comment by Matthias J. Sax (2025-01-07)
Just failed two times in a row on [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/18402]
[S3] Comment by Szymon Blumczynski (2026-08-21)
Duplicate of KAFKA-18310, fixed by https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/18945 (commit 19d8a414ef (https://github.com/apache/kafka/commit/19d8a414ef6d86596d5f8d33828d8d7560cc8678), fix version 4.1.0). That ticket covered all three AbstractCoordinatorTest sync-group wakeup tests, including this one.

Cause: ensureActiveGroup() starts the real HeartbeatThread before joinGroupIfNeeded(). The heartbeat loop calls client.pollNoWakeup(), whose trySend() can transmit the queued SyncGroupRequest and MockClient.send() is where the test's RequestMatcher (and therefore consumerClient.wakeup()) runs. Because pollNoWakeup() passes disableWakeup=true, that thread sets the wakeup flag and completes the future without raising anything. The main thread sits in ConsumerNetworkClient.poll(future, timer), whose do/while only checks the flag inside poll(); seeing future.isDone() it exits without another iteration, so maybeTriggerWakeup() never runs and ensureActiveGroup() returns normally.

The fix extracted BaseHeartbeatThread and injects a Mockito mock in these tests, so the SyncGroup request is always sent by the main thread and the wakeup is observed deterministically. The test has carried no @Flaky annotation on trunk since then.

Hey [~apoorvmittal10], I believe we can close this one as it is a Duplicate of KAFKA-18310.

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1386: Per-call record limit for Consumer poll
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1386: Per-call record limit for Consumer poll
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21350
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
max.poll.records and max.poll.interval.ms are read when a consumer is constructed and neither can be changed afterwards.
If processing slows down, a batch that used to fit inside the poll interval stops fitting. The consumer misses its deadline and leaves the group. The assignment is released through onPartitionsLost, so the in-flight batch was never committed and the next owner reprocesses it.
The consumer rejoins and asks for the same batch size without any changes to config. It misses the deadline again. This continues until the slowdown ends. A shared dependency degrades for all members at once, so they hit it together and the group rebalances repeatedly. The common response is a process restart after increasing max.poll.interval.ms or decreasing max.poll.records, which reassigns every group in that JVM.
The existing levers do not help. pause() postpones records without reducing them, so SmallRye's Kafka connector pauses partitions for backpressure and keeps its own queue, sized at max.poll.records times a factor. Spring Integration's KafkaMessageSource returns one record per receive(), so it rewrites the user's ConsumerFactory with max.poll.records=1 or refuses to start; allowMultiFetch instead buffers the batch and drains it one record at a time, and the documentation then warns you to process the batch and poll again within max.poll.interval.ms.
max.poll.interval.ms does two jobs. It detects a dead member, and it gives a live member headroom. It is also not local: the consumer sends it to the coordinator as a rebalance timeout, so it sets how long the rest of the group waits for this member to hand its partitions back, and varying it per call would change that wait for everyone else. It is unchanged by this proposal.
max.poll.records is read inside the consumer and sent nowhere, and it is already only a maximum, because the consumer returns fewer records whenever fewer are buffered. Choosing it on each call changes when the value is picked rather than what it means. An application measures its own throughput and knows whether a smaller batch means less work. This KIP lets it set the batch size per call.
Public Interfaces
javaPollOptions.java
max.poll.records
No change to the default, the type or the behaviour. The documentation gains a sentence naming the per-call override:javamax.poll.records
Consumer
javaConsumer.java
KafkaConsumer
javaConsumer.java
Metrics
Five metrics in the consumer-metrics group, tagged client-id. They are for an operator reading JMX. An application sizes the limit from its own clock.
MetricGroupTypeMeaning
poll-interval-remaining-msconsumer-metricsgaugeTime left before the poll interval expires.
poll-budget-used-ratio-avg, -maxconsumer-metricssampledProcessing time between polls, as a fraction of max.poll.interval.ms.
records-per-poll-avg, -maxconsumer-metricssampledRecords returned per call.
configured-max-poll-recordsconsumer-metricsgaugeThe configured max.poll.records. Constant.
effective-max-poll-recordsconsumer-metricsgaugeLimit in force on the last call.
A metric already in consumer-metrics look close, but does not answer the question, which is how much of the deadline is left right now.
last-poll-seconds-ago counts seconds since the last poll() invocation rather than since the poll timer reset, so it diverges from the deadline for a caller using a long timeout.
configured-max-poll-records never changes. It is there so the ceiling and the limit actually in force plot on one chart, which is what shows how far a member has backed off.
Proposed Changes
Same shape as CloseOptions in this package: private constructor, static factory, build pattern to mutate. It is mutable so a caller can hold one instance and change maxRecords between calls rather than rebuilding it. The timeout comes from the factory and is required. There is no default poll timeout to fall back on. maxRecords is OptionalInt; absent means max.poll.records. withMaxRecords stores the value without validating it, as CloseOptions.withTimeout does. Negative values are rejected by poll(). A call to poll() can take less work than the configured value, never more, so an application that adopts this cannot end up with larger batches than it has today. The bound is applied inside poll() rather than at the setter, because PollOptions is built without a consumer and cannot read max.poll.records.
FetchCollector takes the limit as a parameter in addition to the FetchBuffer, passed down from the poll() method for both Classic and Async KafkaConsumer. FetchConfig is unchanged.

[S1] Page: KIP-432: Additional Broker-Side Opt-In for Default, Unsecure SASL/OAUTHBEARER Implementation
This page is meant as a template for writing a . To create a KIP choose Tools->Copy on this page and modify with your content and replace the heading with the next KIP number and a description of your issue. Replace anything in italics with your own description.
Status
Current state: DISCARDED
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: KAFKA-7960
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
The default implementation of SASL/OAUTHBEARER, as per , is unsecured.  This is useful for development and testing purposes, and it provides a great out-of-the-box experience, but it must not be used in production because it allows the client to authenticate with any principal name it wishes.  To enable the default unsecured SASL/OAUTHBEARER implementation on the broker side simply requires the addition of OAUTHBEARER to the sasl.enabled.mechanisms configuration value (for example: sasl.enabled.mechanisms=GSSAPI,OAUTHBEARER instead of simply sasl.enabled.mechanisms=GSSAPI). To secure the implementation requires the explicit setting of the listener.name.{sasl_plaintext|sasl_ssl}.oauthbearer.sasl.{login,server}.callback.handler.class properties on the broker.  The question then arises: what if someone either accidentally or maliciously appended OAUTHBEARER to the sasl.enabled.mechanisms configuration value?  Doing so would enable the unsecured implementation on the broker, and clients could then authenticate with any principal name they desired.
This KIP proposes to add an additional opt-in configuration property on the broker side for the default, unsecured SASL/OAUTHBEARER implementation such that simply adding OAUTHBEARER to the sasl.enabled.mechanisms configuration value would be insufficient to enable the feature.  This additional opt-in broker configuration property would have to be explicitly set to true before the default unsecured implementation would successfully authenticate users, and the name of this configuration property would explicitly indicate that the feature is not secure and must not be used in production.  Adding this explicit opt-in is a breaking change; existing uses of the unsecured implementation would have to update their configuration to include this explicit opt-in property before their cluster would accept unsecure tokens again.  Note that this would only result in a breaking change in production if the unsecured feature is either accidentally or maliciously enabled …

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1387: Distribution Snapshots for Kafka client metrics
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1387: Distribution Snapshots for Kafka client metrics
Status
Current state: Under discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21361
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Kafka clients report latency and size as an average and a maximum over a 30-second window, and nothing else reaches a MetricsReporter. clients/src/main/java uses new Avg() 36 times, new Max() 31 times, and Percentiles never, so no client latency or size metric has a percentile today.
An average and a maximum are useful, but they don't show how the values are spread out. Say a producer's requests mostly take 3 to 7 ms, and one request in the window stalls for 2 seconds. The average jumps to about 150 ms, which no longer looks like a normal request. Neither number tells you that most requests finished under 7 ms, or whether the stall was a one-off or the start of a problem. Fetch sizes have the same problem: they stay small while a consumer keeps up and jump when it reads a backlog, so the average lands between the two but does not represent either scenario (low steady state and peaks during lag).
You can't work out p50 or p99 from an average and a maximum. Kafka's Percentiles stat can compute them, but no client metric currently uses it. Using it would mean adding new metrics, which needs a KIP of its own, and it would still give only the few percentiles someone picked in advance, each over the same 30-second window: A p99 for the last 30 seconds can't be combined into a p99 for the hour.
This KIP adds one stat that counts how many values fell into each range, or bin, and gives those counts to the reporter. The reporter can then decide which percentiles to compute and over what period, or publish the raw bin counts to a downstream collector. A Prometheus reporter can publish the counts as _bucket, _sum and _count, an OpenTelemetry reporter can publish them as a histogram, and the client's own telemetry (KIP-714) could send a real histogram instead of single numbers.

Bin 0 is only for zero, which is a common value for record-queue-time. That way a metric that only ever records zero reports zero, rather than a percentile somewhere between 0 and 1. Bin 1 holds everything above zero up to min.
Every client must compute the bin edges in exactly the same way, because a backend adds up buckets from different clients only when their edges match exactly.

The existing bin schemes, ConstantBinScheme and LinearBinScheme, include a bin's lower edge and exclude its upper edge, [low, high). The new scheme does the opposite, (low, high]. This definition aligns with many metric libraries such as  Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. So Histogram.BinScheme gets a method that says which kind a scheme is. It defaults to the existing kind (false), so current and third-party schemes keep working. Distribution refuses a scheme of lower-bounds, so a mistake fails when the metric is registered instead of quietly producing wrong buckets.java

Every other client stat covers a recent window of time. A distribution doesn't: it counts from the moment it is created.
That is because Prometheus and OpenTelemetry understand only two kinds of counts: a running total, or the change since the last read. A sliding window is neither. When old values drop out of the window the total goes down, and both formats take that to mean the client restarted.
A reporter that wants a window can subtract an earlier snapshot from a later one with minus(). If startTimeMs() is later than it was at the previous read, the distribution was recreated and its counts started again from zero.

Kafka already counts values in bins: Percentiles and Frequencies both do. This KIP adds one more way of laying out bins, and gives the bin counts to the reporter instead of turning them into a few numbers.

Each distribution sits next to the existing -avg and -max metrics and replaces nothing. There is one per client, tagged only with client-id, and named like its -avg and -max but with a -distribution suffix.

The number of bins is ceil(d * 2^scale) + 3, where d is how many times the range doubles. latencyMs() covers 1 ms to 65,536 ms, which is 16 doublings, and longLatencyMs() covers 1 ms to 1,048,576 ms, which is 20. The lowest allowed scale is -1, where each bin is four times as wide as the one before; anything coarser is too rough to use.
scale2^scaleeach bin isbins, latencyMs() (d = 16)bins, longLatencyMs() (d = 20)max quantile error

241.19× the last16 × 4 + 3 = 6720 × 4 + 3 = 8319%
4161.04× the last16 × 16 + 3 = 25920 × 16 + 3 = 3234%
The config only changes latency distributions. Size distributions always use scale 0, where each bin is twice the last, because byte sizes are usually powers of two and scale 0 puts them exactly on bin edges. Ratio distributions use bins of equal width, so the scale doesn't apply to them.
Most fleets should keep the default, 2, where each bin is about 19% wider than the one before. Raise it to 4 to tell apart latencies that differ by less than that, at about four times as many series. Lower it to 0 for fewer series, if bins that double are precise enough. Whoever runs the metrics backend for a fleet makes this choice, once, for every client that reports to it.
It has to be one value for the whole fleet. When a query combines histograms from many clients, it adds up buckets that have the same bounds. Clients on different scales have different bounds, so the combined histogram is wrong, and nothing warns you: the query still returns a number. While a scale change rolls out, fleet-wide percentiles are wrong until every client has the new value. Queries about a single client are not affected.
Proposed Changes

Counts are cumulative, not windowed
Every other client stat covers a recent window of time. A distribution doesn't: it counts from the moment it is created.
That is because Prometheus and OpenTelemetry understand only two kinds of counts: a running total, or the change since the last read. A sliding window is neither. When old values drop out of the window the total goes down, and both formats take that to mean the client restarted.
A reporter that wants a window can subtract an earlier snapshot from a later one with minus(). If startTimeMs() is later than it was at the previous read, the distribution was recreated and its counts started again from zero.
Why geometric bins
Kafka already counts values in bins: Percentiles and Frequencies both do. This KIP adds one more way of laying out bins, and gives the bin counts to the reporter instead of turning them into a few numbers.
Each bin is a fixed percentage wider than the one before, because latencies and sizes range from tiny to huge. With bins of equal width you would need a huge number of them to see small values clearly, or you would lose all detail at the small end. Bins that grow keep the same relative precision everywhere with a modest number of bins.
The growth is set by a whole-number scale, the same way OpenTelemetry's exponential histograms set theirs. A bin includes its upper edge, because that is what a bucket bound means in both Prometheus and OpenTelemetry.
Where to use it
Each distribution sits next to the existing -avg and -max metrics and replaces nothing. There is one per client, tagged only with client-id, and named like its -avg and -max but with a -distribution suffix.

<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1388: Add a committed-offsets filter to ListGroups
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: KAFKA-21366
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Tools that replicate consumer group offsets between clusters typically use two RPCs, with client-side filtering in between:
Admin.listGroups(ListGroupsOptions.forConsumerGroups()) (the ListGroups RPC, sent to every broker) to enumerate the consumer groups on the source cluster.
Apply a user-supplied group filter (an allow list, deny list or pattern) to the listed group ids.
Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets(...) (the OffsetFetch RPC, batched per group coordinator) for the groups that passed the filter.
MirrorMaker 2 does exactly this in MirrorCheckpointConnector, and the group offset synchronization in KIP-1279 (Cluster Mirroring) follows the same pattern. Other cross-cluster replication tools built on the Admin API do the same.
A group exists in the group coordinator while it has at least one member or at least one committed offset; a group with neither is removed by the periodic group cleanup. In some scenarios, a large number of the groups returned by ListGroups have members but no committed offsets at all. Typical examples are:
consumers that disable auto-commit and never commit, for example because they store offsets outside Kafka, or because they are short-lived command-line consumers such as kafka-console-consumer.sh;
consumers that have joined a group but have not committed yet, which is a permanent condition for applications that only read and never commit.
In some large deployments, we have seen thousands of such groups. For each of them, the replication tool still fetches offsets, receives nothing and discards the group. OffsetFetch can carry several groups per request to a coordinator, but every offset-less group still costs coordinator work, response bytes and client-side handling.
ListGroups already supports server-side filtering by group state (KIP-518) and by group type (KIP-848). The group coordinator holds both the group metadata and the committed offsets of a group in the same coordinator shard, so it can answer "does this group have any committed offsets?" with a local lookup while it builds the ListGroups response. This KIP adds that filter.
The change is deliberately made to the newer Admin.listGroups API introduced by KIP-1043 and not to Admin.listConsumerGroups, which has been deprecated since 4.1.
Public Interfaces

Client API changes

ListGroupsOptions
A new filter is added to org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ListGroupsOptions.java
The default value is false , which preserves the existing behavior.
Example: list all consumer groups that have committed offsets.java
all() is used so that a broker that does not support the filter fails the call instead of silently returning a partial listing (see the compatibility section).
No changes are made to Admin, ListGroupsResult or GroupListing.
Kafka protocol changes

ListGroups API
The ListGroups API is bumped to version 6. The request gains one field. The response is unchanged, and its version is bumped only to keep request and response versions aligned.
Request schema
jsonResponse schemajson
No new error codes are introduced.
Proposed Changes

Group coordinator
When a ListGroups request has RequireCommittedOffsets set to true, the group coordinator returns only groups with at least one committed offset. This condition is combined with the existing state and type filters using AND semantics.
A group matches if the committed state of its group coordinator contains a committed offset for at least one topic partition of that group. The offset predicate and the existing state filter are evaluated consistently against the coordinator’s committed state.
Pending transactional offsets do not count because the transaction may still abort. A group with only pending offsets becomes eligible once the transaction commits and the resulting offsets take effect in the coordinator’s committed state. A group with an existing committed offset continues to match even if it also has pending transactional offsets.
Group’s offset stateMatches
At least one committed offset, whether or not pending transactional offsets also existYes
Only pending transactional offsetsNo
Neither committed nor pending offsetsNo
Offsets eligible for expiration continue to count until their deletion takes effect in the coordinator’s committed state. Once deletion of the last committed offset takes effect, the group no longer matches.
The predicate concerns stored committed offsets, not the offsets visible to a particular caller through OffsetFetch, which also applies authorization and stability checks.
The coordinator creates group metadata when processing an offset commit for an unknown group ID, so offset-only groups are included in the group metadata that ListGroups enumerates. The new filter adds a per-group in-memory existence check; it does not enumerate the group’s topic partitions or require additional external I/O.
The filter considers only offsets stored by the group coordinator. It is applicable to Classic, Consumer, and Streams groups. Share-group consumption state is maintained separately by the share coordinator and does not count toward this predicate. Share groups therefore do not match, and ListGroupsOptions.forShareGroups().requireCommittedOffsets(true) returns an empty result. Querying share-group consumption state is outside the scope of this KIP.
Admin client
ListGroupsOptions gets a new option. When it is set, the admin client sets the new field in the ListGroups request. The request is sent with version 6 or later. If a broker does not support version 6, the request to that broker fails with UnsupportedVersionException, because the client cannot emulate the filter without fetching the offsets of every group, which is exactly the cost this KIP removes. The field is deliberately not ignorable; see Rejected Alternatives. listGroups is asynchronous and fans out to every broker, so this failure surfaces through ListGroupsResult: all() completes exceptionally with the first failure, errors() contains one Throwable per failed broker, and valid() contains the groups from the brokers that succeeded. When the option is not set, the request is unchanged and continues to work with brokers of any version supported by the client.
The authorization model of ListGroups is unchanged: a principal with DESCRIBE on the cluster receives all groups, otherwise only groups the principal has DESCRIBE on. The new filter only removes groups from that set. Note that this exposes one additional bit of information per listed group, namely whether the group has committed offsets, to any principal that can list the group. A principal with cluster DESCRIBE but without DESCRIBE on a given group can learn this bit although OffsetFetch for that group would be denied. The filter does not reveal which topics have offsets or the offset values themselves, which continue to require DESCRIBE on the group and on the topics. We consider this acceptable because the existence of committed offsets is comparable to the group state and group type that ListGroups already returns, but we call it out explicitly for review.
Command-line tools
No command-line tool changes are proposed. kafka-groups.sh --list and kafka-consumer-groups.sh --list continue to list all groups.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Existing clients against new brokers: unaffected. Clients that send ListGroups version 5 or earlier do not set the new field, and the broker treats the filter as disabled.
New clients against existing brokers: unaffected unless the new option is used. ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(true) requires ListGroups version 6. Against a broker that does not support version 6 the request to that broker fails with UnsupportedVersionException, consistent with how the states filter from KIP-518 behaves against brokers that predate it. Because listGroups is asynchronous, the exception is not thrown by the method call; it is the cause of the ExecutionException from all().get(), and it appears in errors(). Callers that must support older brokers should check that the cause is UnsupportedVersionException (the same exception can also come from another unsupported filter, so the retry can fail again and that failure must propagate) and then retry the listing without requireCommittedOffsets, keeping their state, type and protocol-type filters. Callers that use valid() must also inspect errors(), otherwise an unsupported broker looks like a broker with no groups.
Behavior of existing calls: the default value of the option is false, so the set of groups returned by Admin.listGroups and the command-line tools does not change.
Deprecation: nothing is deprecated. The option is intentionally not added to the deprecated Admin.listConsumerGroups API or ListConsumerGroupsOptions.
Mixed-version clusters: Admin.listGroups sends one …

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1388: Add a committed-offsets filter to ListGroups
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1388: Add a committed-offsets filter to ListGroups
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: here
JIRA: KAFKA-21366
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
Tools that replicate consumer group offsets between clusters typically use two RPCs, with client-side filtering in between:
Admin.listGroups(ListGroupsOptions.forConsumerGroups()) (the ListGroups RPC, sent to every broker) to enumerate the consumer groups on the source cluster.
Apply a user-supplied group filter (an allow list, deny list or pattern) to the listed group ids.
Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets(...) (the OffsetFetch RPC, batched per group coordinator) for the groups that passed the filter.
MirrorMaker 2 does exactly this in MirrorCheckpointConnector, and the group offset synchronization in KIP-1279 (Cluster Mirroring) follows the same pattern. Other cross-cluster replication tools built on the Admin API do the same.
A group exists in the group coordinator while it has at least one member or at least one committed offset; a group with neither is removed by the periodic group cleanup. In some scenarios, a large number of the groups returned by ListGroups have members but no committed offsets at all. Typical examples are:
consumers that disable auto-commit and never commit, for example because they store offsets outside Kafka, or because they are short-lived command-line consumers such as kafka-console-consumer.sh;
consumers that have joined a group but have not committed yet, which is a permanent condition for applications that only read and never commit.
In some large deployments, we have seen thousands of such groups. For each of them, the replication tool still fetches offsets, receives nothing and discards the group. OffsetFetch can carry several groups per request to a coordinator, but every offset-less group still costs coordinator work, response bytes and client-side handling.
ListGroups already supports server-side filtering by group state (KIP-518) and by group type (KIP-848). The group coordinator holds both the group metadata and the committed offsets of a group in the same coordinator shard, so it can answer "does this group have any committed offsets?" with a local lookup while it builds the ListGroups response. This KIP adds that filter.
The change is deliberately made to the newer Admin.listGroups API introduced by KIP-1043 and not to Admin.listConsumerGroups, which has been deprecated since 4.1.
Public Interfaces

Client API changes

ListGroupsOptions
A new filter is added to org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ListGroupsOptions.java
The default value is false , which preserves the existing behavior.
Example: list all consumer groups that have committed offsets.java
all() is used so that a broker that does not support the filter fails the call instead of silently returning a partial listing (see the compatibility section).
No changes are made to Admin, ListGroupsResult or GroupListing.
Kafka protocol changes

ListGroups API
The ListGroups API is bumped to version 6. The request gains one field. The response is unchanged, and its version is bumped only to keep request and response versions aligned.
Request schema
jsonResponse schemajson
No new error codes are introduced.
Proposed Changes

Group coordinator
When a ListGroups request has RequireCommittedOffsets set to true, the group coordinator returns only groups with at least one committed offset. This condition is combined with the existing state and type filters using AND semantics.
A group matches if the committed state of its group coordinator contains a committed offset for at least one topic partition of that group. The offset predicate and the existing state filter are evaluated consistently against the coordinator’s committed state.
Pending transactional offsets do not count because the transaction may still abort. A group with only pending offsets becomes eligible once the transaction commits and the resulting offsets take effect in the coordinator’s committed state. A group with an existing committed offset continues to match even if it also has pending transactional offsets.
Group’s offset stateMatches
At least one committed offset, whether or not pending transactional offsets also existYes
Only pending transactional offsetsNo
Neither committed nor pending offsetsNo
Offsets eligible for expiration continue to count until their deletion takes effect in the coordinator’s committed state. Once deletion of the last committed offset takes effect, the group no longer matches.
The predicate concerns stored committed offsets, not the offsets visible to a particular caller through OffsetFetch, which also applies authorization and stability checks.
The coordinator creates group metadata when processing an offset commit for an unknown group ID, so offset-only groups are included in the group metadata that ListGroups enumerates. The new filter adds a per-group in-memory existence check; it does not enumerate the group’s topic partitions or require additional external I/O.
The filter considers only offsets stored by the group coordinator. It is applicable to Classic, Consumer, and Streams groups. Share-group consumption state is maintained separately by the share coordinator and does not count toward this predicate. Share groups therefore do not match, and ListGroupsOptions.forShareGroups().requireCommittedOffsets(true) returns an empty result. Querying share-group consumption state is outside the scope of this KIP.
Admin client
ListGroupsOptions gets a new option. When it is set, the admin client sets the new field in the ListGroups request. The request is sent with version 6 or later. If a broker does not support version 6, the request to that broker fails with UnsupportedVersionException, because the client cannot emulate the filter without fetching the offsets of every group, which is exactly the cost this KIP removes. The field is deliberately not ignorable; see Rejected Alternatives. listGroups is asynchronous and fans out to every broker, so this failure surfaces through ListGroupsResult: all() completes exceptionally with the first failure, errors() contains one Throwable per failed broker, and valid() contains the groups from the brokers that succeeded. When the option is not set, the request is unchanged and continues to work with brokers of any version supported by the client.
The authorization model of ListGroups is unchanged: a principal with DESCRIBE on the cluster receives all groups, otherwise only groups the principal has DESCRIBE on. The new filter only removes groups from that set. Note that this exposes one additional bit of information per listed group, namely whether the group has committed offsets, to any principal that can list the group. A principal with cluster DESCRIBE but without DESCRIBE on a given group can learn this bit although OffsetFetch for that group would be denied. The filter does not reveal which topics have offsets or the offset values themselves, which continue to require DESCRIBE on the group and on the topics. We consider this acceptable because the existence of committed offsets is comparable to the group state and group type that ListGroups already returns, but we call it out explicitly for review.
Command-line tools
No command-line tool changes are proposed. kafka-groups.sh --list and kafka-consumer-groups.sh --list continue to list all groups.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Existing clients against new brokers: unaffected. Clients that send ListGroups version 5 or earlier do not set the new field, and the broker treats the filter as disabled.
New clients against existing brokers: unaffected unless the new option is used. ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(true) requires ListGroups version 6. Against a broker that does not support version 6 the request to that broker fails with UnsupportedVersionException, consistent with how the states filter from KIP-518 behaves against brokers that predate it. Because listGroups is asynchronous, the exception is not thrown by the method call; it is the cause of the ExecutionException from all().get(), and it appears in errors(). Callers that must support older brokers should check that the cause is UnsupportedVersionException (the same exception can also come from another unsupported filter, so the retry can fail again and that failure must propagate) and then retry the listing without requireCommittedOffsets, keeping their state, type and protocol-type filters. Callers that use valid() must also inspect errors(), otherwise an unsupported broker looks like a broker with no groups.
Behavior of existing calls: the default value of the option is false, so the set of groups returned by Admin.listGroups and the command-line tools does not change.
Deprecation: nothing is deprecated. The option is intentionally not added to the deprecated Admin.listConsumerGroups API or ListConsumerGroupsOptions.

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1389: Surface effective group configurations to clients
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1389: Surface effective group configurations to clients
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/gctkxrg2y664jt4sq18znrgl0omd93tp
JIRA: KAFKA-20848
Release: TBD
Motivation
With the consumer group protocol (KIP-848), share groups (KIP-932) and the Streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071), settings that shape how a client behaves are group configurations owned by the broker. Some of them, such as the session timeout and the heartbeat interval of consumer groups, used to be client configurations; others, such as a share group's record lock duration, were introduced as group configurations. Settings such as session timeouts and heartbeat intervals have broker-level defaults and bounds, and an administrator can override them for a single group. None of these values are set in the client's configuration.
The client sees only some of these values. The heartbeat responses of all three protocols carry the heartbeat interval, and the Streams heartbeat response also carries the task offset interval and the acceptable recovery lag. Clients recently started logging these values (KAFKA-20761 for consumer and share groups, and the equivalent change for Streams). A share consumer also receives the record lock duration in the ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses, as AcquisitionLockTimeoutMs, and exposes it through ShareConsumer#acquisitionLockTimeoutMs(). Other values, including the session timeout of every group type, are not included in any response. When diagnosing unexpected group behavior from the client's logs, one cannot tell which of these values the brokers are applying.
The values in effect can also differ from the configured ones. KIP-1240 lets a broker start even if a stored group configuration lies outside the broker's current bounds, and clamps the effective value to those bounds. The broker logs a warning when it does so, but the client is not told. In a reproduction attached to KAFKA-20848, consumer.session.timeout.ms was set to 60000 for a group, and the broker was then restarted with the session timeout bounds narrowed to 20000–30000 (group.consumer.min.session.timeout.ms=20000, group.consumer.session.timeout.ms=25000, group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms=30000):
The broker logged that the value is capped to 30000.
Describing the group configuration still returned 60000, the stored value.
The consumer received no indication that its effective session timeout had been reduced, because the session timeout is not part of the heartbeat response.
After the consumer was killed, the member was fenced approximately 30 seconds after the coordinator processed its last heartbeat, so 30000 was the value in effect.
A user who chose 60 seconds to tolerate long pauses therefore sees members fenced after 30 seconds, and nothing on the client side explains why. Similar discrepancies between configured and effective values can arise when other settings are clamped to their lower or upper bounds, or when a group names a Streams task assignor that is not available and the coordinator falls back to the default assignor. Even for values that are sent to the client, such as the heartbeat interval or the record lock duration, the client receives the effective value but cannot tell that it differs from the configured one.
The protocols already carry this kind of information in places. The share fetch path sends the effective record lock duration to the client, and Streams uses the heartbeat response to report a misconfiguration: the MISSING_CLIENT_TAGS status (KAFKA-20744) tells a member that client tags required for rack-aware standby task assignment are missing. This KIP exposes the effective group configurations relevant to each protocol through responses from the broker that applies them. For the group heartbeats that broker is the group coordinator. The share configurations that govern record delivery, such as the record lock duration and the delivery count limit, are applied by each share partition leader against its own bounds and defaults, so they are reported in the ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses of the leader rather than in the share group heartbeat. Clients log these values on first receipt and when they change, and warn when a stored group override differs from the value in effect.
Public Interfaces
This KIP adds a new version of five RPCs. In each, the response gains two tagged fields, an opaque state token and a list of effective group configurations, and the request gains one tagged field to echo the token.
RPCCurrent versionsNew versionBroker that sends the listEntries
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat0-1N (2 today)group coordinator4
ShareGroupHeartbeat1N (2 today)group coordinator4
StreamsGroupHeartbeat0-1N (2 today)group coordinator11
ShareFetch1-2N (3 today)share partition leader8
ShareAcknowledge1-2N (3 today)share partition leader8
N is the next unreleased version of each RPC when this KIP is implemented. KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in Apache Kafka 4.5; if this KIP lands in the same release, the fields are added to that version in coordination with KAFKA-20925 instead of a separate bump (see Compatibility). The new fields are tagged because they are optional: the token is absent from responses with a top-level error, and after the first exchange the list is absent from most responses.
Request schema
The same field is added to ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest, ShareGroupHeartbeatRequest, StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest, ShareFetchRequest and ShareAcknowledgeRequest. Shown for ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest:// Version N adds GroupConfigsToken (KIP-1389).
{ "name": "GroupConfigsToken", "type": "int64", "versions": "N+", "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 0,
  "default": "-1", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The token of the group configurations the client holds for this broker, or -1 if it holds none." }
Response schema
The same fields are added to ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse, ShareGroupHeartbeatResponse, StreamsGroupHeartbeatResponse, ShareFetchResponse and ShareAcknowledgeResponse. Shown for ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse:// Version N adds GroupConfigsToken and GroupConfigs (KIP-1389).
{ "name": "GroupConfigsToken", "type": "int64", "versions": "N+", "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 0,
  "default": "-1", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "Identifies the group configuration state of this broker for the group, or -1 if this response carries no group configuration information." },
{ "name": "GroupConfigs", "type": "[]EffectiveGroupConfig", "versions": "N+", "nullableVersions": "N+",
  "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 1, "default": "null", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The effective group configurations applied by this broker, or null if they are unchanged from the state identified by the request's GroupConfigsToken.",
  "fields": [
    { "name": "Name", "type": "string", "versions": "N+",
      "about": "The group configuration name." },
    { "name": "Value", "type": "string", "versions": "N+",
      "about": "The effective value." },
    { "name": "ConfiguredValue", "type": "string", "versions": "N+", "nullableVersions": "N+", "default": "null",
      "about": "The value of the stored group override if it is not the value in effect, null otherwise." }
  ]
}
Tag numbers 0 and 1 are free in all ten schemas today; they are coordinated with any other KIP adding tagged fields to the same versions.
Field semantics
GroupConfigsToken (response)
-1: this response carries no group configuration information. A broker returns -1, with a null list, in any response with a top-level error (for example NOT_COORDINATOR or an authorization error), in any response where it cannot resolve the group, and in responses to a member leaving the group. Such a response does not change the client's cache.
Any other value: identifies the state of the exposed content (every entry's Name, Value and ConfiguredValue) on this broker. The value is opaque; clients store and echo it and never compute it. A broker never issues -1. Different states may in rare cases share a token (see Rejected Alternatives).
GroupConfigs (response)
Present: the full list for the token in the same response. Never empty.
Null with a token other than -1: the broker's current state is the one identified by the token in the request.
In a response that carries a token, a broker includes the list when the request's token is -1 or differs from its current token.
GroupConfigsToken (request)
The token the client holds, together with the list it identifies, for the broker it sends the request to; -1 if it holds none.
Entries
One entry per group configuration in the table below, for the RPC that carries it. A configuration added to Apache Kafka later is not included automatically.
Value is the configuration as resolved by the responding broker when it built the response, through the same resolution the broker uses for its behavior (overrides, broker defaults, bounds, fallbacks). It describes the configuration, not work already in progress: for example, a new record lock duration applies to locks …

CONVERSATION: Document: KIP-1389: Surface effective group configurations to clients
<<<TEXT
[S1] Page: KIP-1389: Surface effective group configurations to clients
Status
Current state: Under Discussion
Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/gctkxrg2y664jt4sq18znrgl0omd93tp
JIRA: KAFKA-20848
Release: TBD
Motivation
With the consumer group protocol (KIP-848), share groups (KIP-932) and the Streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071), settings that shape how a client behaves are group configurations owned by the broker. Some of them, such as the session timeout and the heartbeat interval of consumer groups, used to be client configurations; others, such as a share group's record lock duration, were introduced as group configurations. Settings such as session timeouts and heartbeat intervals have broker-level defaults and bounds, and an administrator can override them for a single group. None of these values are set in the client's configuration.
The client sees only some of these values. The heartbeat responses of all three protocols carry the heartbeat interval, and the Streams heartbeat response also carries the task offset interval and the acceptable recovery lag. Clients recently started logging these values (KAFKA-20761 for consumer and share groups, and the equivalent change for Streams). A share consumer also receives the record lock duration in the ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses, as AcquisitionLockTimeoutMs, and exposes it through ShareConsumer#acquisitionLockTimeoutMs(). Other values, including the session timeout of every group type, are not included in any response. When diagnosing unexpected group behavior from the client's logs, one cannot tell which of these values the brokers are applying.
The values in effect can also differ from the configured ones. KIP-1240 lets a broker start even if a stored group configuration lies outside the broker's current bounds, and clamps the effective value to those bounds. The broker logs a warning when it does so, but the client is not told. In a reproduction attached to KAFKA-20848, consumer.session.timeout.ms was set to 60000 for a group, and the broker was then restarted with the session timeout bounds narrowed to 20000–30000 (group.consumer.min.session.timeout.ms=20000, group.consumer.session.timeout.ms=25000, group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms=30000):
The broker logged that the value is capped to 30000.
Describing the group configuration still returned 60000, the stored value.
The consumer received no indication that its effective session timeout had been reduced, because the session timeout is not part of the heartbeat response.
After the consumer was killed, the member was fenced approximately 30 seconds after the coordinator processed its last heartbeat, so 30000 was the value in effect.
A user who chose 60 seconds to tolerate long pauses therefore sees members fenced after 30 seconds, and nothing on the client side explains why. Similar discrepancies between configured and effective values can arise when other settings are clamped to their lower or upper bounds, or when a group names a Streams task assignor that is not available and the coordinator falls back to the default assignor. Even for values that are sent to the client, such as the heartbeat interval or the record lock duration, the client receives the effective value but cannot tell that it differs from the configured one.
The protocols already carry this kind of information in places. The share fetch path sends the effective record lock duration to the client, and Streams uses the heartbeat response to report a misconfiguration: the MISSING_CLIENT_TAGS status (KAFKA-20744) tells a member that client tags required for rack-aware standby task assignment are missing. This KIP exposes the effective group configurations relevant to each protocol through responses from the broker that applies them. For the group heartbeats that broker is the group coordinator. The share configurations that govern record delivery, such as the record lock duration and the delivery count limit, are applied by each share partition leader against its own bounds and defaults, so they are reported in the ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses of the leader rather than in the share group heartbeat. Clients log these values on first receipt and when they change, and warn when a stored group override differs from the value in effect.
Public Interfaces
This KIP adds a new version of five RPCs. In each, the response gains two tagged fields, an opaque state token and a list of effective group configurations, and the request gains one tagged field to echo the token.
RPCCurrent versionsNew versionBroker that sends the listEntries
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat0-1N (2 today)group coordinator4
ShareGroupHeartbeat1N (2 today)group coordinator4
StreamsGroupHeartbeat0-1N (2 today)group coordinator11
ShareFetch1-2N (3 today)share partition leader8
ShareAcknowledge1-2N (3 today)share partition leader8
N is the next unreleased version of each RPC when this KIP is implemented. KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in Apache Kafka 4.5; if this KIP lands in the same release, the fields are added to that version in coordination with KAFKA-20925 instead of a separate bump (see Compatibility). The new fields are tagged because they are optional: the token is absent from responses with a top-level error, and after the first exchange the list is absent from most responses.
Request schema
The same field is added to ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest, ShareGroupHeartbeatRequest, StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest, ShareFetchRequest and ShareAcknowledgeRequest. Shown for ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest:// Version N adds GroupConfigsToken (KIP-1389).
{ "name": "GroupConfigsToken", "type": "int64", "versions": "N+", "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 0,
  "default": "-1", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The token of the group configurations the client holds for this broker, or -1 if it holds none." }
Response schema
The same fields are added to ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse, ShareGroupHeartbeatResponse, StreamsGroupHeartbeatResponse, ShareFetchResponse and ShareAcknowledgeResponse. Shown for ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse:// Version N adds GroupConfigsToken and GroupConfigs (KIP-1389).
{ "name": "GroupConfigsToken", "type": "int64", "versions": "N+", "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 0,
  "default": "-1", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "Identifies the group configuration state of this broker for the group, or -1 if this response carries no group configuration information." },
{ "name": "GroupConfigs", "type": "[]EffectiveGroupConfig", "versions": "N+", "nullableVersions": "N+",
  "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 1, "default": "null", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The effective group configurations applied by this broker, or null if they are unchanged from the state identified by the request's GroupConfigsToken.",
  "fields": [
    { "name": "Name", "type": "string", "versions": "N+",
      "about": "The group configuration name." },
    { "name": "Value", "type": "string", "versions": "N+",
      "about": "The effective value." },
    { "name": "ConfiguredValue", "type": "string", "versions": "N+", "nullableVersions": "N+", "default": "null",
      "about": "The value of the stored group override if it is not the value in effect, null otherwise." }
  ]
}
Tag numbers 0 and 1 are free in all ten schemas today; they are coordinated with any other KIP adding tagged fields to the same versions.
Field semantics
GroupConfigsToken (response)
-1: this response carries no group configuration information. A broker returns -1, with a null list, in any response with a top-level error (for example NOT_COORDINATOR or an authorization error), in any response where it cannot resolve the group, and in responses to a member leaving the group. Such a response does not change the client's cache.
Any other value: identifies the state of the exposed content (every entry's Name, Value and ConfiguredValue) on this broker. The value is opaque; clients store and echo it and never compute it. A broker never issues -1. Different states may in rare cases share a token (see Rejected Alternatives).
GroupConfigs (response)
Present: the full list for the token in the same response. Never empty.
Null with a token other than -1: the broker's current state is the one identified by the token in the request.
In a response that carries a token, a broker includes the list when the request's token is -1 or differs from its current token.
GroupConfigsToken (request)
The token the client holds, together with the list it identifies, for the broker it sends the request to; -1 if it holds none.
Entries
One entry per group configuration in the table below, for the RPC that carries it. A configuration added to Apache Kafka later is not included automatically.
Value is the configuration as resolved by the responding broker when it built the response, through the same resolution the broker uses for its behavior (overrides, broker defaults, bounds, fallbacks). It describes the configuration, not work already in progress: for example, a new record lock duration applies to locks …

CONVERSATION: Mail thread: [DISCUSS] KIP-1354: Single purpose TLS extended key usages (EKU) support
<<<TEXT
[S1] EmailMessage by Kondrát Bertalan (2026-07-29)
Hi,
I’d like to start a discussion on a KIP to improve public Certificate
Authorities (CA) compatibility after public CAs are actively deprecating
and will soon stop providing multipurpose certificates.
This presents a breaking operational challenge for Kafka environments
relying on public CAs. A Kafka broker is simultaneously a TLS server (it
accepts connections on its listeners) and a TLS client (it dials other
brokers and controllers). With a single keystore, the same certificate is
presented in both roles.

https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/430408110/KIP-1354+Single+purpose+TLS+extended+key+usages+EKU+support

Thanks,
Berci
[S2] EmailMessage by Aditya Kousik (2026-07-30)
Hi Kondrát,

Thanks for the KIP. I took a look and the use case does make sense - even within private CA certs, the policy seems to be to move away from issuing both client and server webAuth EKUs. And the inter-broker roles do present a real scenario that can pose a challenge currently.

However,
AK1. The proliferation of the SSL configs essentially 2x for client config seems like overkill to me. JCA is already notorious for the myriad of config options I have to set and the keytool/openssl tools makes my head spin usually. So, I think looking for a solution with fewer knobs to tweak might make it more digestible for me.

AK2. The SSL config values are in the common clients module reused between all clients/admin/broker alike. So if we introduce ssl.client.*, then you’re going to cause some confusion for producer/consumer clients which are essentially just client EKUs.

AK3. I realise you’re tweaking the configs because the DefaultSSLEngineFactory reads these params and yes it makes sense to create new props to do something different. But I think you’re on the right but parallel track to the solution. KIP-519 introduced an ssl.engine.factory.class that will implement all the hooks that you need. So, I think you can implement a custom ssl engine factory that can initialise a different SSLEngine for createClientSslEngine and createServerSslEngine by reading different key material and different SSLContexts. You can even extend DefaultSSLEngineFactory since it’s in the public …
[S3] EmailMessage by Kondrát Bertalan (2026-07-31)
Hi Aditya Kousik,
Thank you for your feedback, you are right.
I dug deeper into the key manager, and it turned out that if you change it
from the default SunX509 to NewSunX509 Then it will be able to select based
on the cert EKU and based on the purpose Kafka will use the cert for.

I am going to conduct some tests, but maybe the whole KIP can be avoided
this way.

Thanks,
Berci

Motivation
Currently, a task in Kafka Streams has its "partition time" determined by the latest timestamp of the records it has received. This could introduce problems because when records pass through a processor whose function is to filter certain records out, some messages with the largest timestamps might be removed, allowing only records with smaller timestamps to proceed to the next task. Consequently, this means that some tasks would have the incorrect partition time.
For instance, if four records (their timestamp in the parantheses) r1(2), r2(3), r3(7), and r4(9) are making their way down the topologies, but r3 and r4 was removed, the downstream tasks would incorrectly assume that the timestamp was 3 (since last received record was r2) when in reality it should be 9 (timestamp of r4). This requires us to propagate the correct stream time through the DAG of tasks, which Kafka Streams currently does not do. However, the only manner in which an upstream and a downstream task could communicate is through the repartition topic they share. This means that any metadata related to partition time must be stored in the ProducerRecord that is sent from SinkNode to SourceNode. Currently, any modification to records, including the addition of headers or extra metadata, is fundamentally still a public API change, hence why this KIP is necessary.
Public Interfaces
The core problem that we wish to solve here is how to transmit the relevant partition time data in between tasks (via Producer/Consumer records). The following is the description of what is currently stored in a ProducerRecord:
Key and value (serialized into a byte array)
Topic, partition, and timestamp (A String, a 32-bit Integer, and a 64-bit Integer respectively)
Headers (used to store extra metadata which the user wishes to pass in between tasks)

Hi,
I’d like to start a discussion on a KIP to improve public Certificate
Authorities (CA) compatibility after public CAs are actively deprecating
and will soon stop providing multipurpose certificates.
This presents a breaking operational challenge for Kafka environments
relying on public CAs. A Kafka broker is simultaneously a TLS server (it
accepts connections on its listeners) and a TLS client (it dials other
brokers and controllers). With a single keystore, the same certificate is
presented in both roles.

Berci
[S2] EmailMessage by Aditya Kousik (2026-07-30)
Hi Kondrát,

Thanks for the KIP. I took a look and the use case does make sense - even within private CA certs, the policy seems to be to move away from issuing both client and server webAuth EKUs. And the inter-broker roles do present a real scenario that can pose a challenge currently.

However,
AK1. The proliferation of the SSL configs essentially 2x for client config seems like overkill to me. JCA is already notorious for the myriad of config options I have to set and the keytool/openssl tools makes my head spin usually. So, I think looking for a solution with fewer knobs to tweak might make it more digestible for me.

AK2. The SSL config values are in the common clients module reused between all clients/admin/broker alike. So if we introduce ssl.client.*, then you’re going to cause some confusion for producer/consumer clients which are essentially just client EKUs.

AK3. I realise you’re tweaking the configs because the DefaultSSLEngineFactory reads these params and yes it makes sense to create new props to do something different. But I think you’re on the right but parallel track to the solution. KIP-519 introduced an ssl.engine.factory.class that will implement all the hooks that you need. So, I think you can implement a custom ssl engine factory that can initialise a different SSLEngine for createClientSslEngine and createServerSslEngine by reading different key material and different SSLContexts. You can even extend DefaultSSLEngineFactory since it’s in the public …

Thank you for your feedback, you are right.
I dug deeper into the key manager, and it turned out that if you change it
from the default SunX509 to NewSunX509 Then it will be able to select based
on the cert EKU and based on the purpose Kafka will use the cert for.

I am going to conduct some tests, but maybe the whole KIP can be avoided
this way.

Thanks,
Berci

CONVERSATION: Ticket KAFKA-17754: A delayed EndTxn message can cause aborted read, lost writes, atomicity violation
<<<TEXT
[S1] Comment by Justine Olshan (2024-10-10)
Hey [~aphyr] . Thanks for filing. I will take a look in the next few days.

Skimming the ticket I have a few thoughts that I will investigate more closely:

I am wondering how a new transaction was started while the markers were still being written. We should see concurrent transactions errors until the transaction is complete – meaning we can't add partitions to a new transaction with the same transactional id until all markers are written to all partitions. (We also shouldn't be able to change the decision once the decision is written to the transaction log). The only thing I can think of is if some zombie markers get delivered late (which I believe you mention above). For that, I wonder if some of the KIP-890 changes will help – there every transaction bumps epoch.
[S2] Comment by Kyle Kingsbury (2024-10-10)
I thiiink this is possible because the first transaction actually does commit normally. It just took two tries: the first try left an EndTxn message floating around, ready to create havoc later, but the second try went through and committed just fine. From the client's point of view, producer.commitTransaction() completed normally, and it was free to begin another transaction after that.

I'm definitely not a protocol expert though, and I bet your intuition is better than mine here!
[S3] Comment by Justine Olshan (2024-10-10)
[~aphyr] yes, in that case – where a commit is floating around and doesn't yet reach the server, we could see an issue where the old commit makes a decision for the next transaction. But KIP-890 should prevent this as the delayed message will have an older epoch and it will be fenced.
[S4] Comment by Artem Livshits (2024-10-10)
Hi Kyle,

Thanks for doing the tests and finding the issues!  What you've found is one of many anomalies in the existing protocol that stems from, as you've put correctly "There is no sequence number to order requests from the same client. There is no concept of a transaction number."  This is exactly what we're fixing in https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-890%3A+Transactions+Server-Side+Defense -- in essence, we'll be incrementing epoch for every transaction, which would uniquely identify every transaction and fence stale requests.

With KIP-890 in place, the sequence would look like the following:

1. Client starts txn1 at epoch 42, sends endTxn (commit, epoch 42), gets timeout or etc.
2. Client retries endTxn (commit, epoch 42), succeeds, the epoch is 43 now.
3. Client starts txn2 at epoch 43, adds partitions, produces data.
4. The "zombie" endTxn (commit, epoch 42) from step1 arrives, but is fenced, because epoch is 43 now.
5. Client continues with txn2, ultimately aborts it.

Without KIP-890, step 4 could commit a torn transaction (commit data from step 3 that should've been aborted at step 5).

There are also other anomalies that can happen without KIP-890.

1. Transaction coordinator sends writeTxnMarkers RPC to partition leaders with commit markers, times out.
2. Transaction coordinator retries, succeeds.
3. Data for the new transaction arrives to the partition leader.
4. Transaction commit marker from step1 arrives, commits …
[S5] Comment by Kyle Kingsbury (2024-10-15)
Fantastic, happy to hear it. :)

I am working on repro the problem you mentioned with the tests here [https://github.com/jepsen-io/redpanda.]

I wonder if you have any other special things to repro the problem?

SUBJECT
[S1] Page: KIP-485: Make topic optional when using through() operations in DSL
Status
Current state: Moved to 
Discussion thread: https://www.mail-archive.com/dev@kafka.apache.org/msg99085.html
JIRA:ASF JIRAkey,summary,type,created,updated,due,assignee,reporter,priority,status,resolution5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-8611
Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
When using DSL in Kafka Streams, data re-partition happens only when key-changing operation is followed by stateful operation. On the other hand, in DSL, stateful computation can happen using transform() operation as well. Problem with this approach is that, even if any upstream operation was key-changing before calling transform(), no auto-repartition is triggered. If repartitioning is required, a call to through(String) should be performed before transform(). With the current implementation, burden of managing and creating the topic falls on user and introduces extra complexity of managing Kafka Streams application.
Public Interfaces
java
Proposed Changes
Add two method overloads for through()
KStream#through() - with default serializers, deserializers and producer's DefaultPartitioner
KStream#through(final Produced<K, V> produced) - produced parameter will be used for configuration, in a similar way as for existing through(String topic, final Produced<K, V> produced) method. Topic will be generated based through() processor name.
Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan
Since we're adding two new method overloads without modifying existing API contract, there won't be any compatibility issues.
Rejected Alternatives
N/A

[S4] Comment by Pankraz76 (2026-10-28)
Thanks @xiaoqingwanga for the fix, and @jolshan / @kevin-wu24 for the reviews!

Two small follow-ups, in case they're useful:

1. **Backport**: KAFKA-20734 is a Blocker and the regression comes from KAFKA-17573. Should this be cherry-picked to 4.3 / 4.4?

2. **Retry busy-loop**: with this fix, markers for offline partitions now land in `markersQueueForUnknownBroker` (as intended). However, `addTxnMarkersToBrokerQueue` always ends with `wakeup()`, so on every `generateRequests()` the parked marker is drained, re-parked, and the next `pollOnce` returns immediately. With one parked marker I measured ~30k `getPartitionLeaderEndpoint` calls/s for as long as the partition stays offline. Correctness is fine, since the marker goes out once a leader is registered, but it's a hot loop on the coordinator. A possible fix would be to only `wakeup()` when a marker reaches a real broker queue and retry the unknown-broker queue after `retry.backoff.ms` or on a metadata update. I'm happy to open a JIRA and a PR for this if that sounds reasonable.

I also have an end-to-end test in `TransactionsTest` (offline partition on a non-coordinator broker → commit → bring it back → `read_committed` sees the record) from #23947. Happy to submit it separately if you think it adds value on top of the unit test here; otherwise no worries.
[S5] Comment by Pankraz76 (2026-10-28)
Follow-up on points 2 and 3 from my comment above: opened #23993 under KAFKA-20734, since it fixes a regression from this PR before it ships.

**Busy loop**
- Retrying parked markers from `generateRequests()` no longer calls `wakeup()`. That path already runs on the sender thread, and markers that get a leader are drained to their broker queue in the same call, so the wakeup only made the next `poll` return immediately and re-park the marker.
- While markers sit in `markersQueueForUnknownBroker`, `doWork()` polls with a 100 ms bound instead of `Long.MaxValue`. They are retried after a backoff, not in a tight loop and not only when some unrelated event wakes the thread. It's the same 100 ms backoff `NodeToControllerRequestThread` uses when no controller is known.
- `addTxnMarkersToBrokerQueue` from other threads and from completion handlers still wakes up the sender, so nothing changes there.
- I used a fixed 100 ms rather than `retry.backoff.ms` or a metadata-update hook to keep the change small. Happy to switch if you'd prefer one of those.

**Tests**
- `TransactionMarkerChannelManagerTest`: re-parking a marker does not call `wakeup()`, and `doWork()` uses the bounded poll only while markers are parked. Both tests fail on trunk and pass with the change.
